abstract: Competitive learning is an unsupervised algorithm that classifies input pat(cid:173) terns into mutually exclusive clusters. In a neural net framework, each clus(cid:173) ter is represented by a processing unit that competes with others in a winner(cid:173) take-all pool for an input pattern. I present a simple extension to the algo(cid:173) rithm that allows it to construct discrete, distributed representations. Discrete representations are useful because they are relatively easy to analyze and their information content can readily be measured. Distributed representa(cid:173) tions are useful because they explicitly encode similarity. The basic idea is to apply competitive learning iteratively to an input pattern, and after each stage to subtract from the input pattern the component that was captured in the representation at that stage. This component is simply the weight vector of the winning unit of the competitive pool. The subtraction procedure forces competitive pools at different stages to encode different aspects of the input. The algorithm is essentially the same as a traditional data compression tech(cid:173) nique known as multistep vector quantization, although the neural net per(cid:173) spective suggests potentially powerful extensions to that approach.

paragraphs: Ordinary competitive learning assigns an input to one winning unit from a pool, producing mutually exclusive clusters. This paper extends that procedure so an input receives a discrete, distributed representation. Instead of expressing the input through one cluster assignment, the method builds its representation through a sequence of competitive choices.

After each stage, the weight vector of the winning unit is subtracted from the current input. The next stage then operates on what remains. This subtraction is the crucial mechanism: it forces later competitive pools to represent aspects that earlier pools have not already captured. The representation accumulates distinct contributions across successive stages.

The approach combines two desired properties. Discrete representations are comparatively easy to analyze and measure in terms of information content, while distributed representations explicitly express similarity. The author identifies the algorithm as essentially multistep vector quantization, a data-compression technique. The neural-network formulation offers a different perspective on that procedure and suggests possible extensions, without requiring a separate cluster for every complete input pattern.
summary.tldr: Repeated competitive learning on successive residuals builds discrete codes whose components capture different aspects of an input.

title: Discovering Discrete Distributed Representations with Iterative Competitive Learning

abstract: Current Intra-Cardia defibrillators make use of simple classification algo(cid:173) rithms to determine patient conditions and subsequently to enable proper therapy. The simplicity is primarily due to the constraints on power dissipa(cid:173) tion and area available for implementation. Sub-threshold implementation of artificial neural networks offer potential classifiers with higher perfor(cid:173) mance than commercially available defibrillators. In this paper we explore several classifier architectures and discuss micro-electronic implementation issues.
originalAbstract: Current Intra-Cardia defibrillators make use of simple classification algo(cid:173) rithms to determine patient conditions and subsequently to enable proper therapy. The simplicity is primarily due to the constraints on power dissipa(cid:173) tion and area available for implementation. Sub-threshold implementation of artificial neural networks offer potential classifiers with higher perfor(cid:173) mance than commercially available defibrillators. In this paper we explore several classifier architectures and discuss micro-electronic implementation issues.

paragraphs: The paper examines neural-network classifiers for intracardiac defibrillators. These devices classify a patient's condition to determine when appropriate therapy should be enabled. The abstract explains that existing classifiers are kept simple largely because the available implementation area and allowable power dissipation constrain what computation can be built into the device.

The proposed direction is to implement artificial neural networks using sub-threshold electronics. The authors explore several classifier architectures alongside the microelectronic issues involved in realizing them. This brings the classification problem and its physical implementation into the same discussion: a potentially useful decision method must also fit the device's hardware constraints.

The abstract presents these neural implementations as offering the potential for higher classification performance than commercially available defibrillators. Its contribution is an exploration of architectures and implementation choices under explicit power and area limits. The stated outcome is therefore a promising design direction for more capable classifiers, with practical feasibility tied directly to how the neural computation is implemented.
summary.tldr: The paper explores sub-threshold neural-network classifiers for defibrillators operating under tight power and hardware-area constraints.

title: ANN Based Classification for Heart Defibrillators

abstract: We have designed a neural network which detects the direction of ego(cid:173) motion from optic flow in the presence of eye movements (Lappe and Rauschecker, 1993). The performance of the network is consistent with human psychophysical data, and its output neurons show great similarity to "triple component" cells in area MSTd of monkey visual cortex. We now show that by using assumptions about the kind of eye movements that the obsenrer is likely to perform, our model can generate various other cell types found in MSTd as well.
originalAbstract: We have designed a neural network which detects the direction of ego(cid:173) motion from optic flow in the presence of eye movements (Lappe and Rauschecker, 1993). The performance of the network is consistent with human psychophysical data, and its output neurons show great similarity to "triple component" cells in area MSTd of monkey visual cortex. We now show that by using assumptions about the kind of eye movements that the obsenrer is likely to perform, our model can generate various other cell types found in MSTd as well.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a visual system can infer the direction of its own movement from optic flow, the pattern of motion across the visual field. Eye movements complicate this task because the observed visual motion also changes when the eyes move. The authors use a neural network designed to detect heading under these conditions.

The network's performance agrees with human psychophysical observations, and its output units resemble the triple-component cells found in area MSTd of monkey visual cortex. These two connections give the model both a behavioral interpretation and a relationship to measured neural response types within a visual brain area.

The new result is that assumptions about the eye movements an observer is likely to make allow the model to generate additional MSTd cell types. Those assumptions therefore affect the neural responses produced by the heading computation. The finding links variation among modeled cell types to the conditions under which self-motion must be estimated, within one computational account.
summary.tldr: A heading-estimation network reproduces additional visual-cortex cell types when it incorporates assumptions about likely eye movements.

title: Computation of Heading Direction from Optic Flow in Visual Cortex

abstract: Results of a study of the worst case learning curves for a partic(cid:173) ular class of probability distribution on input space to MLP with hard threshold hidden units are presented. It is shown in partic(cid:173) ular, that in the thermodynamic limit for scaling by the number of connections to the first hidden layer, although the true learning curve behaves as ~ a-I for a ~ 1, its VC-dimension based bound is trivial (= 1) and its VC-entropy bound is trivial for a ::; 6.2. It is also shown that bounds following the true learning curve can be derived from a formalism based on the density of error patterns.
originalAbstract: Results of a study of the worst case learning curves for a partic(cid:173) ular class of probability distribution on input space to MLP with hard threshold hidden units are presented. It is shown in partic(cid:173) ular, that in the thermodynamic limit for scaling by the number of connections to the first hidden layer, although the true learning curve behaves as ~ a-I for a ~ 1, its VC-dimension based bound is trivial (= 1) and its VC-entropy bound is trivial for a ::; 6.2. It is also shown that bounds following the true learning curve can be derived from a formalism based on the density of error patterns.

paragraphs: A generalization bound can be mathematically valid yet give little information about how well a network actually learns. This paper studies that gap for multilayer perceptrons with hard-threshold hidden units. It analyzes worst-case learning curves within a particular class of input probability distributions, giving the comparison a specified distributional setting.

The analysis takes a large-system limit in which sample size is scaled by the number of connections to the first hidden layer. In the regime described, the true learning curve improves approximately inversely with the scaled sample size, while the VC-dimension bound remains at the trivial error bound of one. The VC-entropy bound also stays trivial across a stated range.

The authors additionally derive bounds that follow the true learning curve using a formalism based on the density of error patterns. This shows that the loose VC results reflect the information captured by those bounds, rather than the learning behavior itself. The contribution is both a demonstrated gap and an alternative route to more informative guarantees in the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: For a specified class of threshold networks and input distributions, actual learning substantially outpaces VC bounds, while error-pattern-based bounds track it.

title: MLP Can Provably Generalize Much Better than VC-bounds Indicate

abstract: We consider the microscopic equations for learning problems in neural networks. The aligning fields of an example are obtained from the cavity fields, which are the fields if that example were absent in the learning process. In a rough energy landscape, we assume that the density of the local minima obey an exponential distribution, yielding macroscopic properties agreeing with the first step replica symmetry breaking solution. Iterating the microscopic equations provide a learning algorithm, which results in a higher stability than conventional algorithms.
originalAbstract: We consider the microscopic equations for learning problems in neural networks. The aligning fields of an example are obtained from the cavity fields, which are the fields if that example were absent in the learning process. In a rough energy landscape, we assume that the density of the local minima obey an exponential distribution, yielding macroscopic properties agreeing with the first step replica symmetry breaking solution. Iterating the microscopic equations provide a learning algorithm, which results in a higher stability than conventional algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies neural network learning through equations that describe individual examples. For a given example, it relates the field involved in aligning the network with that example to a cavity field: the corresponding field when that example is left out of learning. This comparison connects an example’s influence to the system formed by the remaining data.

The analysis addresses a rough energy landscape containing multiple local minima. It assumes that the density of those minima follows an exponential distribution. Under that assumption, the resulting large-scale properties agree with a first-step replica symmetry breaking solution, linking the example-level equations to a broader statistical description of the learning system.

The equations also supply a computational procedure: repeatedly applying them produces a learning algorithm. The authors report that this algorithm achieves higher stability than conventional algorithms. The contribution therefore joins theory and training, using a specific assumption about the landscape’s local minima to derive equations that both reproduce macroscopic behavior and guide iterative learning.
summary.tldr: Example-level equations connect a rough learning landscape to statistical theory and yield an algorithm with higher reported stability.

title: Microscopic Equations in Rough Energy Landscape for Neural Networks

abstract: Output coding is a general method for solving multiclass problems by reducing them to multiple binary classification problems. Previous re(cid:173) search on output coding has employed, almost solely, predefined discrete codes. We describe an algorithm that improves the performance of output codes by relaxing them to continuous codes. The relaxation procedure is cast as an optimization problem and is reminiscent of the quadratic program for support vector machines. We describe experiments with the proposed algorithm, comparing it to standard discrete output codes. The experimental results indicate that continuous relaxations of output codes often improve the generalization performance, especially for short codes.

We describe an algorithm that improves the performance of output codes by relaxing them to continuous codes. The relaxation procedure is cast as an optimization problem and is reminiscent of the quadratic program for support vector machines. We describe experiments with the proposed algorithm, comparing it to standard discrete output codes. The experimental results indicate that continuous relaxations of output codes often improve the generalization performance, especially for short codes.

paragraphs: Output coding solves a multiclass classification problem by expressing it through several binary classification problems. The code determines how these binary tasks represent the original classes. This paper focuses on improving that representation, observing that previous output-coding research had relied almost entirely on predefined discrete codes.

The proposed algorithm relaxes the codes into continuous values and treats their improvement as an optimization problem. This permits adjustments beyond the choices available in the original discrete representation. The authors describe the resulting optimization as reminiscent of the quadratic program used for support vector machines, connecting code design to an established style of classification optimization.

Experiments compare the proposed approach with standard discrete output codes. The results indicate that continuous relaxation often improves generalization, with especially noticeable benefits for short codes. The finding makes the code itself an object of optimization within multiclass learning. Its empirical qualification matters: the reported improvement is frequent in the experiments, and particularly associated with short codes, rather than stated as a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: Optimizing continuous relaxations of output codes often improved multiclass generalization in experiments, especially for short codes.

title: Improved Output Coding for Classification Using Continuous Relaxation

abstract: Query expansion is a long-studied approach for improving retrieval effectiveness by enhancing the userâs original query with additional related terms. Current algorithms for automatic query expansion have been shown to consistently improve retrieval accuracy on average, but are highly unstable and have bad worst-case performance for individual queries. We introduce a novel risk framework that formulates query model estimation as a constrained metric labeling problem on a graph of term relations. Themodel combines assignment costs based on a baseline feedback algorithm, edge weights based on term similarity, and simple constraints to enforce aspect balance, aspect coverage, and term centrality. Results across multiple standard test collections show consistent and dramatic reductions in the number and magnitude of expansion failures, while retaining the strong positive gains of the baseline algorithm.

Current algorithms for automatic query expansion have been shown to consistently improve retrieval accuracy on average, but are highly unstable and have bad worst-case performance for individual queries. We introduce a novel risk framework that formulates query model estimation as a constrained metric labeling problem on a graph of term relations. Themodel combines assignment costs based on a baseline feedback algorithm, edge weights based on term similarity, and simple constraints to enforce aspect balance, aspect coverage, and term centrality. Results across multiple standard test collections show consistent and dramatic reductions in the number and magnitude of expansion failures, while retaining the strong positive gains of the baseline algorithm.

paragraphs: Automatic query expansion adds related terms to a user's search to improve retrieval. Its average benefits can hide serious failures on individual queries. This paper focuses on that instability, asking how query models can preserve the gains of expansion while reducing the frequency and severity of cases where expansion makes retrieval worse.

The method represents relationships between terms as a graph and formulates query-model estimation as a constrained metric-labeling problem. Assignment costs incorporate a baseline feedback algorithm, while edge weights capture similarity between terms. Additional constraints enforce balance among query aspects, coverage of those aspects, and term centrality. These ingredients make relationships and coverage explicit parts of the estimation problem.

Across multiple standard test collections, the authors report consistent, substantial reductions in both the number and magnitude of expansion failures. At the same time, the method retains the baseline algorithm's strong positive gains. The findings therefore concern reliability across individual queries as well as retrieval effectiveness: the proposed framework reduces damaging outcomes without surrendering the benefits that motivated expansion.
summary.tldr: A graph-based constrained query model reduces expansion failures while retaining the retrieval gains of its baseline feedback method.

title: Estimating Robust Query Models with Convex Optimization

abstract: We present a general inference framework for inter-domain Gaussian Processes (GPs), focusing on its usefulness to build sparse GP models. The state-of-the-art sparse GP model introduced by Snelson and Ghahramani in [1] relies on finding a small, representative pseudo data set of m elements (from the same domain as the n available data elements) which is able to explain existing data well, and then uses it to perform inference. This reduces inference and model selection computation time from O(n^3) to O(m^2n), where m << n. Inter-domain GPs can be used to find a (possibly more compact) representative set of features lying in a different domain, at the same computational cost. Being able to specify a different domain for the representative features allows to incorporate prior knowledge about relevant characteristics of data and detaches the functional form of the covariance and basis functions. We will show how previously existing models fit into this framework and will use it to develop two new sparse GP models. Tests on large, representative regression data sets suggest that significant improvement can be achieved, while retaining computational efficiency.

Being able to specify a different domain for the representative features allows to incorporate prior knowledge about relevant characteristics of data and detaches the functional form of the covariance and basis functions. We will show how previously existing models fit into this framework and will use it to develop two new sparse GP models. Tests on large, representative regression data sets suggest that significant improvement can be achieved, while retaining computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Gaussian process inference can be expensive as the number of observations grows. Sparse methods address this by using a small representative collection of pseudo-data. The existing approach described in the paper places those representatives in the same domain as the observations, reducing computation from O(n^3) to O(m^2 n), where m is much smaller than n.

This paper allows the representatives to be features in a different domain. Such features may provide a more compact summary while keeping the same computational cost. Choosing another domain also lets the model incorporate prior knowledge about relevant data characteristics and separates the functional form of covariance functions from that of basis functions.

The authors develop a general inter-domain inference framework, show how earlier models fit within it, and construct two new sparse Gaussian process models. Tests on large regression datasets suggest significant improvement is possible without sacrificing computational efficiency. The central benefit is greater freedom in how the data are represented for sparse inference.
summary.tldr: Inter-domain Gaussian processes use representative features outside the observation domain to improve sparse modeling while retaining its computational efficiency.

title: Inter-domain Gaussian Processes for Sparse Inference using Inducing Features

abstract: We develop a convex relaxation of maximum a posteriori estimation of a mixture of regression models. Although our relaxation involves a semidefinite matrix variable, we reformulate the problem to eliminate the need for general semidefinite programming. In particular, we provide two reformulations that admit fast algorithms. The first is a max-min spectral reformulation exploiting quasi-Newton descent. The second is a min-min reformulation consisting of fast alternating steps of closed-form updates. We evaluate the methods against Expectation-Maximization in a real problem of motion segmentation from video data.
originalAbstract: We develop a convex relaxation of maximum a posteriori estimation of a mixture of regression models. Although our relaxation involves a semidefinite matrix variable, we reformulate the problem to eliminate the need for general semidefinite programming. In particular, we provide two reformulations that admit fast algorithms. The first is a max-min spectral reformulation exploiting quasi-Newton descent. The second is a min-min reformulation consisting of fast alternating steps of closed-form updates. We evaluate the methods against Expectation-Maximization in a real problem of motion segmentation from video data.

paragraphs: A mixture of regression models represents data through several regression relationships. This paper develops a convex relaxation of maximum a posteriori estimation for such a mixture. The relaxation provides an alternative optimization formulation for fitting the model, while retaining a connection to the original estimation task.

The initial formulation includes a semidefinite matrix variable, which could suggest using a general semidefinite-programming solver. The authors instead derive two reformulations that support faster specialized algorithms. One expresses the problem through a max-min spectral formulation and uses quasi-Newton descent. The other uses a min-min formulation with alternating steps whose updates are available in closed form.

The practical point is that the mathematical relaxation and its computational implementation are developed together: a convex formulation is paired with ways to avoid general semidefinite programming. The authors evaluate both methods against Expectation-Maximization on motion segmentation from real video data. This supplies an application-based comparison, although the abstract does not state a performance ranking or quantify an advantage over that comparator.
summary.tldr: Two specialized reformulations make a convex relaxation of mixture-regression estimation computationally practical without general semidefinite programming.

title: Convex Relaxation of Mixture Regression with Efficient Algorithms

abstract: Sparse coding has recently become a popular approach in computer vision to learn dictionaries of natural images. In this paper we extend sparse coding to learn interpretable spatio-temporal primitives of human motion. We cast the problem of learning spatio-temporal primitives as a tensor factorization problem and introduce constraints to learn interpretable primitives. In particular, we use group norms over those tensors, diagonal constraints on the activations as well as smoothness constraints that are inherent to human motion. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach to learn interpretable representations of human motion from motion capture data, and show that our approach outperforms recently developed matching pursuit and sparse coding algorithms.
originalAbstract: Sparse coding has recently become a popular approach in computer vision to learn dictionaries of natural images. In this paper we extend sparse coding to learn interpretable spatio-temporal primitives of human motion. We cast the problem of learning spatio-temporal primitives as a tensor factorization problem and introduce constraints to learn interpretable primitives. In particular, we use group norms over those tensors, diagonal constraints on the activations as well as smoothness constraints that are inherent to human motion. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach to learn interpretable representations of human motion from motion capture data, and show that our approach outperforms recently developed matching pursuit and sparse coding algorithms.

paragraphs: Sparse coding learns a dictionary of building blocks for representing data. This paper extends that idea from natural images to human motion, where useful building blocks must capture both spatial structure and change over time. The aim is to learn motion primitives that can be interpreted as meaningful components of movement.

The authors formulate learning as tensor factorization and introduce constraints that encourage interpretable results. These include group norms over the tensors, diagonal constraints on activations, and smoothness constraints reflecting properties of human motion. The constraints shape both the learned primitives and their activation patterns, bringing motion-specific structure into the representation-learning problem.

Experiments on motion-capture data demonstrate that the method learns interpretable human-motion representations. The authors also report better performance than recently developed matching-pursuit and sparse-coding algorithms. The results support combining sparse representation learning with structured constraints: the method is designed to produce components whose spatial and temporal organization remains meaningful while representing the observed movements.
summary.tldr: Constrained tensor factorization extends sparse coding to interpretable human-motion primitives and outperforms the compared representation methods.

title: Sparse Coding for Learning Interpretable Spatio-Temporal Primitives

abstract: From a functional viewpoint, a spiking neuron is a device that transforms input spike trains on its various synapses into an output spike train on its axon. We demonstrate in this paper that the function mapping underlying the device can be tractably learned based on input and output spike train data alone. We begin by posing the problem in a classification based framework. We then derive a novel kernel for an SRM0 model that is based on PSP and AHP like functions. With the kernel we demonstrate how the learning problem can be posed as a Quadratic Program. Experimental results demonstrate the strength of our approach.
originalAbstract: From a functional viewpoint, a spiking neuron is a device that transforms input spike trains on its various synapses into an output spike train on its axon. We demonstrate in this paper that the function mapping underlying the device can be tractably learned based on input and output spike train data alone. We begin by posing the problem in a classification based framework. We then derive a novel kernel for an SRM0 model that is based on PSP and AHP like functions. With the kernel we demonstrate how the learning problem can be posed as a Quadratic Program. Experimental results demonstrate the strength of our approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies a neuron as an input-output system: spike sequences arrive at its synapses, and another spike sequence leaves through its axon. The learning task is to recover this transformation from recorded input and output spikes alone. This focuses on reproducing the neuron's functional behavior using observations of what enters and what emerges.

The authors express the task as a classification problem and develop a kernel for the SRM0 neuron model. A kernel supplies the comparison structure used by the learning method. Here, it is built from functions resembling postsynaptic potentials and after-hyperpolarization, connecting the learning formulation to the kinds of responses represented by the neuron model.

With this kernel, training becomes a quadratic program, giving the proposed modeling task a tractable optimization formulation. The authors report experiments supporting the approach. The central contribution is the connection between spike-train observations, a neuron-specific kernel, and an optimization problem that can be solved to learn the modeled transformation.
summary.tldr: A neuron-specific kernel turns learning an SRM0 input-output model from spike trains into a tractable quadratic program.

title: A Novel Kernel for Learning a Neuron Model from Spike Train Data

abstract: Unlike existing nonparametric Bayesian models, which rely solely on specially conceived priors to incorporate domain knowledge for discovering improved latent representations, we study nonparametric Bayesian inference with regularization on the desired posterior distributions. While priors can indirectly affect posterior distributions through Bayes' theorem, imposing posterior regularization is arguably more direct and in some cases can be much easier. We particularly focus on developing infinite latent support vector machines (iLSVM) and multi-task infinite latent support vector machines (MT-iLSVM), which explore the large-margin idea in combination with a nonparametric Bayesian model for discovering predictive latent features for classification and multi-task learning, respectively. We present efficient inference methods and report empirical studies on several benchmark datasets. Our results appear to demonstrate the merits inherited from both large-margin learning and Bayesian nonparametrics.
originalAbstract: Unlike existing nonparametric Bayesian models, which rely solely on specially conceived priors to incorporate domain knowledge for discovering improved latent representations, we study nonparametric Bayesian inference with regularization on the desired posterior distributions. While priors can indirectly affect posterior distributions through Bayes' theorem, imposing posterior regularization is arguably more direct and in some cases can be much easier. We particularly focus on developing infinite latent support vector machines (iLSVM) and multi-task infinite latent support vector machines (MT-iLSVM), which explore the large-margin idea in combination with a nonparametric Bayesian model for discovering predictive latent features for classification and multi-task learning, respectively. We present efficient inference methods and report empirical studies on several benchmark datasets. Our results appear to demonstrate the merits inherited from both large-margin learning and Bayesian nonparametrics.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to guide latent-feature discovery in nonparametric Bayesian models toward useful predictions. Its central choice is to regularize the desired posterior distributions directly. Priors influence the posterior through Bayesian inference, whereas posterior regularization provides another place to express preferences about the representations that learning should produce.

The authors combine this idea with large-margin learning in two models: infinite latent support vector machines for classification and a multitask version for learning related tasks. Both combine a nonparametric Bayesian model with a predictive objective for discovering latent features. The aim is to bring representation learning and the requirements of classification into the same inference framework.

The paper supplies efficient inference methods and evaluates the models on several benchmark datasets. The authors describe the results as appearing to demonstrate advantages inherited from both large-margin learning and Bayesian nonparametrics. That is qualified empirical support for the combination. The broader methodological contribution is showing how predictive requirements can act directly on Bayesian posterior inference, rather than entering solely through specially designed priors.
summary.tldr: Infinite latent SVMs combine posterior regularization, large-margin prediction, and Bayesian nonparametric feature discovery for classification and multitask learning.

title: Infinite Latent SVM for Classification and Multi-task Learning

abstract: Despite the variety of robust regression methods that have been developed, current regression formulations are either NP-hard, or allow unbounded response to even a single leverage point. We present a general formulation for robust regression --Variational M-estimation--that unifies a number of robust regression methods while allowing a tractable approximation strategy. We develop an estimator that requires only polynomial-time, while achieving certain robustness and consistency guarantees. An experimental evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the new estimation approach compared to standard methods.
originalAbstract: Despite the variety of robust regression methods that have been developed, current regression formulations are either NP-hard, or allow unbounded response to even a single leverage point. We present a general formulation for robust regression --Variational M-estimation--that unifies a number of robust regression methods while allowing a tractable approximation strategy. We develop an estimator that requires only polynomial-time, while achieving certain robustness and consistency guarantees. An experimental evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the new estimation approach compared to standard methods.

paragraphs: Robust regression aims to fit relationships without allowing unusual observations to dominate the answer. The paper identifies a difficult tradeoff in existing formulations: they can be computationally intractable, or they can respond without bound to even one leverage point. That makes computational feasibility and resistance to influential observations joint concerns.

The authors introduce Variational M-estimation, a general formulation that brings several robust regression methods into a common framework. Its practical purpose is to permit a tractable approximation strategy. From this formulation, they develop an estimator with polynomial-time computation and certain guarantees concerning robustness and consistency. The claim concerns this estimator and its stated guarantees, rather than exact efficient solutions to every robust regression problem.

Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed estimation approach relative to standard methods. Together, the theoretical and experimental contributions show a route toward balancing manageable computation with statistically meaningful protection against problematic observations. The unifying formulation matters because it connects that route to a broader family of robust regression approaches.
summary.tldr: Variational M-estimation supports a polynomial-time robust regression estimator with qualified robustness and consistency guarantees.

title: A Polynomial-time Form of Robust Regression

abstract: This paper concerns the problem of matrix completion, which is to estimate a matrix from observations in a small subset of indices. We propose a calibrated spectrum elastic net method with a sum of the nuclear and Frobenius penalties and develop an iterative algorithm to solve the convex minimization problem. The iterative algorithm alternates between imputing the missing entries in the incomplete matrix by the current guess and estimating the matrix by a scaled soft-thresholding singular value decomposition of the imputed matrix until the resulting matrix converges. A calibration step follows to correct the bias caused by the Frobenius penalty. Under proper coherence conditions and for suitable penalties levels, we prove that the proposed estimator achieves an error bound of nearly optimal order and in proportion to the noise level. This provides a unified analysis of the noisy and noiseless matrix completion problems. Simulation results are presented to compare our proposal with previous ones.
originalAbstract: This paper concerns the problem of matrix completion, which is to estimate a matrix from observations in a small subset of indices. We propose a calibrated spectrum elastic net method with a sum of the nuclear and Frobenius penalties and develop an iterative algorithm to solve the convex minimization problem. The iterative algorithm alternates between imputing the missing entries in the incomplete matrix by the current guess and estimating the matrix by a scaled soft-thresholding singular value decomposition of the imputed matrix until the resulting matrix converges. A calibration step follows to correct the bias caused by the Frobenius penalty. Under proper coherence conditions and for suitable penalties levels, we prove that the proposed estimator achieves an error bound of nearly optimal order and in proportion to the noise level. This provides a unified analysis of the noisy and noiseless matrix completion problems. Simulation results are presented to compare our proposal with previous ones.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates an entire matrix from observations of only some entries. The paper proposes a convex estimation method that combines nuclear and Frobenius penalties. This combination is called a spectrum elastic net, and its calibration step addresses bias introduced by the Frobenius part of the penalty.

The algorithm repeatedly fills missing entries using its current estimate, then updates the matrix through a scaled, soft-thresholded singular value decomposition. These two operations alternate until the matrix converges. Calibration follows this iterative fitting process. The procedure therefore separates obtaining a regularized estimate from correcting the particular bias caused by one of its penalties.

Under appropriate coherence conditions and suitable penalty levels, the authors prove an error bound with nearly optimal order that scales with the noise level. Those conditions are part of the guarantee. The same analysis covers both noisy observations and the noiseless case, providing a unified account of the estimator’s behavior. Simulations compare the proposal with earlier methods, although the abstract does not claim a particular empirical ranking.
summary.tldr: A calibrated combination of matrix penalties yields nearly optimal, noise-proportional recovery guarantees under stated structural and tuning conditions.

title: Calibrated Elastic Regularization in Matrix Completion

abstract: We present PAC-Bayes-Empirical-Bernstein inequality. The inequality is based on combination of PAC-Bayesian bounding technique with Empirical Bernstein bound. It allows to take advantage of small empirical variance and is especially useful in regression. We show that when the empirical variance is significantly smaller than the empirical loss PAC-Bayes-Empirical-Bernstein inequality is significantly tighter than PAC-Bayes-kl inequality of Seeger (2002) and otherwise it is comparable. PAC-Bayes-Empirical-Bernstein inequality is an interesting example of application of PAC-Bayesian bounding technique to self-bounding functions. We provide empirical comparison of PAC-Bayes-Empirical-Bernstein inequality with PAC-Bayes-kl inequality on a synthetic example and several UCI datasets.

paragraphs: Learning bounds can use more than the average loss observed in data. This paper introduces an inequality that also benefits from low empirical variance, meaning relatively little variation in the observed losses. It combines a PAC-Bayesian bounding technique with an Empirical Bernstein bound to make that information useful.

The authors compare the resulting PAC-Bayes-Empirical-Bernstein inequality with the PAC-Bayes-kl inequality. When empirical variance is substantially smaller than empirical loss, the new bound is significantly tighter. Otherwise, the bounds are comparable. The advantage is therefore tied to a property of the observed losses, giving a specific condition under which the new construction is especially valuable.

Empirical comparisons use a synthetic example and several UCI datasets. The central significance is that observed variability can sharpen a learning guarantee: two situations with similar average loss need not warrant equally loose bounds when their empirical variances differ.
summary.tldr: A variance-sensitive PAC-Bayesian bound is substantially tighter than PAC-Bayes-kl when empirical variance is much smaller than empirical loss.

title: PAC-Bayes-Empirical-Bernstein Inequality

abstract: We propose a model for demand estimation in multi-agent, differentiated product settings and present an estimation algorithm that uses reversible jump MCMC techniques to classify agents' types. Our model extends the popular setup in Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995) to allow for the data-driven classification of agents' types using agent-level data. We focus on applications involving data on agents' ranking over alternatives, and present theoretical conditions that establish the identifiability of the model and uni-modality of the likelihood/posterior. Results on both real and simulated data provide support for the scalability of our approach.

Results on both real and simulated data provide support for the scalability of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper develops a model for estimating demand when multiple agents choose among differentiated products. A central concern is that agents can have different types, reflecting differences in their preferences. The proposed model extends an established demand-estimation framework so that these types can be classified from individual-level data.

The estimation algorithm uses reversible jump MCMC to classify agents' types. The paper focuses on settings where observations describe agents' rankings over alternatives. This makes the ordering of preferences the information used for estimation, while the type structure is learned from the data within the proposed modeling framework.

The authors give theoretical conditions under which the model is identifiable and the likelihood or posterior is unimodal. Identifiability concerns whether the model can be distinguished from the available observations; unimodality concerns the shape of the estimation objective. These are conditional results, rather than unrestricted properties of every dataset. Experiments with real and simulated data provide evidence supporting the scalability of the approach.
summary.tldr: A demand model learns agent types from individual rankings, with conditional identifiability and unimodality guarantees and empirical support for scalability.

title: Generalized Random Utility Models with Multiple Types

abstract: There are two major routes to address linear inverse problems. Whereas regularization-based approaches build estimators as solutions of penalized regression optimization problems, Bayesian estimators rely on the posterior distribution of the unknown, given some assumed family of priors. While these may seem radically different approaches, recent results have shown that, in the context of additive white Gaussian denoising, the Bayesian conditional mean estimator is always the solution of a penalized regression problem. The contribution of this paper is twofold. First, we extend the additive white Gaussian denoising results to general linear inverse problems with colored Gaussian noise. Second, we characterize conditions under which the penalty function associated to the conditional mean estimator can satisfy certain popular properties such as convexity, separability, and smoothness. This sheds light on some tradeoff between computational efficiency and estimation accuracy in sparse regularization, and draws some connections between Bayesian estimation and proximal optimization.

These approaches appear different, but earlier results connected them for additive white Gaussian denoising: the Bayesian conditional mean can be expressed as the solution of a penalized regression problem.

This paper extends that connection to general linear inverse problems with colored Gaussian noise. The extension broadens the setting in which a posterior-based estimate can be understood through an optimization problem. It makes the associated penalty an object of study, linking the statistical estimator to the structure of the objective used to compute it.

The authors also characterize conditions under which this penalty can be convex, separable, or smooth. These properties matter to the relationship between estimation and optimization, and they are established conditionally rather than asserted for every penalty. The analysis sheds light on tradeoffs between computational efficiency and estimation accuracy in sparse regularization. It also connects Bayesian estimation with proximal optimization, providing a shared perspective on two ways of solving inverse problems.
summary.tldr: The paper connects Bayesian conditional means with penalized regression for linear inverse problems with colored Gaussian noise and characterizes possible penalty properties.

title: Reconciling "priors" & "priors" without prejudice?

abstract: We study an online learning setting where the player is temporarily deprived of feedback each time it switches to a different action. Such model of \emph{adaptive feedback} naturally occurs in scenarios where the environment reacts to the player's actions and requires some time to recover and stabilize after the algorithm switches actions. This motivates a variant of the multi-armed bandit problem, which we call the \emph{blinded multi-armed bandit}, in which no feedback is given to the algorithm whenever it switches arms. We develop efficient online learning algorithms for this problem and prove that they guarantee the same asymptotic regret as the optimal algorithms for the standard multi-armed bandit problem. This result stands in stark contrast to another recent result, which states that adding a switching cost to the standard multi-armed bandit makes it substantially harder to learn, and provides a direct comparison of how feedback and loss contribute to the difficulty of an online learning problem. We also extend our results to the general prediction framework of bandit linear optimization, again attaining near-optimal regret bounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential learning when changing actions temporarily removes feedback. Such a setting can arise when the environment needs time to settle after a change. The authors formalize it as a blinded multi-armed bandit problem, where switching arms means the learner receives no feedback at the switch.

They develop efficient algorithms and prove that these attain the same asymptotic regret as optimal algorithms for the standard multi-armed bandit problem. Regret expresses the performance shortfall associated with learning which actions to take. The result shows that the specified feedback loss can be handled without worsening its optimal asymptotic rate.

The paper contrasts this finding with a result in which charging a switching cost makes the standard bandit problem substantially harder. Losing information when switching and directly increasing loss when switching can therefore affect learning difficulty differently. The authors also extend their approach to bandit linear optimization, obtaining near-optimal regret bounds there. This broadens the analysis beyond choosing among individual arms to a more general prediction framework.
summary.tldr: Efficient bandit algorithms tolerate feedback loss when switching actions while retaining the standard problem's optimal asymptotic regret rate.

title: The Blinded Bandit: Learning with Adaptive Feedback

abstract: In this paper, we propose a very deep fully convolutional encoding-decoding framework for image restoration such as denoising and super-resolution. The network is composed of multiple layers of convolution and deconvolution operators, learning end-to-end mappings from corrupted images to the original ones. The convolutional layers act as the feature extractor, which capture the abstraction of image contents while eliminating noises/corruptions. Deconvolutional layers are then used to recover the image details. We propose to symmetrically link convolutional and deconvolutional layers with skip-layer connections, with which the training converges much faster and attains a higher-quality local optimum. First, the skip connections allow the signal to be back-propagated to bottom layers directly, and thus tackles the problem of gradient vanishing, making training deep networks easier and achieving restoration performance gains consequently. Second, these skip connections pass image details from convolutional layers to deconvolutional layers, which is beneficial in recovering the original image. Significantly, with the large capacity, we can handle different levels of noises using a single model. Experimental results show that our network achieves better performance than recent state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a very deep encoder–decoder network for restoring corrupted images, including denoising and super-resolution. It learns the mapping from degraded images to their originals end to end. Convolutional layers extract representations of image content while removing corruption, and deconvolutional layers reconstruct image details from those representations.

Its central design choice is to connect corresponding convolutional and deconvolutional layers through symmetric skip connections. These links serve two purposes. They give training signals a direct route back to lower layers, addressing vanishing gradients, and they carry image details forward to the reconstruction layers. The same connections therefore support both optimization and preservation of useful visual information.

The authors report faster convergence, a higher-quality local optimum, and improved restoration performance from this design. They also state that the network's capacity allows one model to handle different noise levels. Experiments show better performance than recent leading methods, supporting the combination of network depth with direct paths for gradients and image details.
summary.tldr: Symmetric skip connections help a deep image-restoration network train more effectively and preserve details during reconstruction.

title: Image Restoration Using Very Deep Convolutional Encoder-Decoder Networks with Symmetric Skip Connections

abstract: Variational methods that rely on a recognition network to approximate the posterior of directed graphical models offer better inference and learning than previous methods. Recent advances that exploit the capacity and flexibility in this approach have expanded what kinds of models can be trained. However, as a proposal for the posterior, the capacity of the recognition network is limited, which can constrain the representational power of the generative model and increase the variance of Monte Carlo estimates. To address these issues, we introduce an iterative refinement procedure for improving the approximate posterior of the recognition network and show that training with the refined posterior is competitive with state-of-the-art methods. The advantages of refinement are further evident in an increased effective sample size, which implies a lower variance of gradient estimates.

To address these issues, we introduce an iterative refinement procedure for improving the approximate posterior of the recognition network and show that training with the refined posterior is competitive with state-of-the-art methods. The advantages of refinement are further evident in an increased effective sample size, which implies a lower variance of gradient estimates.

paragraphs: Recognition networks provide approximate posterior distributions for directed generative models, making variational inference and learning possible for flexible model families. However, their capacity is limited. An inadequate posterior approximation can restrict what the generative model learns and increase the variability of Monte Carlo estimates used during training.

The paper introduces an iterative procedure that refines the posterior approximation produced by a recognition network. Instead of treating the network's initial proposal as the final inference result, the procedure improves that proposal through additional refinement. Training then uses the refined posterior, directly connecting better approximate inference to the learning process.

The authors report that training with refinement is competitive with state-of-the-art methods. They also find an increase in effective sample size, indicating that the samples provide more useful information for estimation and implying lower variance in gradient estimates. These findings support refinement as a way to address the recognition network's inference bottleneck while improving the statistical quality of the training signal.
summary.tldr: Iteratively refining a recognition network's posterior approximation yields competitive training results and lower-variance gradient estimates.

title: Iterative Refinement of the Approximate Posterior for Directed Belief Networks

abstract: We present an architecture which lets us train deep, directed generative models with many layers of latent variables. We include deterministic paths between all latent variables and the generated output, and provide a richer set of connections between computations for inference and generation, which enables more effective communication of information throughout the model during training. To improve performance on natural images, we incorporate a lightweight autoregressive model in the reconstruction distribution. These techniques permit end-to-end training of models with 10+ layers of latent variables. Experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard image modelling benchmarks, can expose latent class structure in the absence of label information, and can provide convincing imputations of occluded regions in natural images.

To improve performance on natural images, we incorporate a lightweight autoregressive model in the reconstruction distribution. These techniques permit end-to-end training of models with 10+ layers of latent variables. Experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard image modelling benchmarks, can expose latent class structure in the absence of label information, and can provide convincing imputations of occluded regions in natural images.

paragraphs: This paper develops an architecture for directed generative models containing many layers of latent variables. These hidden variables provide a hierarchy through which the model represents and generates observations. The architectural goal is to make information travel more effectively throughout that hierarchy during training, allowing substantially deep latent-variable models to be trained together.

The design adds deterministic paths from every latent variable to the generated output. It also creates richer connections between the computations used to infer hidden variables and those used to generate observations. For natural images, a lightweight autoregressive component enriches the reconstruction distribution. Together, these choices enable end-to-end training with more than ten latent-variable layers.

Experiments report leading performance on standard image modeling benchmarks. The models can also reveal latent class structure without receiving class labels and plausibly fill in obscured regions of natural images. These findings show that the architecture supports both image modeling and useful hidden representations. The reported capabilities are experimental results, rather than guarantees that any learned hierarchy will recover meaningful classes or reconstruct every missing region correctly.
summary.tldr: Richer information paths enable training generative models with more than ten latent layers and strong image modeling results.

title: An Architecture for Deep, Hierarchical Generative Models

abstract: Computationally intensive distributed and parallel computing is often bottlenecked by a small set of slow workers known as stragglers. In this paper, we utilize the emerging idea of ``coded computation'' to design a novel error-correcting-code inspired technique for solving linear inverse problems under specific iterative methods in a parallelized implementation affected by stragglers. Example machine-learning applications include inverse problems such as personalized PageRank and sampling on graphs. We provably show that our coded-computation technique can reduce the mean-squared error under a computational deadline constraint. In fact, the ratio of mean-squared error of replication-based and coded techniques diverges to infinity as the deadline increases. Our experiments for personalized PageRank performed on real systems and real social networks show that this ratio can be as large as $10^4$. Further, unlike coded-computation techniques proposed thus far, our strategy combines outputs of all workers, including the stragglers, to produce more accurate estimates at the computational deadline. This also ensures that the accuracy degrades ``gracefully'' in the event that the number of stragglers is large.

paragraphs: Parallel computations can be held back by a few slow workers, often called stragglers. This paper develops a technique inspired by error-correcting codes for linear inverse problems solved with particular iterative methods. Its goal is to improve the estimate available when a computational deadline arrives, even when workers have progressed at different speeds.

The method combines outputs from all workers, including the slow ones. Their partial contributions therefore help determine the final estimate. This design also makes accuracy degrade gradually when many workers are slow. The applications discussed include personalized PageRank and sampling on graphs, both presented as examples of relevant inverse problems.

The authors prove that their approach can reduce mean-squared error under a deadline constraint. In their analysis, the error ratio between replication-based and coded methods grows without bound as the deadline increases. Personalized PageRank experiments on real systems and social networks produce ratios as large as 10,000. These results demonstrate substantial gains within the iterative-computation setting studied.
summary.tldr: An error-correcting-code-inspired method uses all workers' outputs to improve deadline-limited inverse-problem estimates despite stragglers.

title: Coded Distributed Computing for Inverse Problems

abstract: Density ratio estimation is a vital tool in both machine learning and statistical community. However, due to the unbounded nature of density ratio, the estimation proceudre can be vulnerable to corrupted data points, which often pushes the estimated ratio toward infinity. In this paper, we present a robust estimator which automatically identifies and trims outliers. The proposed estimator has a convex formulation, and the global optimum can be obtained via subgradient descent. We analyze the parameter estimation error of this estimator under high-dimensional settings. Experiments are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the estimator.

The proposed estimator has a convex formulation, and the global optimum can be obtained via subgradient descent. paragraphs: Density ratio estimation compares two probability distributions through the ratio of their densities. Because that ratio can be unbounded, corrupted observations can have a severe effect on its estimation, potentially driving the estimated value toward infinity. This paper addresses that sensitivity by designing an estimator that automatically identifies and trims outliers.

The proposed estimator has a convex formulation, and the authors state that its global optimum can be obtained using subgradient descent. This connects the robustness mechanism to an optimization problem with a global solution. Automatic trimming is central to the approach: the method incorporates the identification of problematic observations into estimation rather than requiring their removal beforehand.

The paper also analyzes parameter estimation error in high-dimensional settings and conducts experiments to verify the estimator's effectiveness. These contributions address both the statistical behavior of the recovered parameters and the practical usefulness of trimming. The resulting method targets the specific failure mode in which corrupted observations exert excessive influence on an otherwise useful distribution-comparison tool.
summary.tldr: A convex density-ratio estimator automatically trims outliers to reduce corruption sensitivity, with high-dimensional error analysis and experimental support.

title: Trimmed Density Ratio Estimation

abstract: Stochastic regularisation is an important weapon in the arsenal of a deep learning practitioner. However, despite recent theoretical advances, our understanding of how noise influences signal propagation in deep neural networks remains limited. By extending recent work based on mean field theory, we develop a new framework for signal propagation in stochastic regularised neural networks. Our \textit{noisy signal propagation} theory can incorporate several common noise distributions, including additive and multiplicative Gaussian noise as well as dropout. We use this framework to investigate initialisation strategies for noisy ReLU networks. We show that no critical initialisation strategy exists using additive noise, with signal propagation exploding regardless of the selected noise distribution. For multiplicative noise (e.g.\ dropout), we identify alternative critical initialisation strategies that depend on the second moment of the noise distribution. Simulations and experiments on real-world data confirm that our proposed initialisation is able to stably propagate signals in deep networks, while using an initialisation disregarding noise fails to do so. Furthermore, we analyse correlation dynamics between inputs. Stronger noise regularisation is shown to reduce the depth to which discriminatory information about the inputs to a noisy ReLU network is able to propagate, even when initialised at criticality. We support our theoretical predictions for these trainable depths with simulations, as well as with experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: Noise-based regularization changes how signals move through deep networks, so initialization strategies that ignore noise may fail to preserve useful signals. This paper extends mean field theory to analyze signal propagation under stochastic regularization. Its framework accommodates additive and multiplicative Gaussian noise as well as dropout.

For the noisy ReLU networks studied, the theory finds no critical initialization under additive noise: signal propagation explodes regardless of the selected noise distribution. Simulations and real-data experiments show stable signal propagation with the proposed initialization, while initialization that disregards noise fails to achieve it.

Stronger noise reduces how far information that distinguishes inputs can propagate, even at critical initialization. Simulations and experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 support these predictions. The results distinguish stabilizing signal propagation from preserving discriminatory information throughout a deep network.
summary.tldr: Noise-aware theory identifies critical initialization for multiplicative-noise ReLU networks and shows that stronger noise still limits useful propagation depth.

title: Critical initialisation for deep signal propagation in noisy rectifier neural networks

abstract: Dense event captioning aims to detect and describe all events of interest contained in a video. Despite the advanced development in this area, existing methods tackle this task by making use of dense temporal annotations, which is dramatically source-consuming. This paper formulates a new problem: weakly supervised dense event captioning, which does not require temporal segment annotations for model training. Our solution is based on the one-to-one correspondence assumption, each caption describes one temporal segment, and each temporal segment has one caption, which holds in current benchmark datasets and most real world cases. We decompose the problem into a pair of dual problems: event captioning and sentence localization and present a cycle system to train our model. Extensive experimental results are provided to demonstrate the ability of our model on both dense event captioning and sentence localization in videos.

paragraphs: Dense event captioning requires finding events within a video and describing each one. Training typically relies on annotations that specify where those events occur in time, which are expensive to produce. This paper formulates a weakly supervised version of the task that does not require temporal-segment annotations during training.

The method assumes a one-to-one relationship between captions and temporal segments: each caption describes one segment, and each segment has one caption. Under that assumption, the authors connect two complementary problems. Event captioning produces a sentence for an event, while sentence localization identifies the video segment described by a sentence. A cyclic system trains these tasks together.

Experiments demonstrate the model's ability to perform both dense captioning and sentence localization. The approach matters because it uses the relationship between description and localization to reduce the required annotation burden. Its formulation depends on the correspondence assumption, which the authors state holds in current benchmark datasets and most real-world cases.
summary.tldr: A cyclic captioning-and-localization system learns dense video descriptions without temporal annotations under a one-to-one caption–segment assumption.

title: Weakly Supervised Dense Event Captioning in Videos

abstract: In order to achieve state-of-the-art performance, modern machine learning techniques require careful data pre-processing and hyperparameter tuning. Moreover, given the ever increasing number of machine learning models being developed, model selection is becoming increasingly important. Automating the selection and tuning of machine learning pipelines, which can include different data pre-processing methods and machine learning models, has long been one of the goals of the machine learning community. In this paper, we propose to solve this meta-learning task by combining ideas from collaborative filtering and Bayesian optimization. Specifically, we use a probabilistic matrix factorization model to transfer knowledge across experiments performed in hundreds of different datasets and use an acquisition function to guide the exploration of the space of possible ML pipelines. In our experiments, we show that our approach quickly identifies high-performing pipelines across a wide range of datasets, significantly outperforming the current state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Choosing a machine learning pipeline involves decisions about preprocessing, the predictive model, and hyperparameters. Evaluating these combinations can require substantial experimentation. This paper treats pipeline selection as a meta-learning problem: results from previous datasets provide information that can guide the search on another dataset.

The method combines collaborative filtering with Bayesian optimization. A probabilistic matrix factorization model transfers knowledge from experiments across hundreds of datasets, while an acquisition function chooses which pipelines to explore. These components connect learning from historical evaluations with making decisions about new evaluations, so the search can use more than the results obtained on the current dataset alone.

Experiments show that the approach quickly finds high-performing pipelines across a wide range of datasets and significantly outperforms the contemporary state of the art in those evaluations. The contribution is an integrated way to reuse accumulated experimentation and guide further search. Its reported advantage concerns how effectively the system identifies good pipelines, with performance evidence drawn from the paper's experiments.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic matrix factorization transfers past pipeline results across datasets to guide efficient automated machine learning search.

title: Probabilistic Matrix Factorization for Automated Machine Learning

abstract: The problem of learning-to-learn (LTL) or meta-learning is gaining increasing attention due to recent empirical evidence of its effectiveness in applications. The goal addressed in LTL is to select an algorithm that works well on tasks sampled from a meta-distribution. In this work, we consider the family of algorithms given by a variant of Ridge Regression, in which the regularizer is the square distance to an unknown mean vector. We show that, in this setting, the LTL problem can be reformulated as a Least Squares (LS) problem and we exploit a novel meta- algorithm to efficiently solve it. At each iteration the meta-algorithm processes only one dataset. Specifically, it firstly estimates the stochastic LS objective function, by splitting this dataset into two subsets used to train and test the inner algorithm, respectively. Secondly, it performs a stochastic gradient step with the estimated value. Under specific assumptions, we present a bound for the generalization error of our meta-algorithm, which suggests the right splitting parameter to choose. When the hyper-parameters of the problem are fixed, this bound is consistent as the number of tasks grows, even if the sample size is kept constant. Preliminary experiments confirm our theoretical findings, highlighting the advantage of our approach, with respect to independent task learning.
originalAbstract: The problem of learning-to-learn (LTL) or meta-learning is gaining increasing attention due to recent empirical evidence of its effectiveness in applications. The goal addressed in LTL is to select an algorithm that works well on tasks sampled from a meta-distribution. In this work, we consider the family of algorithms given by a variant of Ridge Regression, in which the regularizer is the square distance to an unknown mean vector. We show that, in this setting, the LTL problem can be reformulated as a Least Squares (LS) problem and we exploit a novel meta- algorithm to efficiently solve it. At each iteration the meta-algorithm processes only one dataset. Specifically, it firstly estimates the stochastic LS objective function, by splitting this dataset into two subsets used to train and test the inner algorithm, respectively. Secondly, it performs a stochastic gradient step with the estimated value. Under specific assumptions, we present a bound for the generalization error of our meta-algorithm, which suggests the right splitting parameter to choose. When the hyper-parameters of the problem are fixed, this bound is consistent as the number of tasks grows, even if the sample size is kept constant. Preliminary experiments confirm our theoretical findings, highlighting the advantage of our approach, with respect to independent task learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies meta-learning through a family of ridge regression algorithms that penalize distance from a shared, learned mean vector. The objective is to select a learning algorithm that performs well on tasks drawn from a task distribution. Learning the mean gives those tasks a common reference point for regularization.

The authors reformulate this meta-learning problem as least squares and develop an algorithm that processes one task dataset per iteration. Each dataset is split into two subsets: one trains the inner learner and the other tests it. The resulting estimate of the meta-objective is used for a stochastic gradient update.

Under specific assumptions, a generalization bound guides the choice of the split. With fixed hyperparameters, the bound is consistent as the number of tasks increases, even if each task's sample size stays constant. Preliminary experiments support the theory and show an advantage over learning tasks independently. The result highlights how accumulating tasks can improve learning without requiring larger datasets for every task.
summary.tldr: Learning a shared regularization mean across tasks yields a least-squares meta-learning method with conditional generalization guarantees.

title: Learning To Learn Around A Common Mean

abstract: Distributed implementations of mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) suffer from communication overheads, attributed to the high frequency of gradient updates inherent in small-batch training. Training with large batches can reduce these overheads; however it besets the convergence of the algorithm and the generalization performance. In this work, we take a first step towards analyzing how the structure (width and depth) of a neural network affects the performance of large-batch training. We present new theoretical results which suggest that--for a fixed number of parameters--wider networks are more amenable to fast large-batch training compared to deeper ones. We provide extensive experiments on residual and fully-connected neural networks which suggest that wider networks can be trained using larger batches without incurring a convergence slow-down, unlike their deeper variants.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient descent can spend substantial effort communicating frequent updates when batches are small. Larger batches reduce that overhead, but can impair convergence and generalization. This paper asks whether network structure helps explain which models are better suited to large-batch training, focusing on the allocation of capacity between width and depth.

The theoretical results suggest that, for a fixed parameter count, wider networks are more amenable to fast large-batch training than deeper ones. Holding the number of parameters fixed makes the comparison about how capacity is arranged. The result points to architecture as a factor in the effectiveness of using larger batches.

Experiments on residual and fully connected networks support that direction: wider networks can use larger batches without the convergence slowdown observed in their deeper variants. The authors frame the work as an initial step toward analyzing this relationship. Its stated findings concern the compatibility of width with fast large-batch training, providing evidence for considering architecture alongside batch size when studying distributed optimization.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments suggest wider networks can accommodate larger training batches more effectively than deeper networks with comparable parameter budgets.

title: The Effect of Network Width on the Performance of Large-batch Training

abstract: Fueled by algorithmic advances, AI algorithms are increasingly being deployed in settings subject to unanticipated challenges with complex social effects. Motivated by real-world deployment of AI driven, social-network based suicide prevention and landslide risk management interventions, this paper focuses on a robust graph covering problem subject to group fairness constraints. We show that, in the absence of fairness constraints, state-of-the-art algorithms for the robust graph covering problem result in biased node coverage: they tend to discriminate individuals (nodes) based on membership in traditionally marginalized groups. To remediate this issue, we propose a novel formulation of the robust covering problem with fairness constraints and a tractable approximation scheme applicable to real world instances. We provide a formal analysis of the price of group fairness (PoF) for this problem, where we show that uncertainty can lead to greater PoF. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several real-world social networks. Our method yields competitive node coverage while significantly improving group fairness relative to state-of-the-art methods.
