paragraphs: Graph covering problems arise when an intervention must reach people or locations connected through a network. This paper studies robust covering under uncertainty, motivated by social-network suicide prevention and landslide risk management. It finds that existing robust covering algorithms can produce biased coverage when fairness is absent from the optimization problem.

The authors introduce a formulation with group fairness constraints and a tractable approximation scheme intended for real-world instances. Fairness becomes an explicit requirement alongside coverage and robustness. They also analyze the price of group fairness: the cost associated with imposing fairness requirements. Their analysis shows that uncertainty can increase this price, linking equitable allocation to how unpredictable deployment conditions are.

Experiments on several real-world social networks show competitive overall node coverage alongside significantly improved group fairness compared with state-of-the-art methods. The result demonstrates that addressing biased coverage need not eliminate useful coverage performance in the tested settings. It also shows why uncertainty and fairness deserve joint analysis when designing network-based interventions.
summary.tldr: Fairness-constrained robust graph covering improves group equity while retaining competitive coverage, and uncertainty can increase the cost of fairness.

title: Exploring Algorithmic Fairness in Robust Graph Covering Problems

abstract: Object detectors are usually equipped with backbone networks designed for image classification. It might be sub-optimal because of the gap between the tasks of image classification and object detection. In this work, we present DetNAS to use Neural Architecture Search (NAS) for the design of better backbones for object detection. It is non-trivial because detection training typically needs ImageNetpre-training while NAS systems require accuracies on the target detection task as supervisory signals. Based on the technique of one-shot supernet, which contains all possible networks in the search space, we propose a framework for backbone search on object detection. We train the supernet under the typical detector training schedule: ImageNet pre-training and detection fine-tuning. Then, the architecture search is performed on the trained supernet, using the detection task as the guidance. This framework makes NAS on backbones very efficient. In experiments, we show the effectiveness of DetNAS on various detectors, for instance, one-stage RetinaNetand the two-stage FPN. We empirically find that networks searched on object detection shows consistent superiority compared to those searched on ImageNet classification. The resulting architecture achieves superior performance than hand-crafted networks on COCO with much less FLOPs complexity.

paragraphs: Object detectors commonly reuse feature-extraction backbones designed for image classification. Because classification and detection are different tasks, those designs may be suboptimal for detection. DetNAS searches directly for detection backbones while addressing a practical complication: detector training typically needs classification pre-training, but architecture selection should be guided by detection performance.

The method uses a one-shot supernet that contains all candidate networks in the search space. It trains this shared structure through ImageNet pre-training followed by detection fine-tuning. Architecture search then operates on the trained supernet, using the target detection task to judge candidates. Sharing the training in this way makes backbone search efficient.

Experiments demonstrate the approach with detectors including RetinaNet and FPN. Networks searched using detection performance consistently outperform classification-searched networks in the reported comparisons. The resulting architecture also exceeds the performance of hand-designed networks on COCO while requiring substantially fewer floating-point operations. The findings support aligning architecture search with the task where the backbone will ultimately be used.
summary.tldr: DetNAS efficiently searches for detection-specific backbones and reports better detection performance with less computation than the compared hand-designed networks.

title: DetNAS: Backbone Search for Object Detection

abstract: Forecasting high-dimensional time series plays a crucial role in many applications such as demand forecasting and financial predictions. Modern datasets can have millions of correlated time-series that evolve together, i.e they are extremely high dimensional (one dimension for each individual time-series). There is a need for exploiting global patterns and coupling them with local calibration for better prediction. However, most recent deep learning approaches in the literature are one-dimensional, i.e, even though they are trained on the whole dataset, during prediction, the future forecast for a single dimension mainly depends on past values from the same dimension. In this paper, we seek to correct this deficiency and propose DeepGLO, a deep forecasting model which thinks globally and acts locally. In particular, DeepGLO is a hybrid model that combines a global matrix factorization model regularized by a temporal convolution network, along with another temporal network that can capture local properties of each time-series and associated covariates. Our model can be trained effectively on high-dimensional but diverse time series, where different time series can have vastly different scales, without a priori normalization or rescaling. Empirical results demonstrate that DeepGLO can outperform state-of-the-art approaches; for example, we see more than 25% improvement in WAPE over other methods on a public dataset that contains more than 100K-dimensional time series.

paragraphs: Large forecasting datasets can contain many correlated time series that evolve together. A model may train on the whole collection yet predict each series mainly from its own past, leaving cross-series information underused. DeepGLO addresses this by combining a global model of shared patterns with a local model of each individual series.

Its global component uses matrix factorization regularized by a temporal convolution network. A second temporal network captures local behavior and associated covariates. Together, these components connect collection-wide structure with series-specific prediction. The authors also state that the model can train effectively on diverse series with substantially different scales without prior normalization or rescaling.

On one public dataset with more than 100,000 time-series dimensions, the reported improvement in weighted absolute percentage error exceeds 25% over other methods. That result illustrates the potential benefit of combining global dependence and local calibration, while remaining a finding for the reported dataset rather than a guaranteed improvement on every forecasting problem.
summary.tldr: DeepGLO combines global matrix factorization with local temporal modeling to improve forecasting across large collections of correlated time series.

title: Think Globally, Act Locally: A Deep Neural Network Approach to High-Dimensional Time Series Forecasting

abstract: There are many surprising and perhaps counter-intuitive properties of optimization of deep neural networks. We propose and experimentally verify a unified phenomenological model of the loss landscape that incorporates many of them. High dimensionality plays a key role in our model. Our core idea is to model the loss landscape as a set of high dimensional \emph{wedges} that together form a large-scale, inter-connected structure and towards which optimization is drawn. We first show that hyperparameter choices such as learning rate, network width and $L_2$ regularization, affect the path optimizer takes through the landscape in similar ways, influencing the large scale curvature of the regions the optimizer explores. Finally, we predict and demonstrate new counter-intuitive properties of the loss-landscape. We show an existence of low loss subspaces connecting a set (not only a pair) of solutions, and verify it experimentally. Finally, we analyze recently popular ensembling techniques for deep networks in the light of our model.

paragraphs: Deep-network optimization exhibits behaviors that can be difficult to reconcile within a single picture of the loss landscape. This paper proposes a phenomenological model: a geometric description intended to organize observed behavior. High dimensionality is central, with interconnected high-dimensional wedges forming a large-scale structure that attracts optimization.

The authors experimentally examine how learning rate, network width, and L2 regularization affect the optimizer's path. They find that these choices influence the large-scale curvature of explored regions in similar ways. The proposed geometry therefore connects several apparently different training choices through their effects on where optimization travels.

The model also leads to predictions about connections among trained solutions. The paper demonstrates low-loss subspaces connecting a set of solutions, extending the idea of connections between only two solutions. It additionally interprets deep-network ensembling techniques through the same geometric perspective. The contribution is an experimentally supported organizing model that relates optimization paths, connected solutions, and ensembling within one account.
summary.tldr: An experimentally supported wedge-based model connects hyperparameter effects, optimization paths, and low-loss subspaces joining multiple neural-network solutions.

title: Large Scale Structure of Neural Network Loss Landscapes

abstract: Causal effect identification considers whether an interventional probability distribution can be uniquely determined from a passively observed distribution in a given causal structure. If the generating system induces context-specific independence (CSI) relations, the existing identification procedures and criteria based on do-calculus are inherently incomplete. We show that deciding causal effect non-identifiability is NP-hard in the presence of CSIs. Motivated by this, we design a calculus and an automated search procedure for identifying causal effects in the presence of CSIs. The approach is provably sound and it includes standard do-calculus as a special case. With the approach we can obtain identifying formulas that were unobtainable previously, and demonstrate that a small number of CSI-relations may be sufficient to turn a previously non-identifiable instance to identifiable.

paragraphs: Causal effect identification asks whether observational data and a specified causal structure uniquely determine the distribution produced by an intervention. This paper considers additional information in the form of context-specific independence: independence relationships that hold in particular contexts. Existing identification methods based on do-calculus are incomplete when these relationships are present.

The authors first show that deciding non-identifiability in the presence of context-specific independence is NP-hard. They then develop a calculus and an automated search procedure that use these relationships to identify causal effects. The calculus includes standard do-calculus as a special case, extending the reasoning tools available for deriving intervention formulas.

The approach is provably sound, meaning its derivations justify the effects it identifies. Soundness does not itself claim that the search can identify every identifiable effect. The authors obtain formulas unavailable to previous procedures and show that even a small number of context-specific independence relations may make a previously non-identifiable instance identifiable. Such information can therefore change what causal conclusions observational evidence supports.
summary.tldr: A sound extension of do-calculus uses context-specific independence to identify causal effects beyond the reach of previous procedures.

title: Identifying Causal Effects via Context-specific Independence Relations

abstract: The long-short-term memory (LSTM), though powerful, is memory and computa\x02tion expensive. To alleviate this problem, one approach is to compress its weights by quantization. However, existing quantization methods usually have inferior performance when used on LSTMs. In this paper, we first show theoretically that training a quantized LSTM is difficult because quantization makes the exploding gradient problem more severe, particularly when the LSTM weight matrices are large. We then show that the popularly used weight/layer/batch normalization schemes can help stabilize the gradient magnitude in training quantized LSTMs. Empirical results show that the normalized quantized LSTMs achieve significantly better results than their unnormalized counterparts. Their performance is also comparable with the full-precision LSTM, while being much smaller in size.

paragraphs: LSTMs can require substantial memory and computation, making weight quantization an attractive compression strategy. Yet quantization methods that compress weights often produce inferior results when applied to these networks. This paper investigates the training dynamics behind that performance loss and considers normalization as a way to address it.

The theoretical analysis shows that quantization makes exploding gradients more severe, particularly for large LSTM weight matrices. Exploding gradients create excessively large training signals, making weight updates difficult to control. The authors then show that commonly used weight, layer, and batch normalization schemes can help stabilize gradient magnitudes when training quantized LSTMs.

In the reported experiments, normalized quantized LSTMs perform significantly better than their unnormalized counterparts. They also achieve performance comparable to full-precision LSTMs while using much smaller models. The contribution links a specific theoretical explanation for training difficulty to a practical intervention. The results indicate that managing gradient behavior can preserve much of an LSTM’s predictive performance while retaining the size benefits of quantized weights.
summary.tldr: Normalization stabilizes gradients in quantized LSTMs, enabling much smaller models with performance comparable to full-precision networks in the reported experiments.

title: Normalization Helps Training of Quantized LSTM

abstract: We address the problem of credit assignment in reinforcement learning and explore fundamental questions regarding the way in which an agent can best use additional computation to propagate new information, by planning with internal models of the world to improve its predictions. Particularly, we work to understand the gains and peculiarities of planning employed as forethought via forward models or as hindsight operating with backward models. We establish the relative merits, limitations and complementary properties of both planning mechanisms in carefully constructed scenarios. Further, we investigate the best use of models in planning, primarily focusing on the selection of states in which predictions should be (re)-evaluated. Lastly, we discuss the issue of model estimation and highlight a spectrum of methods that stretch from environment dynamics predictors to planner-aware models.

paragraphs: Credit assignment in reinforcement learning concerns how new information should change an agent's earlier predictions. Internal world models let an agent spend additional computation on this process through planning. This paper asks how that computation is best used, comparing planning that looks forward with planning that reasons backward from later states.

Forward models support forethought by predicting what can happen next. Backward models support hindsight by reasoning about what could have preceded a state. Through carefully constructed scenarios, the authors establish merits, limitations, and complementary properties of these mechanisms. Their comparison examines how the direction of planning affects the propagation of information within an agent's predictions.

The paper also studies which states should be selected for prediction updates, making the allocation of planning effort a central question. It then considers model estimation across a spectrum from predictors of environmental dynamics to models designed with the planner in mind. Together, these investigations treat effective planning as a combination of model direction, update location, and model purpose.
summary.tldr: The paper examines how forward and backward planning complement one another in reinforcement-learning credit assignment.

title: Forethought and Hindsight in Credit Assignment

abstract: This paper focuses on estimating probability distributions over the set of 3D ro- tations (SO(3)) using deep neural networks. Learning to regress models to the set of rotations is inherently difficult due to differences in topology between R^N and SO(3). We overcome this issue by using a neural network to out- put the parameters for a matrix Fisher distribution since these parameters are homeomorphic to R^9 . By using a negative log likelihood loss for this distri- bution we get a loss which is convex with respect to the network outputs. By optimizing this loss we improve state-of-the-art on several challenging applica- ble datasets, namely Pascal3D+, ModelNet10-SO(3). Our code is available at https://github.com/Davmo049/Public_prob_orientation_estimation_with_matrix _fisher_distributions

paragraphs: Estimating three-dimensional orientation with a neural network involves a geometric mismatch: ordinary network outputs live in a Euclidean space, while rotations form the differently structured space SO(3). This paper addresses the issue by predicting a probability distribution over rotations. That formulation makes the output a probabilistic description of orientation.

The network outputs parameters of a matrix Fisher distribution. Their parameter space is homeomorphic to nine-dimensional Euclidean space, providing a compatible space for the network's outputs while the distribution itself describes rotations. The authors train with the distribution's negative log likelihood and show that this loss is convex with respect to those outputs.

The scope of that convexity statement is the predicted distribution parameters; it does not establish convexity of the entire neural-network training problem. Optimizing the proposed loss improves the state of the art on Pascal3D+ and ModelNet10-SO(3), according to the reported results. The contribution connects a rotation-aware probabilistic representation with a favorable output-level loss property and demonstrated orientation-estimation performance.
summary.tldr: Predicting matrix Fisher distributions provides a probabilistic rotation representation with a loss convex in network outputs and improved reported benchmark performance.

title: Probabilistic Orientation Estimation with Matrix Fisher Distributions

abstract: Language exhibits structure at different scales, ranging from subwords to words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents. To what extent do deep models capture information at these scales, and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy? We approach this question by focusing on individual neurons, analyzing the behavior of their activations at different timescales. We show that signal processing provides a natural framework for separating structure across scales, enabling us to 1) disentangle scale-specific information in existing embeddings and 2) train models to learn more about particular scales. Concretely, we apply spectral filters to the activations of a neuron across an input, producing filtered embeddings that perform well on part of speech tagging (word-level), dialog speech acts classification (utterance-level), or topic classification (document-level), while performing poorly on the other tasks. We also present a prism layer for training models, which uses spectral filters to constrain different neurons to model structure at different scales. Our proposed BERT + Prism model can better predict masked tokens using long-range context and produces multiscale representations that perform better at utterance- and document-level tasks. Our methods are general and readily applicable to other domains besides language, such as images, audio, and video.

title: Language Through a Prism: A Spectral Approach for Multiscale Language Representations

abstract: Noninvasive behavioral tracking of animals is crucial for many scientific investigations. Recent transfer learning approaches for behavioral tracking have considerably advanced the state of the art. Typically these methods treat each video frame and each object to be tracked independently. In this work, we improve on these methods (particularly in the regime of few training labels) by leveraging the rich spatiotemporal structures pervasive in behavioral video --- specifically, the spatial statistics imposed by physical constraints (e.g., paw to elbow distance), and the temporal statistics imposed by smoothness from frame to frame. We propose a probabilistic graphical model built on top of deep neural networks, Deep Graph Pose (DGP), to leverage these useful spatial and temporal constraints, and develop an efficient structured variational approach to perform inference in this model. The resulting semi-supervised model exploits both labeled and unlabeled frames to achieve significantly more accurate and robust tracking while requiring users to label fewer training frames. In turn, these tracking improvements enhance performance on downstream applications, including robust unsupervised segmentation of behavioral ``syllables,'' and estimation of interpretable ``disentangled'' low-dimensional representations of the full behavioral video. Open source code is available at \href{\CodeLink}{https://github.com/paninski-lab/deepgraphpose}.

In turn, these tracking improvements enhance performance on downstream applications, including robust unsupervised segmentation of behavioral ``syllables,'' and estimation of interpretable ``disentangled'' low-dimensional representations of the full behavioral video. Open source code is available at \href{\CodeLink}{https://github.com/paninski-lab/deepgraphpose}.

paragraphs: Tracking animal movement in video supports many scientific investigations, but manually labeling training frames takes effort. Existing transfer-learning approaches often predict each tracked object in each frame independently. This leaves useful information unused: body parts have constrained spatial relationships, and movement usually changes smoothly between neighboring frames.

Deep Graph Pose places a probabilistic graphical model on top of deep neural networks to incorporate these spatial and temporal relationships. A distance constraint between a paw and an elbow is one example of the physical structure it can exploit. The authors also develop an efficient structured variational inference method to make predictions within the combined model.

The resulting system learns from both labeled and unlabeled frames. The paper reports more accurate and robust tracking with fewer manually labeled examples, especially when training labels are scarce. These improvements also carry through to downstream behavior analysis, including unsupervised segmentation into recurring behavioral units and interpretable low-dimensional video representations. The approach matters because it turns the organization already present in animal motion into additional information for learning and prediction.
summary.tldr: Deep Graph Pose uses physical and temporal constraints to improve animal tracking while reducing the number of labeled video frames needed.

title: Deep Graph Pose: a semi-supervised deep graphical model for improved animal pose tracking

abstract: Exponential bounds on the estimation error are given for the plug-in estimator of weighted areas under the ROC curve. The bounds hold for single score functions and uniformly over classes of functions, whose complexity can be controlled by Gaussian or Rademacher averages. The results justify learning algorithms which select score functions to maximize the empirical partial area under the curve (pAUC). They also illustrate the use of some recent advances in the theory of nonlinear empirical processes.

paragraphs: A scoring function can be evaluated through weighted areas under its ROC curve, allowing evaluation to emphasize selected portions of that curve. This paper studies how accurately such quantities can be estimated from data. It analyzes a plug-in estimator, which substitutes empirical information for the unknown population quantities needed to calculate the weighted area.

The main results are exponential bounds on estimation error. They apply both to a single score function and uniformly across classes of score functions whose complexity can be controlled using Gaussian or Rademacher averages. Uniform control is especially relevant when the same data are used to compare and choose among candidate scoring functions, rather than simply evaluate one fixed choice.

These guarantees provide theoretical justification for learning algorithms that maximize empirical partial area under the curve. They connect an objective measured on available data to its population counterpart under the stated complexity conditions. The paper also demonstrates how advances in nonlinear empirical-process theory can be used to analyze this kind of evaluation and learning objective.
summary.tldr: Exponential estimation-error bounds justify learning score functions by maximizing empirical partial area under the ROC curve.

title: Estimating weighted areas under the ROC curve

abstract: Learning equivariant representations is a promising way to reduce sample and model complexity and improve the generalization performance of deep neural networks. The spherical CNNs are successful examples, producing SO(3)-equivariant representations of spherical inputs. There are two main types of spherical CNNs. The first type lifts the inputs to functions on the rotation group SO(3) and applies convolutions on the group, which are computationally expensive since SO(3) has one extra dimension. The second type applies convolutions directly on the sphere, which are limited to zonal (isotropic) filters, and thus have limited expressivity. In this paper, we present a new type of spherical CNN that allows anisotropic filters in an efficient way, without ever leaving the spherical domain. The key idea is to consider spin-weighted spherical functions, which were introduced in physics in the study of gravitational waves. These are complex-valued functions on the sphere whose phases change upon rotation. We define a convolution between spin-weighted functions and build a CNN based on it. The spin-weighted functions can also be interpreted as spherical vector fields, allowing applications to tasks where the inputs or outputs are vector fields. Experiments show that our method outperforms previous methods on tasks like classification of spherical images, classification of 3D shapes and semantic segmentation of spherical panoramas.

Existing approaches face a tradeoff: operating on the full rotation group adds a computational dimension, while convolving directly on the sphere restricts filters to isotropic forms. This paper introduces directional filters that remain within the spherical domain.

The key representation uses spin-weighted spherical functions, complex-valued functions whose phases change under rotation. The authors define a convolution for these functions and construct a neural network around it. This permits anisotropic filtering without moving computation to the higher-dimensional rotation group. The functions also admit an interpretation as spherical vector fields, allowing tasks with vector-field inputs or outputs.

The contribution combines a mathematical representation suited to rotation with a more expressive form of filtering on the sphere. The reported results show that this design can translate into better performance across several evaluated types of spherical data.
summary.tldr: Spin-weighted spherical CNNs enable efficient directional filtering on the sphere and outperform previous methods on the reported spherical-data tasks.

title: Spin-Weighted Spherical CNNs

abstract: In the context of learning to map an input $I$ to a function $h_I:\mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}$, two alternative methods are compared: (i) an embedding-based method, which learns a fixed function in which $I$ is encoded as a conditioning signal $e(I)$ and the learned function takes the form $h_I(x) = q(x,e(I))$, and (ii) hypernetworks, in which the weights $\theta_I$ of the function $h_I(x) = g(x;\theta_I)$ are given by a hypernetwork $f$ as $\theta_I=f(I)$. In this paper, we define the property of modularity as the ability to effectively learn a different function for each input instance $I$. For this purpose, we adopt an expressivity perspective of this property and extend the theory of~\cite{devore} and provide a lower bound on the complexity (number of trainable parameters) of neural networks as function approximators, by eliminating the requirements for the approximation method to be robust. Our results are then used to compare the complexities of $q$ and $g$, showing that under certain conditions and when letting the functions $e$ and $f$ be as large as we wish, $g$ can be smaller than $q$ by orders of magnitude. This sheds light on the modularity of hypernetworks in comparison with the embedding-based method. Besides, we show that for a structured target function, the overall number of trainable parameters in a hypernetwork is smaller by orders of magnitude than the number of trainable parameters of a standard neural network and an embedding method.

The authors define modularity as the ability to effectively learn a different function for each input instance.

They study this property through expressivity and parameter complexity. Their theoretical development supplies a lower bound on the number of trainable parameters needed for function approximation while removing a robustness requirement from earlier approximation theory. They then use the bound to compare the network receiving an embedding with the network whose weights are generated.

Under certain conditions, and allowing the embedding encoder and weight generator to be arbitrarily large, the generated network can be smaller by orders of magnitude. That comparison concerns the function-implementing networks. Separately, for a structured target function, the authors show an orders-of-magnitude reduction in total trainable parameters relative to standard networks and embedding methods.
summary.tldr: Expressivity results identify conditions where hypernetworks represent input-specific functions with substantially smaller networks or fewer total parameters.

title: On the Modularity of Hypernetworks

abstract: Time-reversal symmetry, which requires that the dynamics of a system should not change with the reversal of time axis, is a fundamental property that frequently holds in classical and quantum mechanics. In this paper, we propose a novel loss function that measures how well our ordinary differential equation (ODE) networks comply with this time-reversal symmetry; it is formally defined by the discrepancy in the time evolutions of ODE networks between forward and backward dynamics. Then, we design a new framework, which we name as Time-Reversal Symmetric ODE Networks (TRS-ODENs), that can learn the dynamics of physical systems more sample-efficiently by learning with the proposed loss function. We evaluate TRS-ODENs on several classical dynamics, and find they can learn the desired time evolution from observed noisy and complex trajectories. We also show that, even for systems that do not possess the full time-reversal symmetry, TRS-ODENs can achieve better predictive performances over baselines.

paragraphs: Time-reversal symmetry is a property of many physical systems: their dynamics follow the same governing behavior when the time axis is reversed appropriately. This paper uses that property to guide ordinary differential equation networks that learn physical dynamics from observed trajectories. The aim is to make learning more sample-efficient by incorporating a relevant physical structure.

The authors introduce a loss that measures disagreement between the network's forward and backward time evolutions. Training with this loss encourages consistency with time-reversal symmetry. Their resulting framework, Time-Reversal Symmetric ODE Networks, therefore uses the relationship between two directions of evolution as an additional learning signal.

Evaluations on several classical dynamical systems show that the framework can learn the desired evolution from noisy and complex trajectories. The authors also report better predictions than baselines for tested systems that do not have full time-reversal symmetry. This suggests that the proposed loss can remain useful when the symmetry is incomplete, with that extension supported by the reported experiments rather than a claim about every physical system.
summary.tldr: A loss comparing forward and backward dynamics helps ODE networks learn physical trajectories more sample-efficiently, including in tests with incomplete time-reversal symmetry.

title: Time-Reversal Symmetric ODE Network

abstract: Exponential families are widely used in machine learning; they include many distributions in continuous and discrete domains (e.g., Gaussian, Dirichlet, Poisson, and categorical distributions via the softmax transformation). Distributions in each of these families have fixed support. In contrast, for finite domains, there has been recent work on sparse alternatives to softmax (e.g., sparsemax and alpha-entmax), which have varying support, being able to assign zero probability to irrelevant categories. These discrete sparse mappings have been used for improving interpretability of neural attention mechanisms. This paper expands that work in two directions: first, we extend alpha-entmax to continuous domains, revealing a link with Tsallis statistics and deformed exponential families. Second, we introduce continuous-domain attention mechanisms, deriving efficient gradient backpropagation algorithms for alpha in {1,2}. Experiments on attention-based text classification, machine translation, and visual question answering illustrate the use of continuous attention in 1D and 2D, showing that it allows attending to time intervals and compact regions.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms often distribute weight over a finite set of items. Sparse alternatives to softmax can assign zero weight to irrelevant items, allowing the set of attended categories to vary. This paper extends that idea to continuous domains, where attention can describe regions of a continuum instead of only individual categories.

The authors extend alpha-entmax to continuous distributions and establish connections with Tsallis statistics and deformed exponential families. They also construct continuous-domain attention mechanisms and derive efficient gradient backpropagation algorithms for alpha values of one and two. These contributions connect the distributional formulation to the computations needed to train neural networks using it.

The mechanisms can attend to time intervals and compact spatial regions. The results demonstrate a different way to represent what a model attends to, extending sparse attention’s variable-support idea beyond finite lists and showing its use in several attention-based learning tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper extends sparse probability mappings to continuous domains, enabling trainable attention over intervals and compact regions.

title: Sparse and Continuous Attention Mechanisms

abstract: Fairness and robustness are critical elements of Trustworthy AI that need to be addressed together. Fairness is about learning an unbiased model while robustness is about learning from corrupted data, and it is known that addressing only one of them may have an adverse affect on the other. In this work, we propose a sample selection-based algorithm for fair and robust training. To this end, we formulate a combinatorial optimization problem for the unbiased selection of samples in the presence of data corruption. Observing that solving this optimization problem is strongly NP-hard, we propose a greedy algorithm that is efficient and effective in practice. Experiments show that our method obtains fairness and robustness that are better than or comparable to the state-of-the-art technique, both on synthetic and benchmark real datasets. Moreover, unlike other fair and robust training baselines, our algorithm can be used by only modifying the sampling step in batch selection without changing the training algorithm or leveraging additional clean data.

paragraphs: Fairness and robustness can interfere with one another: a method addressing bias alone may worsen learning from corrupted data, and vice versa. This paper approaches the two goals jointly through training-sample selection. The central question is which examples should enter training batches when the available data may be corrupted.

The authors formulate unbiased sample selection as a combinatorial optimization problem and show that solving it is strongly NP-hard. They then propose a greedy algorithm intended to make selection efficient and effective in practice. The resulting procedure changes the batch-sampling step without requiring a different training algorithm or additional clean data.

Experiments on synthetic data and real benchmark datasets show fairness and robustness that are better than or comparable to the state-of-the-art technique used in the comparison. These results support sample selection as a practical intervention point for addressing both goals. The computational finding also explains the role of the greedy method: it provides a usable approach to a selection problem whose exact solution is difficult.
summary.tldr: A greedy batch-selection method jointly addresses fairness and corrupted data without changing the training algorithm or requiring extra clean examples.

title: Sample Selection for Fair and Robust Training

abstract: Studies on self-supervised visual representation learning (SSL) improve encoder backbones to discriminate training samples without labels. While CNN encoders via SSL achieve comparable recognition performance to those via supervised learning, their network attention is under-explored for further improvement. Motivated by the transformers that explore visual attention effectively in recognition scenarios, we propose a CNN Attention REvitalization (CARE) framework to train attentive CNN encoders guided by transformers in SSL. The proposed CARE framework consists of a CNN stream (C-stream) and a transformer stream (T-stream), where each stream contains two branches. C-stream follows an existing SSL framework with two CNN encoders, two projectors, and a predictor. T-stream contains two transformers, two projectors, and a predictor. T-stream connects to CNN encoders and is in parallel to the remaining C-Stream. During training, we perform SSL in both streams simultaneously and use the T-stream output to supervise C-stream. The features from CNN encoders are modulated in T-stream for visual attention enhancement and become suitable for the SSL scenario. We use these modulated features to supervise C-stream for learning attentive CNN encoders. To this end, we revitalize CNN attention by using transformers as guidance. Experiments on several standard visual recognition benchmarks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, show that the proposed CARE framework improves CNN encoder backbones to the state-of-the-art performance.

Its CARE framework uses transformers to guide CNN encoders toward more attentive representations. The goal is to improve the CNN backbone through the way it is trained.

This makes transformer-processed features a source of guidance for the encoder's own representation learning. The authors report state-of-the-art CNN backbone performance, supporting the usefulness of transformer guidance across several visual recognition tasks.
summary.tldr: CARE uses a parallel transformer stream to guide self-supervised CNN training, improving learned visual attention and downstream recognition performance.

title: Revitalizing CNN Attention via Transformers in Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning

abstract: Recent experiments have shown that deep networks can approximate solutions to high-dimensional PDEs, seemingly escaping the curse of dimensionality. However, questions regarding the theoretical basis for such approximations, including the required network size remain open. In this paper, we investigate the representational power of neural networks for approximating solutions to linear elliptic PDEs with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We prove that when a PDE's coefficients are representable by small neural networks, the parameters required to approximate its solution scale polynomially with the input dimension $d$ and proportionally to the parameter counts of the coefficient networks. To this end, we develop a proof technique that simulates gradient descent (in an appropriate Hilbert space) by growing a neural network architecture whose iterates each participate as sub-networks in their (slightly larger) successors, and converge to the solution of the PDE.

In this paper, we investigate the representational power of neural networks for approximating solutions to linear elliptic PDEs with Dirichlet boundary conditions. paragraphs: The paper asks how large a neural network must be to approximate solutions of high-dimensional partial differential equations. It focuses on linear elliptic equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. The motivation is to provide a theoretical basis for experimental successes suggesting that neural networks can sometimes avoid the rapid growth in complexity associated with increasing dimension.

The main result depends on a structural assumption: the equation's coefficients must themselves be representable by small neural networks. Under this condition, the parameter count needed to approximate the solution grows polynomially with input dimension and proportionally to the coefficient networks' parameter counts. This connects the complexity of the solution representation to the representability of the equation's ingredients.

The proof simulates gradient descent in an appropriate Hilbert space by progressively growing a network. Each iterate becomes a subnetwork of its slightly larger successor, and the iterates converge to the PDE solution. The result establishes conditional representational efficiency for this class of equations, explaining why dimension alone need not dictate an exponential network size.
summary.tldr: For linear elliptic PDEs with compact neural coefficient representations, the paper proves polynomial-in-dimension network-size bounds for approximating solutions.

title: Parametric Complexity Bounds for Approximating PDEs with Neural Networks

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) promises to enable autonomous acquisition of complex behaviors for diverse agents. However, the success of current reinforcement learning algorithms is predicated on an often under-emphasised requirement -- each trial needs to start from a fixed initial state distribution. Unfortunately, resetting the environment to its initial state after each trial requires substantial amount of human supervision and extensive instrumentation of the environment which defeats the goal of autonomous acquisition of complex behaviors. In this work, we propose Value-accelerated Persistent Reinforcement Learning (VaPRL), which generates a curriculum of initial states such that the agent can bootstrap on the success of easier tasks to efficiently learn harder tasks. The agent also learns to reach the initial states proposed by the curriculum, minimizing the reliance on human interventions into the learning. We observe that VaPRL reduces the interventions required by three orders of magnitude compared to episodic RL while outperforming prior state-of-the art methods for reset-free RL both in terms of sample efficiency and asymptotic performance on a variety of simulated robotics problems.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often assumes that each trial begins from a fixed distribution of starting states. Making that happen can require people or specialized equipment to reset the environment repeatedly. This creates a practical obstacle to autonomous learning: the agent may learn its task while still depending on substantial outside help to begin each attempt.

Value-accelerated Persistent Reinforcement Learning, or VaPRL, addresses this dependence through a curriculum of starting states. The curriculum lets the agent build on success with easier tasks before tackling harder ones. Crucially, the agent also learns how to reach the proposed starting states, making preparation for another attempt part of what it learns.

Across simulated robotics problems, the authors observe three orders of magnitude fewer interventions than episodic reinforcement learning. VaPRL also outperforms prior reset-free methods in sample efficiency and eventual performance. These findings suggest that learning to arrange useful starting conditions can support both greater autonomy and effective task learning, with the reported evidence coming from simulation.
summary.tldr: VaPRL teaches agents to reach progressively useful starting states, greatly reducing human resets in simulated robotics.

title: Autonomous Reinforcement Learning via Subgoal Curricula

abstract: We investigate the issue of parameter estimation with nonuniform negative sampling for imbalanced data. We first prove that, with imbalanced data, the available information about unknown parameters is only tied to the relatively small number of positive instances, which justifies the usage of negative sampling. However, if the negative instances are subsampled to the same level of the positive cases, there is information loss. To maintain more information, we derive the asymptotic distribution of a general inverse probability weighted (IPW) estimator and obtain the optimal sampling probability that minimizes its variance. To further improve the estimation efficiency over the IPW method, we propose a likelihood-based estimator by correcting log odds for the sampled data and prove that the improved estimator has the smallest asymptotic variance among a large class of estimators. It is also more robust to pilot misspecification. We validate our approach on simulated data as well as a real click-through rate dataset with more than 0.3 trillion instances, collected over a period of a month. Both theoretical and empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: When positive events are rare, retaining every negative example can be expensive. The paper proves that information about unknown parameters is tied to the relatively small positive count, supporting negative sampling. However, reducing negatives to the same number as positives loses information.

The authors study nonuniform sampling, where different negatives have different inclusion probabilities. They derive the asymptotic distribution of an inverse probability weighted estimator and identify sampling probabilities that minimize its variance. This gives a principled way to choose which negatives to retain.

They then develop a likelihood estimator that corrects the sampled data's log odds. It has the smallest asymptotic variance within a large class of estimators and is more robust to misspecification of the pilot estimate. The optimality statement concerns that class and the asymptotic setting.

Validation includes simulations and a click-through dataset containing more than 0.3 trillion observations collected over a month. The theoretical and empirical results support careful sampling and correction as a way to improve estimation efficiency while retaining more of the information relevant to rare events.
summary.tldr: Optimized negative sampling and log-odds correction improve parameter estimation efficiency for rare-event data.

title: Nonuniform Negative Sampling and Log Odds Correction with Rare Events Data

abstract: To help agents reason about scenes in terms of their building blocks, we wish to extract the compositional structure of any given scene (in particular, the configuration and characteristics of objects comprising the scene). This problem is especially difficult when scene structure needs to be inferred while also estimating the agent’s location/viewpoint, as the two variables jointly give rise to the agent’s observations. We present an unsupervised variational approach to this problem. Leveraging the shared structure that exists across different scenes, our model learns to infer two sets of latent representations from RGB video input alone: a set of "object" latents, corresponding to the time-invariant, object-level contents of the scene, as well as a set of "frame" latents, corresponding to global time-varying elements such as viewpoint. This factorization of latents allows our model, SIMONe, to represent object attributes in an allocentric manner which does not depend on viewpoint. Moreover, it allows us to disentangle object dynamics and summarize their trajectories as time-abstracted, view-invariant, per-object properties. We demonstrate these capabilities, as well as the model's performance in terms of view synthesis and instance segmentation, across three procedurally generated video datasets.
originalAbstract: To help agents reason about scenes in terms of their building blocks, we wish to extract the compositional structure of any given scene (in particular, the configuration and characteristics of objects comprising the scene). This problem is especially difficult when scene structure needs to be inferred while also estimating the agent’s location/viewpoint, as the two variables jointly give rise to the agent’s observations. We present an unsupervised variational approach to this problem. Leveraging the shared structure that exists across different scenes, our model learns to infer two sets of latent representations from RGB video input alone: a set of "object" latents, corresponding to the time-invariant, object-level contents of the scene, as well as a set of "frame" latents, corresponding to global time-varying elements such as viewpoint. This factorization of latents allows our model, SIMONe, to represent object attributes in an allocentric manner which does not depend on viewpoint. Moreover, it allows us to disentangle object dynamics and summarize their trajectories as time-abstracted, view-invariant, per-object properties. We demonstrate these capabilities, as well as the model's performance in terms of view synthesis and instance segmentation, across three procedurally generated video datasets.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene as a collection of objects is difficult when the observer's viewpoint is also changing. The image reflects both what is in the scene and where it is viewed from. SIMONe addresses this joint problem by learning representations from RGB video alone through an unsupervised variational approach.

The model separates its latent representation into object and frame components. Object latents capture time-invariant information about individual scene elements, while frame latents capture global changes over time, such as viewpoint. Shared structure across scenes supports this separation. The resulting object descriptions are allocentric: they represent objects independently of the observer's particular view.

The same factorization lets the model separate object dynamics and summarize trajectories as per-object properties across time. The authors demonstrate these capabilities on three procedurally generated video datasets, alongside results for view synthesis and instance segmentation. The significance is that a video can supply both persistent object descriptions and changing frame information within one representation, supporting scene understanding beyond the appearance of any single image.
summary.tldr: SIMONe separates video into object and frame latents to learn viewpoint-independent object descriptions and trajectory summaries without supervision.

title: SIMONe: View-Invariant, Temporally-Abstracted Object Representations via Unsupervised Video Decomposition

abstract: Local treatment effects are a common quantity found throughout the empirical sciences that measure the treatment effect among those who comply with what they are assigned. Most of the literature is focused on estimating the average of such quantity, which is called the ``local average treatment effect (LATE)'' [Imbens and Angrist, 1994]). In this work, we study how to estimate the density of the local treatment effect, which is naturally more informative than its average. Specifically, we develop two families of methods for this task, namely, kernel-smoothing and model-based approaches. The kernel-smoothing-based approach estimates the density through some smooth kernel functions. The model-based approach estimates the density by projecting it onto a finite-dimensional density class. For both approaches, we derive the corresponding double/debiased machine learning-based estimators [Chernozhukov et al., 2018]. We further study the asymptotic convergence rates of the estimators and show that they are robust to the biases in nuisance function estimation. The use of the proposed methods is illustrated through both synthetic and a real dataset called 401(k).

paragraphs: Local treatment effects concern people who comply with the treatment they are assigned. Much existing work summarizes these effects with an average. This paper instead studies estimating their density, which provides information about the distribution of effects beyond a single central value. The change in target is the main motivation for the proposed methods.

The authors develop two approaches. One uses smooth kernel functions to estimate the density. The other projects the density onto a finite-dimensional class of candidate densities. These provide distinct ways to represent the distribution, and the paper derives double or debiased machine learning estimators for both approaches.

The analysis establishes asymptotic convergence rates and shows robustness to biases in estimated nuisance functions, the auxiliary functions needed by the estimation procedure. This matters because errors in those supporting estimates can affect the final treatment-effect estimate. Synthetic data and the 401(k) dataset illustrate the methods. Together, the contributions extend the estimation focus from an average local effect to a more informative distributional description.
summary.tldr: Two debiased machine learning approaches estimate the density of local treatment effects and provide robustness to nuisance-estimation biases.

title: Double Machine Learning Density Estimation for Local Treatment Effects with Instruments

abstract: Strong inductive biases give humans the ability to quickly learn to perform a variety of tasks. Although meta-learning is a method to endow neural networks with useful inductive biases, agents trained by meta-learning may sometimes acquire very different strategies from humans. We show that co-training these agents on predicting representations from natural language task descriptions and programs induced to generate such tasks guides them toward more human-like inductive biases. Human-generated language descriptions and program induction models that add new learned primitives both contain abstract concepts that can compress description length. Co-training on these representations result in more human-like behavior in downstream meta-reinforcement learning agents than less abstract controls (synthetic language descriptions, program induction without learned primitives), suggesting that the abstraction supported by these representations is key.

paragraphs: Meta-learning can give agents useful tendencies for learning new tasks, but those tendencies need not resemble human strategies. This paper investigates whether additional training on language and program representations can guide agents toward more human-like inductive biases. The central question is which kinds of task descriptions provide that guidance.

The authors co-train agents to predict representations derived from natural-language task descriptions and programs induced to generate the tasks. Human-written descriptions and programs with newly learned primitives can express abstract concepts that shorten descriptions. Those representations supply information about how tasks can be organized through reusable ideas.

Downstream meta-reinforcement learning agents show more human-like behavior with these representations than with less abstract controls: synthetic language descriptions and program induction without learned primitives. The comparison suggests that abstraction is an important contributor to the observed behavior. It does not establish that language or programs automatically produce human-like learning; the supported finding concerns the particular representations and controls examined, and the abstract concepts they make available during co-training.
summary.tldr: Co-training on human language and programs with learned abstractions produces more human-like meta-learning behavior than less abstract controls.

title: Using natural language and program abstractions to instill human inductive biases in machines

abstract: Learning world models from their sensory inputs enables agents to plan for actions by imagining their future outcomes. World models have previously been shown to improve sample-efficiency in simulated environments with few objects, but have not yet been applied successfully to environments with many objects. In environments with many objects, often only a small number of them are moving or interacting at the same time. In this paper, we investigate integrating this inductive bias of sparse interactions into the latent dynamics of world models trained from pixels. First, we introduce Variational Sparse Gating (VSG), a latent dynamics model that updates its feature dimensions sparsely through stochastic binary gates. Moreover, we propose a simplified architecture Simple Variational Sparse Gating (SVSG) that removes the deterministic pathway of previous models, resulting in a fully stochastic transition function that leverages the VSG mechanism. We evaluate the two model architectures in the BringBackShapes (BBS) environment that features a large number of moving objects and partial observability, demonstrating clear improvements over prior models.

paragraphs: World models learn to predict future observations so that agents can plan by imagining action outcomes. This paper focuses on environments containing many objects, where earlier world-model successes had been difficult to extend. Its starting observation is that, even in a crowded environment, relatively few objects may be moving or interacting at any one time.

Variational Sparse Gating builds this sparse-interaction assumption into a world model learned from pixels. Stochastic binary gates control which dimensions of the model's internal feature representation update. The architecture therefore gives the latent dynamics a way to change selected features rather than updating every dimension indiscriminately at each transition.

The authors also introduce Simple Variational Sparse Gating, which removes the deterministic pathway used in previous models and makes the transition function fully stochastic. Both architectures are evaluated in BringBackShapes, an environment with many moving objects and partial observability. The reported improvements over prior models support sparse latent updates as a useful modeling bias for this setting, including when the agent cannot observe the complete environment.
summary.tldr: Stochastic gates that selectively update latent features improve pixel-based world models in a many-object, partially observable environment.

title: Learning Robust Dynamics through Variational Sparse Gating

abstract: Commonly in reinforcement learning (RL), rewards are discounted over time using an exponential function to model time preference, thereby bounding the expected long-term reward. In contrast, in economics and psychology, it has been shown that humans often adopt a hyperbolic discounting scheme, which is optimal when a specific task termination time distribution is assumed. In this work, we propose a theory for continuous-time model-based reinforcement learning generalized to arbitrary discount functions. This formulation covers the case in which there is a non-exponential random termination time. We derive a Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation characterizing the optimal policy and describe how it can be solved using a collocation method, which uses deep learning for function approximation. Further, we show how the inverse RL problem can be approached, in which one tries to recover properties of the discount function given decision data. We validate the applicability of our proposed approach on two simulated problems. Our approach opens the way for the analysis of human discounting in sequential decision-making tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly reduces the weight of future rewards exponentially. Human time preferences often follow a hyperbolic pattern instead, and the abstract connects that pattern to a particular distribution of task termination times. This paper develops a continuous-time, model-based theory that accommodates arbitrary discount functions, including cases with non-exponential random termination.

The authors derive a Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation characterizing an optimal policy under this generalized formulation. They describe solving it through collocation with a deep learning function approximator. This provides both a mathematical characterization of the decision problem and a computational approach for working with discounting beyond the usual exponential form.

The paper also addresses an inverse question: how properties of a discount function might be recovered from observed decisions. Two simulated problems demonstrate the applicability of the proposed approach. These results open a route to studying human discounting in sequential decisions, while the reported validation remains in simulation. The central contribution is to make the discount function a more flexible part of both policy computation and behavioral inference.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time reinforcement learning framework supports arbitrary discount functions and inference of discounting properties from decisions.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Non-Exponential Discounting

abstract: Unsupervised out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is essential for the reliability of machine learning. In the literature, existing work has shown that higher-level semantics captured by hierarchical VAEs can be used to detect OOD instances.However, we empirically show that, the inherent issue of hierarchical VAEs, i.e., ``posterior collapse'', would seriously limit their capacity for OOD detection.Based on a thorough analysis for `posterior collapse'', we propose a novel informative hierarchical VAE to alleviate this issue through enhancing the connections between the data sample and its multi-layer stochastic latent representations during training.Furthermore, we propose a novel score function for unsupervised OOD detection, referred to as Adaptive Likelihood Ratio. With this score function, one can selectively aggregate the semantic information on multiple hidden layers of hierarchical VAEs, leading to a strong separability between in-distribution and OOD samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our method can significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art unsupervised OOD detection approaches.

paragraphs: Hierarchical variational autoencoders can capture higher-level semantic information useful for identifying inputs outside a model's training distribution. The paper finds that posterior collapse can seriously restrict this ability. In this context, the problem is that latent representations fail to retain enough useful connection to individual data samples.

The authors propose an informative hierarchical VAE that strengthens connections between each input and its stochastic latent representations across multiple layers during training. This aims to alleviate posterior collapse, making the hierarchy a more useful source of information for detection. The architecture change addresses the quality of the representations before they are combined into a detection decision.

A second contribution, the Adaptive Likelihood Ratio, selectively aggregates semantic information from multiple hidden layers. The resulting score is designed to separate familiar samples from out-of-distribution ones. Experiments show significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art unsupervised detection approaches. The findings support addressing both representation collapse and the way information from different levels is combined, rather than relying on hierarchical semantics alone.
summary.tldr: An informative hierarchical VAE and adaptive likelihood-ratio score improve unsupervised out-of-distribution detection in experiments.

title: Out-of-Distribution Detection with An Adaptive Likelihood Ratio on Informative Hierarchical VAE

abstract: Open-world object detection, as a more general and challenging goal, aims to recognize and localize objects described by arbitrary category names. The recent work GLIP formulates this problem as a grounding problem by concatenating all category names of detection datasets into sentences, which leads to inefficient interaction between category names. This paper presents DetCLIP, a paralleled visual-concept pre-training method for open-world detection by resorting to knowledge enrichment from a designed concept dictionary. To achieve better learning efficiency, we propose a novel paralleled concept formulation that extracts concepts separately to better utilize heterogeneous datasets (i.e., detection, grounding, and image-text pairs) for training. We further design a concept dictionary (with descriptions) from various online sources and detection datasets to provide prior knowledge for each concept. By enriching the concepts with their descriptions,we explicitly build the relationships among various concepts to facilitate the open-domain learning. The proposed concept dictionary is further used to provide sufficient negative concepts for the construction of the word-region alignment loss, and to complete labels for objects with missing descriptions in captions of image-text pair data. The proposed framework demonstrates strong zero-shot detection performances, e.g., on the LVIS dataset, our DetCLIP-T outperforms GLIP-T by 9.9% mAP and obtains a 13.5% improvement on rare categories compared to the fully-supervised model with the same backbone as ours.

paragraphs: Open-world detection seeks to locate objects described by arbitrary category names. DetCLIP addresses this by combining visual learning with a dictionary of concepts and their descriptions. Its motivation includes an inefficiency in GLIP's formulation, which joins detection category names into sentences and thereby introduces interactions among those names.

DetCLIP processes concepts separately, allowing training to draw on detection data, grounding data, and image-text pairs. The concept dictionary supplies descriptive prior knowledge and explicitly connects related concepts. It also provides negative concepts for learning which words match which image regions, and helps complete labels for objects omitted from image captions.

The reported zero-shot results show that this combination improves detection in the evaluated setting. On LVIS, DetCLIP-T exceeds GLIP-T by 9.9% mAP and reports a 13.5% improvement on rare categories over a fully supervised model with the same backbone. These findings support using structured concept descriptions and heterogeneous training data to improve recognition beyond a fixed category vocabulary.
summary.tldr: DetCLIP combines separately processed visual concepts with a descriptive dictionary to improve zero-shot object detection.

title: DetCLIP: Dictionary-Enriched Visual-Concept Paralleled Pre-training for Open-world Detection

abstract: The Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm, which consists of alternating between a few local stochastic gradient updates at client nodes, followed by a model averaging update at the server, is perhaps the most commonly used method in Federated Learning. Notwithstanding its simplicity, several empirical studies have illustrated that the model output by FedAvg leads to a model that generalizes well to new unseen tasks after a few fine-tuning steps. This surprising performance of such a simple method, however, is not fully understood from a theoretical point of view. In this paper, we formally investigate this phenomenon in the multi-task linear regression setting. We show that the reason behind the generalizability of the FedAvg output is FedAvg’s power in learning the common data representation among the clients’ tasks, by leveraging the diversity among client data distributions via multiple local updates between communication rounds. We formally establish the iteration complexity required by the clients for proving such result in the setting where the underlying shared representation is a linear map. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result showing that FedAvg learns an expressive representation in any setting. Moreover, we show that multiple local updates between communication rounds are necessary for representation learning, as distributed gradient methods that make only one local update between rounds provably cannot recover the ground-truth representation in the linear setting, and empirically yield neural network representations that generalize drastically worse to new clients than those learned by FedAvg trained on heterogeneous image classification datasets.

paragraphs: Federated Averaging alternates several local learning updates at clients with model averaging at a server. This paper investigates why that can happen through a theoretical study of multi-task linear regression.

Experiments on heterogeneous image-classification datasets likewise find substantially worse transfer to new clients from single-update neural-network representations. The formal necessity claim belongs to the linear setting, while the image results provide empirical evidence of a related distinction.
summary.tldr: In a shared linear-representation setting, multiple local FedAvg updates enable representation learning that helps explain adaptation to new tasks.

title: FedAvg with Fine Tuning: Local Updates Lead to Representation Learning

abstract: Proving algorithm-dependent generalization error bounds for gradient-type optimization methods has attracted significant attention recently in learning theory. However, most existing trajectory-based analyses require either restrictive assumptions on the learning rate (e.g., fast decreasing learning rate), or continuous injected noise (such as the Gaussian noise in Langevin dynamics). In this paper, we introduce a new discrete data-dependent prior to the PAC-Bayesian framework, and prove a high probability generalization bound of order $O(\frac{1}{n}\cdot \sum_{t=1}^T(\gamma_t/\varepsilon_t)^2\left\|{\mathrm{g}_t}\right\|^2)$ for Floored GD (i.e. a version of gradient descent with precision level $\varepsilon_t$), where $n$ is the number of training samples, $\gamma_t$ is the learning rate at step $t$, $\mathrm{g}_t$ is roughly the difference of the gradient computed using all samples and that using only prior samples. $\left\|{\mathrm{g}_t}\right\|$ is upper bounded by and and typical much smaller than the gradient norm $\left\|{\nabla f(W_t)}\right\|$. We remark that our bound holds for nonconvex and nonsmooth scenarios. Moreover, our theoretical results provide numerically favorable upper bounds of testing errors (e.g., $0.037$ on MNIST). Using similar technique, we can also obtain new generalization bounds for a certain variant of SGD. Furthermore, we study the generalization bounds for gradient Langevin Dynamics (GLD). Using the same framework with a carefully constructed continuous prior, we show a new high probability generalization bound of order $O(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{L^2}{n^2}\sum_{t=1}^T(\gamma_t/\sigma_t)^2)$ for GLD. The new $1/n^2$ rate is due to the concentration of the difference between the gradient of training samples and that of the prior.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds seek to connect a model's training procedure to its performance beyond the training data. Existing analyses of optimization trajectories often require restrictive learning-rate schedules or continuously injected noise. This paper develops PAC-Bayesian analyses using specially constructed priors to obtain bounds for several gradient-based methods.

For Floored GD, a version of gradient descent with a specified precision level, the authors introduce a discrete, data-dependent prior. The resulting high-probability bound depends on accumulated squared gradient differences, scaled by learning rates and precision. These differences compare gradients from all training samples with gradients from prior samples and can be much smaller than full gradient norms. The bound covers nonconvex and nonsmooth settings.

The authors report numerically favorable test-error upper bounds, including 0.037 on MNIST, and extend the technique to a variant of stochastic gradient descent. A continuous-prior construction also yields a new bound for gradient Langevin dynamics. Its accumulated trajectory term scales with inverse sample size squared, alongside a separate inverse-sample-size term.
summary.tldr: Carefully constructed PAC-Bayesian priors yield new generalization bounds based on gradient differences for several optimization methods.

title: Generalization Bounds for Gradient Methods via Discrete and Continuous Prior

abstract: The bias-variance trade-off is a well-known problem in machine learning that only gets more pronounced the less available data there is. In active learning, where labeled data is scarce or difficult to obtain, neglecting this trade-off can cause inefficient and non-optimal querying, leading to unnecessary data labeling. In this paper, we focus on active learning with Gaussian Processes (GPs). For the GP, the bias-variance trade-off is made by optimization of the two hyperparameters: the length scale and noise-term. Considering that the optimal mode of the joint posterior of the hyperparameters is equivalent to the optimal bias-variance trade-off, we approximate this joint posterior and utilize it to design two new acquisition functions. The first one is a Bayesian variant of Query-by-Committee (B-QBC), and the second is an extension that explicitly minimizes the predictive variance through a Query by Mixture of Gaussian Processes (QB-MGP) formulation. Across six simulators, we empirically show that B-QBC, on average, achieves the best marginal likelihood, whereas QB-MGP achieves the best predictive performance. We show that incorporating the bias-variance trade-off in the acquisition functions mitigates unnecessary and expensive data labeling.

paragraphs: Active learning selects which examples should receive labels, making the quality of each selection important when labeling is expensive. This paper studies selection with Gaussian processes. It focuses on the balance between bias and variance, which becomes particularly consequential when only a small amount of labeled data is available.

The approach represents uncertainty jointly over the Gaussian process length scale and noise term, the two hyperparameters used here to control that balance. It approximates their joint posterior and uses it to construct two acquisition functions, which score possible queries. Bayesian Query-by-Committee uses this uncertainty in a committee formulation; Query by Mixture of Gaussian Processes explicitly targets lower predictive variance.

Across six simulators, Bayesian Query-by-Committee obtains the best marginal likelihood on average, while the mixture-based method achieves the best predictive performance. These are distinct empirical outcomes for the two selection objectives. The findings support accounting for the bias-variance trade-off when choosing new labels, helping avoid expensive queries that contribute less to the learning task.
summary.tldr: Two Gaussian-process acquisition functions use uncertainty over hyperparameters to improve active learning and reduce unnecessary labeling.

title: Bayesian Active Learning with Fully Bayesian Gaussian Processes

abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models on downstream tasks has been adopted in a variety of domains recently. However, it is costly to update the entire parameter set of large pre-trained models. Although recently proposed parameter-efficient transfer learning (PETL) techniques allow updating a small subset of parameters (e.g. only using 2% of parameters) inside a pre-trained backbone network for a new task, they only reduce the training memory requirement by up to 30%. This is because the gradient computation for the trainable parameters still requires back-propagation through the large pre-trained backbone model. To address this, we propose Ladder Side-Tuning (LST), a new PETL technique that can reduce training memory requirements by more substantial amounts. Unlike existing parameter-efficient methods that insert additional parameters inside backbone networks, we train a ladder side network, a small and separate network that takes intermediate activations as input via shortcut connections (ladders) from backbone networks and makes predictions. LST has significantly lower memory requirements than previous methods, because it does not require back-propagation through the backbone network, but instead only through the side network and ladder connections. We evaluate our method with various models (T5 and CLIP-T5) on both natural language processing (GLUE) and vision-and-language (VQA, GQA, NLVR2, MSCOCO) tasks. LST saves 69% of the memory costs to fine-tune the whole network, while other methods only save 26% of that in similar parameter usages (hence, 2.7x more memory savings). Moreover, LST achieves higher accuracy than Adapter and LoRA in a low-memory regime. To further show the advantage of this better memory efficiency, we also apply LST to larger T5 models (T5-large, T5-3B), attaining better GLUE performance than full fine-tuning and other PETL methods. The trend also holds in the experiments on vision-and-language tasks, where LST achieves similar accuracy to other PETL methods when training a similar number of parameters while also having 2.7x more memory savings. paragraphs: Updating only a small fraction of a pretrained model’s parameters does not necessarily produce equally large training-memory savings. Ladder Side-Tuning addresses this distinction between the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed to train them.
