Backpropagation runs through the side network and ladder connections, avoiding the need to backpropagate through the backbone. The architecture therefore changes the gradient-computation path as well as reducing the trainable parameter count.

title: LST: Ladder Side-Tuning for Parameter and Memory Efficient Transfer Learning

abstract: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) encoding continuous multi-media data via multi-layer perceptrons has shown undebatable promise in various computer vision tasks. Despite many successful applications, editing and processing an INR remains intractable as signals are represented by latent parameters of a neural network. Existing works manipulate such continuous representations via processing on their discretized instance, which breaks down the compactness and continuous nature of INR. In this work, we present a pilot study on the question: how to directly modify an INR without explicit decoding? We answer this question by proposing an implicit neural signal processing network, dubbed INSP-Net, via differential operators on INR. Our key insight is that spatial gradients of neural networks can be computed analytically and are invariant to translation, while mathematically we show that any continuous convolution filter can be uniformly approximated by a linear combination of high-order differential operators. With these two knobs, INSP-Net instantiates the signal processing operator as a weighted composition of computational graphs corresponding to the high-order derivatives of INRs, where the weighting parameters can be data-driven learned. Based on our proposed INSP-Net, we further build the first Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that implicitly runs on INRs, named INSP-ConvNet. Our experiments validate the expressiveness of INSP-Net and INSP-ConvNet in fitting low-level image and geometry processing kernels (e.g. blurring, deblurring, denoising, inpainting, and smoothening) as well as for high-level tasks on implicit fields such as image classification.

paragraphs: An implicit neural representation stores a continuous signal in a neural network's parameters. Although this can be compact, editing the signal is difficult. Converting it into discrete samples for processing sacrifices its continuous representation. This paper studies how to process such signals directly through the network.

INSP-Net builds processing operators from spatial derivatives of the implicit representation. These derivatives can be computed analytically. The authors show that continuous convolution filters can be uniformly approximated by linear combinations of higher-order differential operators. INSP-Net turns this result into weighted combinations of derivative computation graphs, with weights that can be learned from data.

Experiments support the expressiveness of both approaches for image and geometry processing, including blurring, denoising, inpainting, and smoothing, as well as image classification on implicit fields. The central contribution is a mathematical and computational route for manipulating continuous neural signals without first explicitly decoding them into a discrete representation.
summary.tldr: INSP-Net processes implicit neural signals directly by learning combinations of their spatial derivatives.

title: Signal Processing for Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: We present Neural Shape Deformation Priors, a novel method for shape manipulation that predicts mesh deformations of non-rigid objects from user-provided handle movements. State-of-the-art methods cast this problem as an optimization task, where the input source mesh is iteratively deformed to minimize an objective function according to hand-crafted regularizers such as ARAP. In this work, we learn the deformation behavior based on the underlying geometric properties of a shape, while leveraging a large-scale dataset containing a diverse set of non-rigid deformations. Specifically, given a source mesh and desired target locations of handles that describe the partial surface deformation, we predict a continuous deformation field that is defined in 3D space to describe the space deformation. To this end, we introduce transformer-based deformation networks that represent a shape deformation as a composition of local surface deformations. It learns a set of local latent codes anchored in 3D space, from which we can learn a set of continuous deformation functions for local surfaces. Our method can be applied to challenging deformations and generalizes well to unseen deformations. We validate our approach in experiments using the DeformingThing4D dataset, and compare to both classic optimization-based and recent neural network-based methods.

paragraphs: When a user moves a few handles on a three-dimensional object, a shape-editing system must determine how the rest of its surface should deform. Common approaches repeatedly optimize the mesh using manually designed deformation regularizers. This paper instead learns deformation behavior from shape geometry and a large dataset containing varied non-rigid deformations.

Given a source mesh and target handle positions, the method predicts a continuous deformation field throughout three-dimensional space. A transformer-based network represents the overall deformation by composing local surface deformations. It learns local latent codes anchored at positions in space, then uses those codes to define continuous deformation functions for the corresponding surface regions.

The authors evaluate the method on DeformingThing4D and compare it with both traditional optimization methods and recent neural approaches. They report that it handles challenging shape changes and generalizes well to unseen deformations. The contribution is a learned geometric prior that translates partial user instructions into broader surface changes through a spatially continuous representation.
summary.tldr: A transformer learns local deformation functions that combine into continuous mesh edits guided by user-moved handles.

title: Neural Shape Deformation Priors

abstract: Cellular sheaves equip graphs with a ``geometrical'' structure by assigning vector spaces and linear maps to nodes and edges. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) implicitly assume a graph with a trivial underlying sheaf. This choice is reflected in the structure of the graph Laplacian operator, the properties of the associated diffusion equation, and the characteristics of the convolutional models that discretise this equation. In this paper, we use cellular sheaf theory to show that the underlying geometry of the graph is deeply linked with the performance of GNNs in heterophilic settings and their oversmoothing behaviour. By considering a hierarchy of increasingly general sheaves, we study how the ability of the sheaf diffusion process to achieve linear separation of the classes in the infinite time limit expands. At the same time, we prove that when the sheaf is non-trivial, discretised parametric diffusion processes have greater control than GNNs over their asymptotic behaviour. On the practical side, we study how sheaves can be learned from data. The resulting sheaf diffusion models have many desirable properties that address the limitations of classical graph diffusion equations (and corresponding GNN models) and obtain competitive results in heterophilic settings. Overall, our work provides new connections between GNNs and algebraic topology and would be of interest to both fields.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks spread information between connected nodes. This paper examines how the geometry underlying that process affects heterophily, where connected nodes may belong to different classes, and oversmoothing, where repeated propagation reduces useful distinctions. It uses cellular sheaves, which attach vector spaces and linear maps to nodes and edges, to describe richer graph geometries.

The authors interpret conventional GNNs as implicitly using a trivial sheaf. They then study increasingly general sheaves and show how this expands the ability of diffusion to keep classes linearly separable in the infinite-time limit. They also prove that discretized, parameterized diffusion with a nontrivial sheaf offers greater control over long-run behavior than conventional GNNs.

The practical part investigates learning these sheaves from data and builds corresponding diffusion models. Those models address limitations of classical graph diffusion and obtain competitive results in heterophilic settings. The work connects a mathematical account of long-term information propagation with a trainable modeling approach, showing how changing graph geometry can change what repeated message passing preserves.
summary.tldr: Learned sheaf geometry gives graph diffusion greater control over class separation and long-run behavior, with competitive results on heterophilic graphs.

title: Neural Sheaf Diffusion: A Topological Perspective on Heterophily and Oversmoothing in GNNs

abstract: The strong lottery ticket hypothesis has highlighted the potential for training deep neural networks by pruning, which has inspired interesting practical and theoretical insights into how neural networks can represent functions. For networks with ReLU activation functions, it has been proven that a target network with depth L can be approximated by the subnetwork of a randomly initialized neural network that has double the target's depth 2L and is wider by a logarithmic factor. We show that a depth L+1 is sufficient. This result indicates that we can expect to find lottery tickets at realistic, commonly used depths while only requiring logarithmic overparametrization. Our novel construction approach applies to a large class of activation functions and is not limited to ReLUs. Code is available on Github (RelationalML/LT-existence).

paragraphs: The strong lottery ticket hypothesis concerns whether a randomly initialized neural network already contains a subnetwork that approximates a desired target network. This perspective makes pruning a way to reveal useful computation already present in the initial weights. A central theoretical question is how much larger the random network must be for such a subnetwork to exist.

For ReLU networks, earlier results established that a target of depth L could be approximated inside a random network of depth 2L with a logarithmic increase in width. This paper improves the sufficient depth to L+1 while retaining logarithmic overparameterization. Only one additional layer is needed in the new construction, bringing the depth requirement closer to architectures commonly used in practice.

The authors' construction also applies to a large class of activation functions, extending beyond ReLU. The result broadens the theoretical settings in which suitable subnetworks can exist without substantial extra depth. Its main contribution is an existence and approximation result: it establishes sufficient network size for lottery tickets, rather than reporting that any particular practical pruning procedure will reliably find them.
summary.tldr: A new construction shows that depth L+1 can suffice to contain lottery-ticket approximations of depth-L networks, with logarithmic overparameterization and broad activation support.

title: Most Activation Functions Can Win the Lottery Without Excessive Depth

abstract: Building generally capable agents is a grand challenge for deep reinforcement learning (RL). To approach this challenge practically, we outline two key desiderata: 1) to facilitate generalization, exploration should be task agnostic; 2) to facilitate scalability, exploration policies should collect large quantities of data without costly centralized retraining. Combining these two properties, we introduce the reward-free deployment efficiency setting, a new paradigm for RL research. We then present CASCADE, a novel approach for self-supervised exploration in this new setting. CASCADE seeks to learn a world model by collecting data with a population of agents, using an information theoretic objective inspired by Bayesian Active Learning. CASCADE achieves this by specifically maximizing the diversity of trajectories sampled by the population through a novel cascading objective. We provide theoretical intuition for CASCADE which we show in a tabular setting improves upon naïve approaches that do not account for population diversity. We then demonstrate that CASCADE collects diverse task-agnostic datasets and learns agents that generalize zero-shot to novel, unseen downstream tasks on Atari, MiniGrid, Crafter and the DM Control Suite. Code and videos are available at https://ycxuyingchen.github.io/cascade/

paragraphs: Learning broadly useful agents requires exploration that is not tied to one reward function. It also requires collecting substantial experience without repeatedly paying for centralized retraining. The paper combines these goals in a reward-free deployment efficiency setting, asking how exploration can support later tasks while using only a handful of deployments.

CASCADE collects data through a population of agents to learn a world model. Its information-theoretic objective is inspired by Bayesian active learning, and its cascading objective specifically encourages diversity among the population's trajectories. The design makes the variety of the population's collective experience an explicit part of exploration.

The authors provide theoretical intuition and demonstrate an advantage in a tabular setting over naive approaches that ignore population diversity. Across Atari, MiniGrid, Crafter, and the DM Control Suite, they also report diverse task-agnostic datasets and agents that generalize zero-shot to unseen downstream tasks. These findings support coordinating exploration around diverse experience as a route to more reusable world models and agents.
summary.tldr: CASCADE coordinates diverse reward-free exploration across a population to learn world models and support zero-shot transfer to unseen tasks.

title: Learning General World Models in a Handful of Reward-Free Deployments

abstract: With the emergence of varied visual navigation tasks (e.g., image-/object-/audio-goal and vision-language navigation) that specify the target in different ways, the community has made appealing advances in training specialized agents capable of handling individual navigation tasks well. Given plenty of embodied navigation tasks and task-specific solutions, we address a more fundamental question: can we learn a single powerful agent that masters not one but multiple navigation tasks concurrently? First, we propose VXN, a large-scale 3D dataset that instantiates~four classic navigation tasks in standardized, continuous, and audiovisual-rich environments. Second, we propose Vienna, a versatile embodied navigation agent that simultaneously learns to perform the four navigation tasks with one model. Building upon a full-attentive architecture, Vienna formulates various navigation tasks as a unified, parse-and-query procedure: the target description, augmented with four task embeddings, is comprehensively interpreted into a set of diversified goal vectors, which are refined as the navigation progresses, and used as queries to retrieve supportive context from episodic history for decision making. This enables the reuse of knowledge across navigation tasks with varying input domains/modalities. We empirically demonstrate that, compared with learning each visual navigation task individually, our multitask agent achieves comparable or even better performance with reduced complexity.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether one embodied agent can handle navigation goals expressed in different ways. Existing specialized agents address individual tasks such as navigating toward an image, an object, a sound, or a language-described goal. The authors introduce VXN, a large-scale dataset bringing four navigation tasks into standardized continuous environments with audiovisual information.

Their agent, Vienna, uses one attention-based model for all four tasks. It interprets a target description together with task embeddings into several goal vectors. As navigation proceeds, it refines these vectors and uses them to query the episode's history for information that supports the next decision.

This shared procedure lets knowledge be reused across tasks with different input modalities. Empirical comparisons show that the multitask agent achieves performance comparable to or better than learning the tasks individually, with reduced complexity. The contribution combines a common evaluation environment with a common decision-making architecture, demonstrating the feasibility of sharing navigation capabilities across the four studied tasks.
summary.tldr: Vienna handles four navigation tasks with one model, matching or improving on separate task learning while reducing complexity.

title: Towards Versatile Embodied Navigation

abstract: In this work, we investigate Active Vision Reinforcement Learning (ActiveVision-RL), where an embodied agent simultaneously learns action policy for the task while also controlling its visual observations in partially observable environments. We denote the former as motor policy and the latter as sensory policy. For example, humans solve real world tasks by hand manipulation (motor policy) together with eye movements (sensory policy). ActiveVision-RL poses challenges on coordinating two policies given their mutual influence. We propose SUGARL, Sensorimotor Understanding Guided Active Reinforcement Learning, a framework that models motor and sensory policies separately, but jointly learns them using with an intrinsic sensorimotor reward. This learnable reward is assigned by sensorimotor reward module, incentivizes the sensory policy to select observations that are optimal to infer its own motor action, inspired by the sensorimotor stage of humans. Through a series of experiments, we show the effectiveness of our method across a range of observability conditions and its adaptability to existed RL algorithms. The sensory policies learned through our method are observed to exhibit effective active vision strategies.

paragraphs: An agent with limited vision must decide both how to act and what to observe. These decisions influence each other: the selected view affects the next action, while actions change which observations are useful. The paper studies this coupled problem in partially observable environments, separating task actions into a motor policy and observation choices into a sensory policy.

Its framework, SUGARL, represents the two policies separately but learns them together. A learned reward module supplies an intrinsic sensorimotor reward that encourages the sensory policy to select observations useful for inferring the agent’s own motor action. This gives observation selection a training signal connected to what the agent does.

Experiments report effectiveness across multiple levels of observability and show that the framework can work with existing reinforcement learning algorithms. The learned sensory policies also exhibit effective active vision strategies. These findings support using the relationship between seeing and acting to coordinate the policies, rather than treating observation selection as an unrelated prediction task.
summary.tldr: SUGARL jointly trains action and observation policies using a learned reward that connects visual choices to the agent’s actions.

title: Active Vision Reinforcement Learning under Limited Visual Observability

abstract: Multi-view clustering (MVC) based on non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and its variants have attracted much attention due to their advantages in clustering interpretability. However, existing NMF-based multi-view clustering methods perform NMF on each view respectively and ignore the impact of between-view. Thus, they can't well exploit the within-view spatial structure and between-view complementary information. To resolve this issue, we present orthogonal non-negative tensor factorization (Orth-NTF) and develop a novel multi-view clustering based on Orth-NTF with one-side orthogonal constraint. Our model directly performs Orth-NTF on the 3rd-order tensor which is composed of anchor graphs of views. Thus, our model directly considers the between-view relationship. Moreover, we use the tensor Schatten $p$-norm regularization as a rank approximation of the 3rd-order tensor which characterizes the cluster structure of multi-view data and exploits the between-view complementary information. In addition, we provide an optimization algorithm for the proposed method and prove mathematically that the algorithm always converges to the stationary KKT point. Extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets indicate that our proposed method is able to achieve satisfactory clustering performance.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples using several representations of the same data. Existing methods based on non-negative matrix factorization often factorize each view separately, which can miss relationships between views. This paper develops a tensor-based approach intended to capture both structure within each view and complementary information across the views during clustering.

The method constructs a third-order tensor from the views' anchor graphs and directly applies orthogonal non-negative tensor factorization with a one-sided orthogonality constraint. It also uses tensor Schatten p-norm regularization as an approximation to tensor rank. These choices make cross-view relationships part of the joint representation used to characterize cluster structure.

The authors provide an optimization algorithm and prove that it converges to a stationary point satisfying the KKT conditions. This is a stationarity guarantee, rather than a claim of reaching a global optimum. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets report satisfactory clustering performance, supporting the use of joint tensor factorization to exploit information that separate view-by-view factorizations can overlook.
summary.tldr: Joint tensor factorization captures relationships across data views for clustering, with a proven stationary-point convergence guarantee.

title: Orthogonal Non-negative Tensor Factorization based Multi-view Clustering

abstract: Peer review lies at the core of the academic process, but even well-intentioned reviewers can still provide noisy ratings. While ranking papers by average ratings may reduce noise, varying noise levels and systematic biases stemming from ``cheap'' signals (e.g. author identity, proof length) can lead to unfairness. Detecting and correcting bias is challenging, as ratings are subjective and unverifiable. Unlike previous works relying on prior knowledge or historical data, we propose a one-shot noise calibration process without any prior information. We ask reviewers to predict others' scores and use these predictions for calibration. Assuming reviewers adjust their predictions according to the noise, we demonstrate that the calibrated score results in a more robust ranking compared to average ratings, even with varying noise levels and biases.In detail, we show that the error probability of the calibrated score approaches zero as the number of reviewers increases and is significantly lower compared to average ratings when the number of reviewers is small.

paragraphs: Averaging peer-review scores can reduce random noise, but it can still produce unfair rankings when reviewers have different noise levels or share systematic biases. Signals such as author identity or proof length can influence ratings without reliably reflecting paper quality. Because these judgments are subjective and unverifiable, correcting them is especially challenging.

The proposed procedure asks reviewers to predict the scores that other reviewers will give. It then uses those predictions to calibrate the ratings in a single round, without historical data or prior information. The key assumption is that reviewers adjust their predictions according to the noise. The theoretical results depend on this relationship between predictions and noisy judgments.

Under that assumption, the calibrated scores yield more robust rankings than simple averages despite varying noise and biases. The authors show that ranking error probability tends to zero as reviewer numbers grow and is substantially lower than averaging when reviewer numbers are small. The contribution is a conditional way to extract useful calibration information from reviewers’ expectations.
summary.tldr: Reviewer predictions of others’ scores enable prior-free calibration with stronger ranking guarantees when those predictions adjust appropriately to noise.

title: Calibrating “Cheap Signals” in Peer Review without a Prior

abstract: Optimal Transport is a popular distance metric for measuring similarity between distributions. Exact and approximate combinatorial algorithms for computing the optimal transport distance are hard to parallelize. This has motivated the development of numerical solvers (e.g. Sinkhorn method) that can exploit GPU parallelism and produce approximate solutions. We introduce the first parallel combinatorial algorithm to find an additive $\varepsilon$-approximation of the OT distance. The parallel complexity of our algorithm is $O(\log(n)/ \varepsilon^2)$ where $n$ is the total support size for the input distributions. In Massive Parallel Computation (MPC) frameworks such as Hadoop and MapReduce, our algorithm computes an $\varepsilon$-approximate transport plan in $O(\log (\log (n/\varepsilon))/\varepsilon^2)$ rounds with $O(n/\varepsilon)$ space per machine; all prior algorithms in the MPC framework take $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds. We also provide a GPU-friendly matrix-based interpretation of our algorithm where each step of the algorithm is row or column manipulation of the matrix. Experiments suggest that our combinatorial algorithm is faster than the state-of-the-art approximate solvers in the GPU, especially for higher values of $n$.

This has encouraged numerical approaches that fit GPU computation more naturally.

The paper introduces a parallel combinatorial algorithm with an additive error guarantee: its estimate is within an error tolerance ε of the optimal transport distance. Its parallel complexity is O(log(n)/ε²), where n is the combined support size. summary.tldr: A parallel combinatorial optimal transport algorithm provides approximation guarantees and shows promising GPU speed advantages on larger inputs.

title: A Combinatorial Algorithm for Approximating the Optimal Transport in the Parallel and MPC Settings

abstract: The rise in malicious usage of large language models, such as fake content creation and academic plagiarism, has motivated the development of approaches that identify AI-generated text, including those based on watermarking or outlier detection. However, the robustness of these detection algorithms to paraphrases of AI-generated text remains unclear. To stress test these detectors, we build a 11B parameter paraphrase generation model (DIPPER) that can paraphrase paragraphs, condition on surrounding context, and control lexical diversity and content reordering. Paraphrasing text generated by three large language models (including GPT3.5-davinci-003) with DIPPER successfully evades several detectors, including watermarking, GPTZero, DetectGPT, and OpenAI's text classifier. For example, DIPPER drops detection accuracy of DetectGPT from 70.3% to 4.6% (at a constant false positive rate of 1%), without appreciably modifying the input semantics.To increase the robustness of AI-generated text detection to paraphrase attacks, we introduce a simple defense that relies on retrieving semantically-similar generations and must be maintained by a language model API provider. Given a candidate text, our algorithm searches a database of sequences previously generated by the API, looking for sequences that match the candidate text within a certain threshold. We empirically verify our defense using a database of 15M generations from a fine-tuned T5-XXL model and find that it can detect 80% to 97% of paraphrased generations across different settings while only classifying 1% of human-written sequences as AI-generated. We open-source our models, code and data.

It provides a way to test detection robustness while largely preserving the original meaning.

In one reported example, DetectGPT's detection accuracy falls from 70.3% to 4.6% while the false-positive rate stays at 1%. The result shows that successful detection of original generations does not necessarily carry over to meaning-preserving rewrites.

Using 15 million generations from a fine-tuned T5-XXL model, the defense detects 80%–97% of paraphrased generations across settings while flagging 1% of human-written sequences. title: Paraphrasing evades detectors of AI-generated text, but retrieval is an effective defense

abstract: Providing formal guarantees of algorithmic fairness is of paramount importance to socially responsible deployment of machine learning algorithms. In this work, we study formal guarantees, i.e., certificates, for individual fairness (IF) of neural networks. We start by introducing a novel convex approximation of IF constraints that exponentially decreases the computational cost of providing formal guarantees of local individual fairness. We highlight that prior methods are constrained by their focus on global IF certification and can therefore only scale to models with a few dozen hidden neurons, thus limiting their practical impact. We propose to certify \textit{distributional} individual fairness which ensures that for a given empirical distribution and all distributions within a $\gamma$-Wasserstein ball, the neural network has guaranteed individually fair predictions. Leveraging developments in quasi-convex optimization, we provide novel and efficient certified bounds on distributional individual fairness and show that our method allows us to certify and regularize neural networks that are several orders of magnitude larger than those considered by prior works. Moreover, we study real-world distribution shifts and find our bounds to be a scalable, practical, and sound source of IF guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to give neural networks formal guarantees of individual fairness. Earlier certification approaches focus on global guarantees and, according to the authors, scale only to networks with a few dozen hidden neurons. The work introduces a convex approximation of individual fairness constraints that exponentially reduces the computational cost of local certification.

The authors then formulate distributional individual fairness. The guarantee covers a given empirical data distribution together with every distribution inside a specified Wasserstein neighborhood around it. The radius of that neighborhood determines the distributional changes covered by the certificate. This makes the scope of the guarantee explicit while accommodating uncertainty about the distribution encountered in use.

Using quasi-convex optimization, the method computes certified bounds and supports both certification and regularization of networks several orders of magnitude larger than those considered previously. Evaluations involving real-world distribution shifts find the bounds scalable, practical, and sound. The contribution is a more tractable route to formal fairness guarantees over a defined family of distributions.
summary.tldr: Efficient certified bounds extend individual fairness guarantees to much larger neural networks and defined neighborhoods of data distributions.

title: Certification of Distributional Individual Fairness

abstract: We investigate the mathematical capabilities of two iterations of ChatGPT (released 9-January-2023 and 30-January-2023) and of GPT-4 by testing them on publicly available datasets, as well as hand-crafted ones, using a novel methodology. In contrast to formal mathematics, where large databases of formal proofs are available (e.g., mathlib, the Lean Mathematical Library), current datasets of natural-language mathematics used to benchmark language models either cover only elementary mathematics or are very small. We address this by publicly releasing two new datasets: GHOSTS and miniGHOSTS. These are the first natural-language datasets curated by working researchers in mathematics that (1) aim to cover graduate-level mathematics, (2) provide a holistic overview of the mathematical capabilities of language models, and (3) distinguish multiple dimensions of mathematical reasoning. These datasets test on 1636 human expert evaluations whether ChatGPT and GPT-4 can be helpful assistants to professional mathematicians by emulating use cases that arise in the daily professional activities of mathematicians. We benchmark the models on a range of fine-grained performance metrics. For advanced mathematics, this is the most detailed evaluation effort to date. We find that ChatGPT and GPT-4 can be used most successfully as mathematical assistants for querying facts, acting as mathematical search engines and knowledge base interfaces. GPT-4 can additionally be used for undergraduate-level mathematics but fails on graduate-level difficulty. Contrary to many positive reports in the media about GPT-4 and ChatGPT's exam-solving abilities (a potential case of selection bias), their overall mathematical performance is well below the level of a graduate student. Hence, if you aim to use ChatGPT to pass a graduate-level math exam, you would be better off copying from your average peer!

These findings concern the evaluated model versions and distinguish useful factual assistance from advanced mathematical competence.
summary.tldr: Expert-curated evaluations find the tested ChatGPT and GPT-4 versions more useful for mathematical facts than graduate-level reasoning.

title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT

abstract: Diffusion models have gained significant attention in the realm of image generation due to their exceptional performance. Their success has been recently expanded to text generation via generating all tokens within a sequence concurrently. However, natural language exhibits a far more pronounced sequential dependency in comparison to images, and the majority of existing language models are trained with a left-to-right auto-regressive approach.To account for the inherent sequential characteristic of natural language, we introduce Auto-Regressive Diffusion (AR-Diffusion). AR-Diffusion ensures that the generation of tokens on the right depends on the generated ones on the left, a mechanism achieved through employing a dynamic number of denoising steps that vary based on token position. This results in tokens on the left undergoing fewer denoising steps than those on the right, thereby enabling them to generate earlier and subsequently influence the generation of tokens on the right.In a series of experiments on various text generation tasks, including text summarization, machine translation, and common sense generation, AR-Diffusion clearly demonstrated its superiority over existing diffusion language models and that it can be $100\times\sim600\times$ faster when achieving comparable results. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/ProphetNet/tree/master/AR-diffusion.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based text generation can produce all positions in a sequence concurrently, but language has strong dependencies between earlier and later tokens. AR-Diffusion introduces a directional structure into this process so that tokens on the right depend on generated tokens to their left. The aim is to incorporate the sequential character of language into diffusion generation.

The method assigns different numbers of denoising steps to different token positions. Left-side tokens receive fewer steps and become available earlier, allowing them to influence the generation of tokens farther right. This position-dependent schedule is the mechanism that brings autoregressive dependence into the diffusion model.

The authors evaluate AR-Diffusion on summarization, machine translation, and commonsense generation. They report better performance than existing diffusion language models and generation that can be 100 to 600 times faster at comparable results. These are empirical findings from the reported comparisons, showing that the denoising schedule can improve both generation quality and efficiency within the evaluated text-generation settings.
summary.tldr: AR-Diffusion uses position-dependent denoising to introduce left-to-right dependence and reports large speedups over existing diffusion language models at comparable results.

title: AR-Diffusion: Auto-Regressive Diffusion Model for Text Generation

abstract: This paper studies quasi-Newton methods for solving nonlinear equations. We propose block variants of both good and bad Broyden's methods, which enjoy explicit local superlinear convergence rates. Our block good Broyden's method has faster condition-number-free convergence rate than existing Broyden's methods because it takes the advantage of multiple rank modification on the Jacobian estimator. On the other hand, our block bad Broyden's method directly estimates the inverse of the Jacobian provably, which reduces the computational cost of the iteration. Our theoretical results provide some new insights on why good Broyden's method outperforms bad Broyden's method in most of the cases. The empirical results also demonstrate the superiority of our methods and validate our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: This paper develops methods for solving nonlinear equations by improving an approximation to the local behavior of the equations. It studies Broyden's methods, two quasi-Newton approaches conventionally called good and bad Broyden. The proposed block variants use richer updates to the estimated Jacobian or its inverse, offering different tradeoffs between convergence and iteration cost.

For block good Broyden, the key change is a modification involving multiple ranks of the Jacobian estimate. The authors establish a faster convergence rate than existing Broyden methods, with a rate that does not depend on the condition number. For block bad Broyden, the method directly estimates the inverse Jacobian, which reduces the computational cost of an iteration.

Both variants receive explicit local superlinear convergence guarantees: the stated acceleration concerns behavior near a solution. The theoretical analysis also offers insight into why good Broyden tends to outperform bad Broyden in most cases. Empirical results support the proposed methods and their analysis, connecting the richer updates to observed improvements in solving nonlinear equations.
summary.tldr: Block versions of Broyden's methods provide explicit local superlinear convergence guarantees while improving convergence rates or per-iteration cost.

title: Block Broyden's Methods for Solving Nonlinear Equations

abstract: We study the convergence behavior of the celebrated temporal-difference (TD) learning algorithm. By looking at the algorithm through the lens of optimization, we first argue that TD can be viewed as an iterative optimization algorithm where the function to be minimized changes per iteration. By carefully investigating the divergence displayed by TD on a classical counter example, we identify two forces that determine the convergent or divergent behavior of the algorithm. We next formalize our discovery in the linear TD setting with quadratic loss and prove that convergence of TD hinges on the interplay between these two forces. We extend this optimization perspective to prove convergence of TD in a much broader setting than just linear approximation and squared loss. Our results provide a theoretical explanation for the successful application of TD in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning is widely used in reinforcement learning, but understanding when it converges remains important. This paper studies the algorithm through an optimization viewpoint. It interprets TD as an iterative procedure in which the function being minimized changes at each step, making the evolution of that objective part of the convergence problem.

The authors examine a classical example where TD diverges and identify two forces that govern whether its behavior converges or diverges. They formalize this account for linear TD with quadratic loss and prove that convergence depends on the interaction between those forces. This turns an analysis of failure into a framework for explaining the algorithm's behavior.

The paper then extends the optimization perspective to establish convergence beyond linear approximation and squared loss. The results explain convergence within the settings analyzed, with the changing objective and the balance of the identified forces central to the argument.
summary.tldr: Viewing TD as optimization of a changing objective yields convergence results governed by the interaction of two identified forces.

title: TD Convergence: An Optimization Perspective

abstract: In the past years, YOLO-series models have emerged as the leading approaches in the area of real-time object detection. Many studies pushed up the baseline to a higher level by modifying the architecture, augmenting data and designing new losses. However, we find previous models still suffer from information fusion problem, although Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and Path Aggregation Network (PANet) have alleviated this. Therefore, this study provides an advanced Gatherand-Distribute mechanism (GD) mechanism, which is realized with convolution and self-attention operations. This new designed model named as Gold-YOLO, which boosts the multi-scale feature fusion capabilities and achieves an ideal balance between latency and accuracy across all model scales. Additionally, we implement MAE-style pretraining in the YOLO-series for the first time, allowing YOLOseries models could be to benefit from unsupervised pretraining. Gold-YOLO-N attains an outstanding 39.9% AP on the COCO val2017 datasets and 1030 FPS on a T4 GPU, which outperforms the previous SOTA model YOLOv6-3.0-N with similar FPS by +2.4%. The PyTorch code is available at https://github.com/huawei-noah/Efficient-Computing/tree/master/Detection/Gold-YOLO, and the MindSpore code is available at https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/Gold_YOLO.

This paper identifies information fusion as a remaining weakness in earlier YOLO models, despite existing mechanisms for combining features. Gold-YOLO targets that weakness by improving how information from multiple feature scales is brought together.

Its Gather-and-Distribute mechanism uses convolution and self-attention to strengthen multi-scale feature fusion. The authors report a favorable latency–accuracy balance across model scales. They also introduce masked-autoencoder-style pretraining into the YOLO series, allowing these detectors to benefit from unsupervised pretraining alongside the changes to feature integration.

The speed figure belongs to the stated model and hardware setting, while the broader contribution concerns combining feature integration with unsupervised pretraining.
summary.tldr: Gold-YOLO improves multi-scale feature fusion and adds unsupervised pretraining, achieving higher reported detection accuracy at comparable speed.

title: Gold-YOLO: Efficient Object Detector via Gather-and-Distribute Mechanism

abstract: An important problem in time-series analysis is modeling systems with time-varying dynamics. Probabilistic models with joint continuous and discrete latent states offer interpretable, efficient, and experimentally useful descriptions of such data. Commonly used models include autoregressive hidden Markov models (ARHMMs) and switching linear dynamical systems (SLDSs), each with its own advantages and disadvantages. ARHMMs permit exact inference and easy parameter estimation, but are parameter intensive when modeling long dependencies, and hence are prone to overfitting. In contrast, SLDSs can capture long-range dependencies in a parameter efficient way through Markovian latent dynamics, but present an intractable likelihood and a challenging parameter estimation task. In this paper, we propose _switching autoregressive low-rank tensor_ SALT models, which retain the advantages of both approaches while ameliorating the weaknesses. SALT parameterizes the tensor of an ARHMM with a low-rank factorization to control the number of parameters and allow longer range dependencies without overfitting. We prove theoretical and discuss practical connections between SALT, linear dynamical systems, and SLDSs. We empirically demonstrate quantitative advantages of SALT models on a range of simulated and real prediction tasks, including behavioral and neural datasets. Furthermore, the learned low-rank tensor provides novel insights into temporal dependencies within each discrete state.

Existing autoregressive hidden Markov models support exact inference and straightforward parameter estimation, but capturing long histories requires many parameters and can cause overfitting. Switching linear dynamical systems represent long-range dependencies more compactly, yet their likelihood and parameter estimation are harder to handle.

The proposed model factorizes the parameter tensor of an autoregressive hidden Markov model into a low-rank form. This controls the number of parameters while supporting longer temporal dependencies. The construction aims to retain the useful inference properties of the autoregressive approach while gaining a more compact description of dynamics.

The paper proves theoretical connections and discusses practical relationships between SALT, linear dynamical systems, and switching linear dynamical systems. Experiments show quantitative advantages on simulated and real prediction problems, including behavioral and neural data. The learned low-rank tensor also reveals temporal dependencies within each discrete state, giving the model an interpretive role alongside its predictive one.
summary.tldr: SALT uses low-rank tensor factors to model changing time-series dynamics compactly while retaining useful autoregressive inference and interpretation.

title: Switching Autoregressive Low-rank Tensor Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be seen as atomic units of computation mapping sequences to a distribution over sequences. Thus, they can be seen as stochastic language layers in a language network, where the learnable parameters are the natural language prompts at each layer. By stacking two such layers and feeding the output of one layer to the next, we obtain a Deep Language Network (DLN). We first show how to effectively perform prompt optimization for a 1-Layer language network (DLN-1). Then, we present an extension that applies to 2-layer DLNs (DLN-2), where two prompts must be learned. The key idea is to consider the output of the first layer as a latent variable, which requires inference, and prompts to be learned as the parameters of the generative distribution. We first test the effectiveness of DLN-1 in multiple reasoning and natural language understanding tasks. Then, we show that DLN-2 can reach higher performance than a single layer, showing promise that we might reach comparable performance to GPT-4, even when each LLM in the network is smaller and less powerful.

We first test the effectiveness of DLN-1 in multiple reasoning and natural language understanding tasks. Then, we show that DLN-2 can reach higher performance than a single layer, showing promise that we might reach comparable performance to GPT-4, even when each LLM in the network is smaller and less powerful.

paragraphs: This paper treats a language model as a computational layer that maps input text to a distribution over possible output texts. Its prompt becomes a parameter that can be optimized. Feeding one such layer's output into another creates a Deep Language Network, allowing the researchers to study prompt learning across a sequence of models.

The authors first develop prompt optimization for a single layer, then extend it to a two-layer network with two prompts to learn jointly. The intermediate text produced by the first model is treated as a latent variable requiring inference. Variational inference provides the framing for learning prompts while accounting for that intermediate output.

Experiments test the single-layer method on reasoning and language-understanding tasks and show that the two-layer version can achieve higher performance. The results suggest the possibility of approaching GPT-4 performance using individually smaller, less powerful models. That comparison is presented as a promising direction, while the demonstrated contribution is joint prompt optimization and gains from the tested two-layer composition.
summary.tldr: Treating intermediate text as a latent variable enables joint prompt optimization across two language-model layers, which can outperform one layer.

title: Joint Prompt Optimization of Stacked LLMs using Variational Inference

abstract: Designing and deriving effective model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) algorithms with a performance improvement guarantee is challenging, mainly attributed to the high coupling between model learning and policy optimization. Many prior methods that rely on return discrepancy to guide model learning ignore the impacts of model shift, which can lead to performance deterioration due to excessive model updates. Other methods use performance difference bound to explicitly consider model shift. However, these methods rely on a fixed threshold to constrain model shift, resulting in a heavy dependence on the threshold and a lack of adaptability during the training process. In this paper, we theoretically derive an optimization objective that can unify model shift and model bias and then formulate a fine-tuning process. This process adaptively adjusts the model updates to get a performance improvement guarantee while avoiding model overfitting. Based on these, we develop a straightforward algorithm USB-PO (Unified model Shift and model Bias Policy Optimization). Empirical results show that USB-PO achieves state-of-the-art performance on several challenging benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: In model-based reinforcement learning, an agent learns an environment model and uses it to improve its policy. These two processes interact closely. Updating the model too aggressively can hurt policy performance, even when the update seems helpful for model learning. This paper studies how to account for that interaction during fine-tuning.

The authors identify shortcomings in two existing approaches. Some methods overlook the effect of model shift, while others restrict it using a fixed threshold that can be difficult to adapt throughout training. They derive an optimization objective that jointly accounts for model shift and model bias, then use it to formulate an adaptive model fine-tuning process.

The resulting algorithm, USB-PO, adjusts model updates with a theoretically derived performance-improvement guarantee while avoiding model overfitting. Empirical evaluations report state-of-the-art performance on several challenging benchmark tasks. The contribution is a way to coordinate model revision with policy optimization: the learning objective considers both the model's errors and the consequences of changing the model that policy learning depends on.
summary.tldr: USB-PO jointly accounts for model bias and model shift to adapt environment-model updates during policy optimization.

title: How to Fine-tune the Model: Unified Model Shift and Model Bias Policy Optimization

abstract: Finding new drugs is getting harder and harder. One of the hopes of drug discovery is to use machine learning models to predict molecular properties. That is why models for molecular property prediction are being developed and tested on benchmarks such as MoleculeNet. However, existing benchmarks are unrealistic and are too different from applying the models in practice. We have created a new practical \emph{Lo-Hi} benchmark consisting of two tasks: Lead Optimization (Lo) and Hit Identification (Hi), corresponding to the real drug discovery process. For the Hi task, we designed a novel molecular splitting algorithm that solves the Balanced Vertex Minimum $k$-Cut problem. We tested state-of-the-art and classic ML models, revealing which works better under practical settings. We analyzed modern benchmarks and showed that they are unrealistic and overoptimistic.Review: https://openreview.net/forum?id=H2Yb28qGLVLo-Hi benchmark: https://github.com/SteshinSS/lohi_neurips2023Lo-Hi splitter library: https://github.com/SteshinSS/lohi_splitter

paragraphs: Machine-learning models for molecular properties are often evaluated on standardized benchmarks, but those evaluations may differ from the situations encountered in drug discovery. This paper argues that existing benchmarks can therefore give an overly optimistic picture of practical performance. It introduces Lo-Hi to connect evaluation more closely to the drug-discovery process.

The benchmark contains two tasks, Lead Optimization and Hit Identification. For Hit Identification, the authors design a molecular data-splitting algorithm that solves a Balanced Vertex Minimum k-Cut problem. This makes the construction of the evaluation split a central part of the benchmark’s approach to representing a practical discovery setting.

The authors test both contemporary state-of-the-art methods and classic machine-learning models to examine which perform better under these settings. They also analyze existing benchmarks and report that they are unrealistic and overoptimistic. The contribution is a revised basis for model comparison: judging molecular-property predictors on tasks shaped around intended use, rather than treating strong results on an existing benchmark as sufficient evidence of practical effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Lo-Hi evaluates molecular-property models on lead optimization and hit identification tasks designed to better reflect practical drug discovery.

title: Lo-Hi: Practical ML Drug Discovery Benchmark

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection discerns OOD data where the predictor cannot make valid predictions as in-distribution (ID) data, thereby increasing the reliability of open-world classification. However, it is typically hard to collect real out-of-distribution (OOD) data for training a predictor capable of discerning ID and OOD patterns. This obstacle gives rise to *data generation-based learning methods*, synthesizing OOD data via data generators for predictor training without requiring any real OOD data. Related methods typically pre-train a generator on ID data and adopt various selection procedures to find those data likely to be the OOD cases. However, generated data may still coincide with ID semantics, i.e., mistaken OOD generation remains, confusing the predictor between ID and OOD data. To this end, we suggest that generated data (with mistaken OOD generation) can be used to devise an *auxiliary OOD detection task* to facilitate real OOD detection. Specifically, we can ensure that learning from such an auxiliary task is beneficial if the ID and the OOD parts have disjoint supports, with the help of a well-designed training procedure for the predictor. Accordingly, we propose a powerful data generation-based learning method named *Auxiliary Task-based OOD Learning* (ATOL) that can relieve the mistaken OOD generation. We conduct extensive experiments under various OOD detection setups, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method against its advanced counterparts.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection aims to identify inputs for which a classifier cannot make valid predictions. Obtaining real examples of such inputs can be difficult, so some methods synthesize them using generators trained on in-distribution data. A central problem is that generated examples may still carry familiar semantics, making their assignment as out-of-distribution training data misleading.

This paper proposes using the imperfect generated data to construct an auxiliary detection task. Rather than requiring every generated example to be a correct out-of-distribution example, the approach uses the auxiliary task to assist the real detection problem. The authors establish that this learning can be beneficial when the in-distribution and out-of-distribution parts have disjoint supports and an appropriately designed training procedure is used.

The resulting method, Auxiliary Task-based OOD Learning, or ATOL, is intended to alleviate mistaken generation. Experiments across several detection setups demonstrate effectiveness against advanced comparison methods. The contribution provides a way to make imperfect synthetic sources useful, with a theoretical benefit that explicitly depends on the stated separation condition and training design.
summary.tldr: ATOL uses imperfect generated examples in an auxiliary task to improve out-of-distribution detection, with a conditional theoretical guarantee.

title: Out-of-distribution Detection Learning with Unreliable Out-of-distribution Sources

abstract: This paper presents a new mechanism to facilitate the training of mask transformers for efficient panoptic segmentation, democratizing its deployment. We observe that due to the high complexity in the training objective of panoptic segmentation, it will inevitably lead to much higher penalization on false positive. Such unbalanced loss makes the training process of the end-to-end mask-transformer based architectures difficult, especially for efficient models. In this paper, we present ReMaX that adds relaxation to mask predictions and class predictions during the training phase for panoptic segmentation. We demonstrate that via these simple relaxation techniques during training, our model can be consistently improved by a clear margin without any extra computational cost on inference. By combining our method with efficient backbones like MobileNetV3-Small, our method achieves new state-of-the-art results for efficient panoptic segmentation on COCO, ADE20K and Cityscapes. Code and pre-trained checkpoints will be available at https://github.com/google-research/deeplab2.

paragraphs: This paper examines why efficient mask-transformer models are difficult to train for panoptic segmentation. The authors identify an imbalance in the training objective: its complexity produces much stronger penalties for false positives. That imbalance makes end-to-end learning difficult, especially for the efficient models that are attractive when deployment computation is constrained.

ReMaX addresses the training process by introducing relaxation into both mask predictions and class predictions. These changes reduce the difficulty associated with the unbalanced objective. Because the relaxation is applied during training, the reported performance improvements do not require additional computation when the trained model is used for inference.

The authors report consistent improvements by clear margins. Combined with efficient backbones such as MobileNetV3-Small, ReMaX achieves state-of-the-art results for efficient panoptic segmentation on COCO, ADE20K, and Cityscapes. The findings emphasize that deployment efficiency depends partly on training design: improving how a compact architecture learns can improve its results while retaining its inference cost.
summary.tldr: ReMaX relaxes mask and class predictions during training to improve efficient panoptic segmentation without adding inference cost.

title: ReMaX: Relaxing for Better Training on Efficient Panoptic Segmentation

abstract: Multiple instance learning (MIL) is an effective and widely used approach for weakly supervised machine learning. In histopathology, MIL models have achieved remarkable success in tasks like tumor detection, biomarker prediction, and outcome prognostication. However, MIL explanation methods are still lagging behind, as they are limited to small bag sizes or disregard instance interactions. We revisit MIL through the lens of explainable AI (XAI) and introduce xMIL, a refined framework with more general assumptions. We demonstrate how to obtain improved MIL explanations using layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and conduct extensive evaluation experiments on three toy settings and four real-world histopathology datasets. Our approach consistently outperforms previous explanation attempts with particularly improved faithfulness scores on challenging biomarker prediction tasks. Finally, we showcase how xMIL explanations enable pathologists to extract insights from MIL models, representing a significant advance for knowledge discovery and model debugging in digital histopathology.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning makes predictions from collections of instances, often called bags, under weak supervision. In histopathology, it supports tasks including tumor detection, biomarker prediction, and outcome prediction. Explaining these models is challenging because existing methods may handle only small bags or overlook interactions among the instances contributing to a prediction.

The authors revisit multiple instance learning from an explainability perspective and introduce xMIL, a framework with more general assumptions. They show how layer-wise relevance propagation can produce improved explanations within this framework. The goal is to better reflect how the model uses its inputs, including the importance of considering instance interactions.

Evaluation spans three toy settings and four real-world histopathology datasets. The proposed approach consistently improves on earlier explanation methods, with particularly strong faithfulness gains on difficult biomarker-prediction tasks. The paper also demonstrates how pathologists can use the explanations to extract insights from trained models. These findings connect more faithful explanations with practical opportunities for model debugging and knowledge discovery in digital histopathology.
summary.tldr: xMIL improves explanations of histopathology models through a broader multiple-instance framework and layer-wise relevance propagation.

title: xMIL: Insightful Explanations for Multiple Instance Learning in Histopathology

abstract: Current 4D generation methods have achieved noteworthy efficacy with the aid of advanced diffusion generative models. However, these methods lack multi-view spatial-temporal modeling and encounter challenges in integrating diverse prior knowledge from multiple diffusion models, resulting in inconsistent temporal appearance and flickers. In this paper, we propose a novel 4D generation pipeline, namely $\textbf{4Diffusion}$, aimed at generating spatial-temporally consistent 4D content from a monocular video. We first design a unified diffusion model tailored for multi-view video generation by incorporating a learnable motion module into a frozen 3D-aware diffusion model to capture multi-view spatial-temporal correlations. After training on a curated dataset, our diffusion model acquires reasonable temporal consistency and inherently preserves the generalizability and spatial consistency of the 3D-aware diffusion model. Subsequently, we propose 4D-aware Score Distillation Sampling loss, which is based on our multi-view video diffusion model, to optimize 4D representation parameterized by dynamic NeRF. This aims to eliminate discrepancies arising from multiple diffusion models, allowing for generating spatial-temporally consistent 4D content. Moreover, we devise an anchor loss to enhance the appearance details and facilitate the learning of dynamic NeRF. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to previous methods.

paragraphs: 4Diffusion turns a video from a single viewpoint into a representation of a three-dimensional scene that changes over time. The challenge is keeping appearance consistent across both viewpoints and moments. Existing approaches can produce flicker and temporal inconsistencies when they lack joint spatial and temporal modeling or combine guidance from several diffusion models.

The authors build a unified model for generating videos from multiple views. They add a trainable motion module to a frozen diffusion model that already understands three-dimensional structure. Training on a curated dataset gives the combined model reasonable temporal consistency while preserving the original model's spatial consistency and generalization capabilities.

This model then guides optimization of a dynamic neural radiance field through a proposed 4D-aware score distillation loss. An additional anchor loss improves appearance details and helps the representation learn. Qualitative and quantitative experiments report better performance than previous methods. The central contribution is coordinated guidance across space and time, aimed at reducing the disagreements that arise when separate diffusion models guide the same reconstruction.
summary.tldr: 4Diffusion uses unified multi-view video diffusion guidance to generate more spatially and temporally consistent 4D content from a monocular video.

title: 4Diffusion: Multi-view Video Diffusion Model for 4D Generation

abstract: This paper introduces a LArge-scale Video Interpolation Benchmark (LAVIB) for the low-level video task of Video Frame Interpolation (VFI). LAVIB comprises a large collection of high-resolution videos sourced from the web through an automated pipeline with minimal requirements for human verification. Metrics are computed for each video's motion magnitudes, luminance conditions, frame sharpness, and contrast. The collection of videos and the creation of quantitative challenges based on these metrics are under-explored by current low-level video task datasets. In total, LAVIB includes 283K clips from 17K ultra-HD videos, covering 77.6 hours. Benchmark train, val, and test sets maintain similar video metric distributions. Further splits are also created for out-of-distribution (OOD) challenges, with train and test splits including videos of dissimilar attributes.

paragraphs: Video frame interpolation concerns producing intermediate frames in a video sequence. LAVIB provides a large benchmark for studying this task using high-resolution web videos. Its collection process is automated and requires little human verification, allowing the dataset to include 283,000 clips drawn from 17,000 ultra-high-definition videos, totaling 77.6 hours.

The benchmark characterizes each video's motion magnitude, lighting conditions, frame sharpness, and contrast. These measurements give the collection an explicit account of the visual conditions a model encounters. They also support quantitative challenges based on those properties, addressing an aspect the authors describe as underexplored in existing datasets for low-level video tasks.

The standard training, validation, and test partitions have similar distributions of the measured video properties. Additional out-of-distribution partitions deliberately use different attributes in training and testing. This design supports evaluation under both matched conditions and shifts in the characteristics of the videos. The paper's contribution is the dataset and evaluation structure for investigating interpolation across these conditions.
summary.tldr: LAVIB provides 283,000 high-resolution video clips and attribute-based splits for evaluating frame interpolation under matched and shifted conditions.

title: LAVIB: A Large-scale Video Interpolation Benchmark

abstract: Accurate and smooth shape matching is very hard to achieve. This is because for accuracy, one needs unique descriptors (signatures) on shapes that distinguish different vertices on a mesh accurately while at the same time being invariant to deformations. However, most existing unique shape descriptors are generally not smooth on the shape and are not noise-robust thus leading to non-smooth matches. On the other hand, for smoothness, one needs descriptors that are smooth and continuous on the shape. However, existing smooth descriptors are generally not unique and as such lose accuracy as they match neighborhoods (for smoothness) rather than exact vertices (for accuracy). In this work, we propose to use different k-hop neighborhoods of vertices as pairwise descriptors for shape matching. We use these descriptors in conjunction with local map distortion (LMD) to refine an initialized map for shape matching. We validate the effectiveness of our pipeline on benchmark datasets such as SCAPE, TOSCA, TOPKIDS, and others.

paragraphs: Shape matching seeks corresponding points on different shapes, but accuracy and smoothness can pull in different directions. A highly distinctive descriptor can identify an individual mesh vertex while behaving irregularly across nearby vertices or reacting poorly to noise. A smoother descriptor can preserve neighborhood continuity while losing the detail needed to distinguish exact points.

HOPE uses neighborhoods at different numbers of mesh hops as pairwise descriptors. These neighborhoods describe a vertex through surrounding mesh structure at several extents, rather than relying on a single kind of vertex signature. The method combines these descriptors with local map distortion to refine an already initialized correspondence map.

The authors validate the pipeline on shape-matching benchmarks including SCAPE, TOSCA, and TOPKIDS. The stated results support the effectiveness of using multiple neighborhood scales together with distortion information. The role of initialization is central to interpreting the method: HOPE improves an existing map. Its contribution is a refinement strategy aimed at reconciling precise point correspondence with the continuity expected of a smooth match.
summary.tldr: HOPE refines shape correspondences using multiple mesh-neighborhood scales and local distortion to address the tension between accuracy and smoothness.

title: HOPE: Shape Matching Via Aligning Different K-hop Neighbourhoods

abstract: A crucial aspect of understanding the complex nature of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is the ability to explain learned concepts within their latent representations. While methods exist to connect neurons to human-understandable textual descriptions, evaluating the quality of these explanations is challenging due to the lack of a unified quantitative approach. We introduce CoSy (Concept Synthesis), a novel, architecture-agnostic framework for evaluating textual explanations of latent neurons. Given textual explanations, our proposed framework uses a generative model conditioned on textual input to create data points representing the explanations. By comparing the neuron's response to these generated data points and control data points, we can estimate the quality of the explanation. We validate our framework through sanity checks and benchmark various neuron description methods for Computer Vision tasks, revealing significant differences in quality.

paragraphs: A textual description of a neuron's behavior can make a neural network easier to interpret, but a convincing description is not automatically a good explanation. Evaluating these descriptions is difficult without a shared quantitative procedure. CoSy provides a framework for assessing how well a proposed description matches the behavior of the neuron it is meant to explain.

The framework starts with the text explanation and uses a text-conditioned generative model to create examples representing that concept. It then compares the neuron's responses to these generated examples with its responses to control examples. This turns an interpretation expressed in words into a testable prediction about which inputs should elicit a response.

The authors validate the framework with sanity checks and use it to benchmark neuron-description methods for computer vision. Their evaluation reveals substantial differences in explanation quality. CoSy is designed to work across architectures, providing a common evaluation approach rather than tying the assessment to one network design. Its contribution is an operational estimate of explanation quality grounded in measured neuron responses.
summary.tldr: CoSy evaluates neuron descriptions by generating examples from the text and comparing neuron responses against control examples.

title: CoSy: Evaluating Textual Explanations of Neurons

abstract: Many problems in physical sciences are characterized by the prediction of space-time sequences. Such problems range from weather prediction to the analysis of disease propagation and video prediction. Modern techniques for the solution of these problems typically combine Convolution Neural Networks (CNN) architecture with a time prediction mechanism. However, oftentimes, such approaches underperform in the long-range propagation of information and lack explainability. In this work, we introduce a physically inspired architecture for the solution of such problems. Namely, we propose to augment CNNs with advection by designing a novel semi-Lagrangian push operator. We show that the proposed operator allows for the non-local transformation of information compared with standard convolutional kernels. We then complement it with Reaction and Diffusion neural components to form a network that mimics the Reaction-Advection-Diffusion equation, in high dimensions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our network on a number of spatio-temporal datasets that show their merit. Our code is available at https://github.com/Siddharth-Rout/deepADRnet.

paragraphs: Predicting how a spatial scene changes over time requires tracking information as it moves. The paper targets this problem in settings such as weather, disease propagation, and video prediction. Conventional combinations of convolutional networks and temporal prediction mechanisms can struggle to propagate information over long distances, motivating an architecture with an explicit transport component.

The central addition is an advection operator, implemented through a new semi-Lagrangian push mechanism. Its role is to move information nonlocally, beyond the transformations available from standard local convolutional kernels. The authors combine this mechanism with neural components for reaction and diffusion, producing a high-dimensional network organized around the structure of a reaction-advection-diffusion equation.

This physical organization gives different parts of the network distinct roles in changing, transporting, and spreading information. It connects the architecture to the processes involved in evolving spatial systems. Experiments on several spatiotemporal datasets demonstrate the network's effectiveness. The stated contribution is both a transport mechanism for extending convolutional processing and a physically motivated way to assemble it into a temporal prediction network.
summary.tldr: The paper adds a nonlocal advection operator to convolutional networks and combines it with reaction and diffusion components for spatiotemporal prediction.

title: Advection Augmented Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Although the performance of Temporal Action Segmentation (TAS) has been improved in recent years, achieving promising results often comes with a high computational cost due to dense inputs, complex model structures, and resource-intensive post-processing requirements. To improve the efficiency while keeping the high performance, we present a novel perspective centered on per-segment classification. By harnessing the capabilities of Transformers, we tokenize each video segment as an instance token, endowed with intrinsic instance segmentation. To realize efficient action segmentation, we introduce BaFormer, a boundary-aware Transformer network. It employs instance queries for instance segmentation and a global query for class-agnostic boundary prediction, yielding continuous segment proposals. During inference, BaFormer employs a simple yet effective voting strategy to classify boundary-wise segments based on instance segmentation. Remarkably, as a single-stage approach, BaFormer significantly reduces the computational costs, utilizing only 6% of the running time compared to the state-of-the-art method DiffAct, while producing better or comparable accuracy over several popular benchmarks. The code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/peiyao-w/BaFormer.
