paragraphs: Adam often trains Transformers substantially better than stochastic gradient descent, but the reason for that gap has been unclear. This paper examines the Hessian, which captures the curvature of the training loss. It identifies large differences in Hessian spectra across groups of Transformer parameters, calling this pattern block heterogeneity.

The authors investigate Transformers, convolutional networks, multilayer perceptrons, and quadratic problems. They find that SGD can match Adam on problems without this heterogeneity, while performing worse when the heterogeneity is present. These comparisons connect the optimizer gap to differences between parameter blocks rather than treating it solely as an unexplained property of Transformers.

An initial theoretical analysis points to SGD's shared learning rate: one rate cannot adequately handle the differing behavior of heterogeneous blocks. Coordinate-wise learning rates, as used by Adam, could alleviate that limitation. The contribution combines empirical comparisons with an initial explanation of why adaptive step sizes can help in these settings; it does not establish that every Transformer requires Adam.
summary.tldr: Differences in loss curvature across parameter blocks help explain Adam's advantage over SGD in the Transformer settings studied.

title: Why Transformers Need Adam: A Hessian Perspective

abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown remarkable capabilitiesin integrating vision and language for complex reasoning. While most existing benchmarks evaluate models under offline settings with a fixed set of pre-recorded inputs, we introduce OST-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate Online Spatio-Temporal understanding from the perspective of an agent actively exploring a scene. The “Online” aspect emphasizes the need to process and reason over incrementally acquired observations, while the “Spatio-Temporal” component requires integrating current visual inputs with historical memory to support dynamic spatial reasoning. OST-Bench better reflects the challenges of real-world embodied perception. Built on an efficient data collection pipeline, OST-Bench consists of 1.4k scenes and 10k question-answer pairs collected from ScanNet, Matterport3D, and ARKitScenes. We evaluate several leading MLLMs on OST-Bench and observe that they fall short on tasks requiring complex spatio-temporal reasoning. Under the online setting, their accuracy declines as the exploration horizon extends and the memory grows. Through further experimental analysis, we identify common error patterns across models and find that both complex clue-based spatial reasoning demands and long-term memory retrieval requirements significantly drop model performance along two separate axes, highlighting the core challenges that must be addressed to improve online embodied reasoning. To foster further research and development in the field, our codes, dataset, and benchmark are available at https://github.com/InternRobotics/OST-Bench.

paragraphs: An agent exploring a scene receives observations gradually and must connect what it sees now with what it saw earlier. OST-Bench evaluates this online form of spatial and temporal understanding. It shifts attention from fixed collections of recorded inputs toward reasoning that depends on accumulating observations and remembering relevant past information.

The benchmark includes 1.4 thousand scenes and 10 thousand question-answer pairs drawn from ScanNet, Matterport3D, and ARKitScenes. It tests whether multimodal language models can integrate current visual evidence with historical memory to answer questions during exploration. This setting captures demands of embodied perception that require both spatial reasoning and use of an expanding observation history.

Evaluated models struggle with complex spatial and temporal reasoning, and accuracy falls as exploration lasts longer and memory grows. Further analysis identifies two separate sources of difficulty: reasoning from complex spatial clues and retrieving information from long-term memory. The results help distinguish failures of reasoning from failures of retrieval, pointing to two capabilities that need improvement for online scene understanding.
summary.tldr: OST-Bench exposes separate spatial-reasoning and memory-retrieval difficulties in models processing observations during scene exploration.

title: OST-Bench: Evaluating the Capabilities of MLLMs in Online Spatio-temporal Scene Understanding

abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have achieved impressive image generation quality and are increasingly fine-tuned for personalized applications. However, these models often inherit unsafe behaviors from toxic pretraining data, raising growing safety concerns. While recent safety-driven unlearning methods have made promising progress in suppressing model toxicity, they are found to be fragile to downstream fine-tuning, as we reveal that state-of-the-art methods largely fail to retain their effectiveness even when fine-tuned on entirely benign datasets. To mitigate this problem, in this paper, we propose ResAlign, a safety-driven unlearning framework with enhanced resilience against downstream fine-tuning. By modeling downstream fine-tuning as an implicit optimization problem with a Moreau envelope-based reformulation, ResAlign enables efficient gradient estimation to minimize the recovery of harmful behaviors. Additionally, a meta-learning strategy is proposed to simulate a diverse distribution of fine-tuning scenarios to improve generalization. Extensive experiments across a wide range of datasets, fine-tuning methods, and configurations demonstrate that ResAlign consistently outperforms prior unlearning approaches in retaining safety, while effectively preserving benign generation capability. Our code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/AntigoneRandy/ResAlign.

paragraphs: Removing unsafe behavior from an image generator may not keep that behavior suppressed after subsequent customization. This paper finds that existing safety-driven unlearning methods can largely lose their effectiveness even when downstream fine-tuning uses entirely benign data. ResAlign is designed to make the initial unlearning step more resilient to those later changes.

The framework incorporates downstream fine-tuning into an implicit optimization problem. A Moreau-envelope reformulation enables efficient gradient estimation, allowing the unlearning process to target the later recovery of harmful behavior. A meta-learning strategy also simulates a varied distribution of fine-tuning scenarios so that resilience is trained across different possible adaptations.

Experiments span multiple datasets, fine-tuning methods, and configurations. ResAlign consistently retains safety better than prior unlearning approaches in these evaluations while preserving benign image-generation capability. The findings highlight the importance of evaluating unlearning after further training, not only immediately after removal. They also support anticipating downstream optimization during unlearning as a practical way to reduce the return of unwanted behaviors.
summary.tldr: ResAlign trains safety-driven unlearning to better withstand later diffusion-model fine-tuning, including customization on benign data.

title: Towards Resilient Safety-driven Unlearning for Diffusion Models against Downstream Fine-tuning

abstract: We initiate a systematic investigation of distribution testing in the framework of algorithmic replicability. Specifically, given independent samples from a collection of probability distributions, the goal is to characterize the sample complexity of replicably testing natural properties of the underlying distributions. On the algorithmic front, we develop new replicable algorithms for testing closeness and independence of discrete distributions. On the lower bound front, we develop a new methodology for proving sample complexity lower bounds for replicable testing that may be of broader interest. As an application of our technique, we establish near-optimal sample complexity lower bounds for replicable uniformity testing---answering an open question from prior work---and closeness testing.
originalAbstract: We initiate a systematic investigation of distribution testing in the framework of algorithmic replicability. Specifically, given independent samples from a collection of probability distributions, the goal is to characterize the sample complexity of replicably testing natural properties of the underlying distributions. On the algorithmic front, we develop new replicable algorithms for testing closeness and independence of discrete distributions. On the lower bound front, we develop a new methodology for proving sample complexity lower bounds for replicable testing that may be of broader interest. paragraphs: Distribution testing asks whether probability distributions have a specified property using samples rather than complete knowledge of the distributions. This paper studies those questions within algorithmic replicability, where stability of the testing outcome across independently sampled data is part of the objective. The main resource of interest is sample complexity: how much data a replicable test needs.

The authors develop new replicable algorithms for testing closeness and independence of discrete distributions. These tasks concern whether distributions are sufficiently similar and whether variables behave independently. Placing them in the replicability framework adds a requirement beyond ordinary property testing, so identifying suitable algorithms and their data requirements becomes a distinct theoretical problem.

The paper also introduces a method for proving sample-complexity lower bounds. Applied to uniformity and closeness testing, it gives near-optimal bounds on the data required by replicable procedures. The uniformity result resolves an open question from earlier work. Together, the algorithmic and lower-bound contributions help characterize both what replicable testing can achieve and the statistical cost it cannot avoid.
summary.tldr: The paper develops replicable distribution tests and near-optimal sample-complexity lower bounds for uniformity and closeness testing.

title: Replicable Distribution Testing

abstract: Understanding the dynamics of optimization algorithms in deep learning has become increasingly critical, especially as models grow in scale and complexity. Despite the empirical success of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants in finding solutions that generalize well, the precise mechanisms underlying this generalization remain poorly understood. A particularly intriguing aspect of this phenomenon is the bias of optimization algorithms towards certain types of minima—often flatter or simpler—especially in overparameterized regimes. While prior works have associated flatness of the loss landscape with better generalization, tools to mechanistically connect data, optimization algorithms, and the nature of the resulting minima are still limited. For instance, methods like Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) have shown practical gains by explicitly promoting flatness, but lack a unified theoretical framework explaining their influence across different data structures and model architectures. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive linear stability analysis framework to dissect the behavior of optimization algorithms—SGD, random perturbations, and SAM—in neural networks, focusing particularly on two-layer ReLU models. Our approach is built upon a novel coherence measure that captures the interaction between data geometry and gradient similarity, providing new insights into why and how certain solutions are favored.

paragraphs: Why does a training algorithm favor one solution over another when a neural network can fit its data in many ways? This paper studies that question through stability: how an optimization procedure behaves near a candidate solution. The motivation is to connect the structure of the training data with the kinds of solutions that optimization tends to favor.

The authors introduce a common linear stability framework for studying stochastic gradient descent, random perturbations, and Sharpness-Aware Minimization. Their analysis focuses particularly on two-layer networks with ReLU activations. Comparing these procedures within one framework provides a way to investigate their different preferences without treating each optimizer as an entirely separate theoretical problem.

The central ingredient is a new coherence measure connecting data geometry with similarity between gradients. This gives the analysis a concrete link between the examples being learned and the local behavior of optimization. The contribution is a framework for explaining solution preferences; the abstract does not establish that SAM universally generalizes better, or that flatter solutions always produce better predictions.
summary.tldr: A shared stability framework connects data geometry and gradient similarity to the solution preferences of SGD, random perturbations, and SAM.

title: A Unified Stability Analysis of SAM vs SGD: Role of Data Coherence and Emergence of Simplicity Bias

abstract: Air pollution remains one of the most critical environmental challenges globally, posing severe threats to public health, ecological sustainability, and climate governance. While existing physics-based and data-driven models have made progress in air quality forecasting, they often struggle to jointly capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics and ensure spatial continuity of pollutant distributions. In this study, we introduce CTENet, a novel chemical transport deep learning model that embeds the Advection-Diffusion-Reaction equation into a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) framework using an Eulerian representation to model the spatiotemporal evolution of pollutants. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that CTENet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines, achieving a remarkable RMSE improvement of 45.8% on the USA dataset and 21.0% on the China dataset.

CTENet addresses the problem by bringing a chemical transport equation into a neural forecasting framework.

Specifically, it embeds the advection-diffusion-reaction equation within a physics-informed neural network. The equation represents pollutant transport, spreading, and reactions, giving the learned model a physical description of how concentrations evolve. An Eulerian representation describes that evolution at spatial locations. This connects the forecasting task to the processes governing pollutant distributions rather than relying solely on learned statistical relationships.

title: Eulerian Neural Network Informed by Chemical Transport for Air Quality Forecasting

abstract: Finetuning large language models (LLMs) is a resource-intensive task for researchers in academia, with memory constraints posing a key bottleneck. A classic optimization method, block coordinate descent (BCD), significantly reduces memory cost by segmenting the trainable parameters into multiple blocks and optimizing one active block at a time while freezing the others. However, we identify that blindly applying BCD to train LLMs can be inefficient for two reasons. First, optimizing only the active block requires backpropagating through multiple deeper yet inactive blocks, resulting in wasteful computations. Second, the frozen blocks, when they are not quite close to optimality, can narrow the optimization landscape, potentially misguiding the training of the active block. To address these issues simultaneously, we propose integrating BCD with *landscape expansion*, which unfreezes the inactive blocks and updates them in a cost-efficient manner during the same backpropagation as the update to the active block. Experiments on 8B and 70B models demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses memory-efficient baselines and matches Adam's downstream performance while requiring only 24 GB of memory for the 8B model and 300 GB for the 70B model.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large language models can require more memory than researchers have available. Block coordinate descent reduces this burden by dividing parameters into blocks and training one block while holding the others fixed. This paper identifies two reasons that applying this strategy directly to language models can make training inefficient.

First, updating the active block still requires backward computation through deeper, frozen blocks, leaving some of that computation underused. Second, frozen blocks that are far from their best settings can restrict the possibilities available to the active block and potentially steer its training poorly. The proposed landscape expansion method updates those inactive blocks cheaply during the same backward pass used for the active block.

Experiments on models with 8 billion and 70 billion parameters show better results than the memory-efficient baselines tested. The method matches Adam’s downstream performance while using 24 GB and 300 GB of memory, respectively. These findings support updating otherwise frozen blocks as a way to improve the usefulness of memory-constrained training.
summary.tldr: Landscape expansion makes block coordinate fine-tuning more effective by cheaply updating inactive blocks during the existing backward pass.

title: Accelerating Block Coordinate Descent for LLM Finetuning via Landscape Expansion

abstract: DeepSeek-R1 has successfully enhanced Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning capabilities through its rule-based reward system. While it's a ''perfect'' reward system that effectively mitigates reward hacking, such reward functions are often discrete. Our experimental observations suggest that discrete rewards can lead to gradient anomaly, unstable optimization, and slow convergence. To address this issue, we propose ReDit (Reward Dithering), a method that dithers the discrete reward signal by adding simple random noise. With this perturbed reward, exploratory gradients are continuously provided throughout the learning process, enabling smoother gradient updates and accelerating convergence. The injected noise also introduces stochasticity into flat reward regions, encouraging the model to explore novel policies and escape local optima. Experiments across diverse tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of ReDit. On average, ReDit achieves performance comparable to vanilla GRPO with only approximately 10% the training steps, and furthermore, still exhibits a 4% performance improvement over vanilla GRPO when trained for a similar duration. Visualizations confirm significant mitigation of gradient issues with ReDit. Moreover, theoretical analyses are provided to further validate these advantages.

title: ReDit: Reward Dithering for Improved LLM Policy Optimization

abstract: Open-vocabulary part segmentation (OVPS) struggles with structurally connected boundaries due to the inherent conflict between continuous image features and discrete classification mechanism. To address this, we propose PBAPS, a novel training-free framework specifically designed for OVPS. PBAPS leverages structural knowledge of object-part relationships to guide a progressive segmentation from objects to fine-grained parts. To further improve accuracy at challenging boundaries, we introduce a Boundary-Aware Refinement (BAR) module that identifies ambiguous boundary regions by quantifying classification uncertainty, enhances the discriminative features of these ambiguous regions using high-confidence context, and adaptively refines part prototypes to better align with the specific image. Experiments on Pascal-Part-116, ADE20K-Part-234, PartImageNet demonstrate that PBAPS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 46.35\% mIoU and 34.46\% bIoU on Pascal-Part-116. Our code is available at https://github.com/TJU-IDVLab/PBAPS.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary part segmentation assigns image regions to fine-grained object parts. Connected parts are particularly difficult to separate because image features vary continuously while the final labels must make discrete distinctions. PBAPS addresses this problem through a training-free process that uses object structure and pays special attention to uncertain boundaries.

The framework segments progressively, moving from objects to their finer parts using knowledge of object-part relationships. Its Boundary-Aware Refinement module identifies ambiguous regions through classification uncertainty. It then uses high-confidence context to strengthen the features needed to distinguish those regions and adapts part prototypes to the particular image being segmented.

This combination connects global structural guidance with local boundary correction. Experiments on Pascal-Part-116, ADE20K-Part-234, and PartImageNet report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. On Pascal-Part-116, the reported scores are 46.35% mIoU and 34.46% bIoU. These findings support the value of refining uncertain part boundaries within a progressive segmentation procedure, without requiring additional training for the proposed framework.
summary.tldr: PBAPS improves training-free object-part segmentation by progressing from objects to parts and refining uncertain boundaries with confident context.

title: Open-Vocabulary Part Segmentation via Progressive and Boundary-Aware Strategy

abstract: Image deblurring plays a crucial role in enhancing visual clarity across various applications. Although most deep learning approaches primarily focus on sRGB images, which inherently lose critical information during the image signal processing pipeline, RAW images, being unprocessed and linear, possess superior restoration potential but remain underexplored. Deblurring RAW images presents unique challenges, particularly in handling frequency-dependent blur while maintaining computational efficiency. To address these issues, we propose Frequency Enhanced Network (FrENet), a framework specifically designed for RAW-to-RAW deblurring that operates directly in the frequency domain. We introduce a novel Adaptive Frequency Positional Modulation module, which dynamically adjusts frequency components according to their spectral positions, thereby enabling precise control over the deblurring process. Additionally, frequency domain skip connections are adopted to further preserve high-frequency details. Experimental results demonstrate that FrENet surpasses state-of-the-art deblurring methods in RAW image deblurring, achieving significantly better restoration quality while maintaining high efficiency in terms of reduced MACs. Furthermore, FrENet's adaptability enables it to be extended to sRGB images, where it delivers comparable or superior performance compared to methods specifically designed for sRGB data. The source code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Most learned image-deblurring methods work on processed sRGB images, after the image-processing pipeline has already discarded information. This paper instead focuses on RAW images, whose unprocessed, linear values offer greater restoration potential. The central challenge is to address blur that affects frequency components differently while keeping the computation needed for restoration manageable.

The proposed Frequency Enhanced Network, or FrENet, performs RAW-to-RAW deblurring directly in the frequency domain. An Adaptive Frequency Positional Modulation module changes frequency components according to their spectral positions, allowing the restoration process to respond differently across frequencies. Frequency-domain skip connections further preserve high-frequency information, which matters for retaining fine image details during deblurring.

The reported experiments show better RAW restoration quality than state-of-the-art deblurring methods while reducing multiply-accumulate operations. The framework also extends to sRGB images, where it achieves comparable or better performance than methods designed specifically for that format. These results indicate that explicitly adapting processing to frequency position can support both restoration quality and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: FrENet improves RAW-image deblurring efficiency and quality by adaptively processing frequency components and preserving high-frequency detail.

title: Efficient RAW Image Deblurring with Adaptive Frequency Modulation

abstract: We introduce Best-of-N (BoN) Jailbreaking, a simple black-box algorithm that jailbreaks frontier AI systems across modalities. BoN Jailbreaking works by repeatedly sampling variations of a prompt with a combination of augmentations---such as random shuffling or capitalization for textual prompts---until a harmful response is elicited. We find that BoN Jailbreaking achieves high attack success rates (ASRs) on closed-source language models, such as 89% on GPT-4o and 78% on Claude 3.5 Sonnet when sampling 10,000 augmented prompts. Further, it is similarly effective at circumventing state-of-the-art open-source defenses like circuit breakers and reasoning models like o1. BoN also seamlessly extends to other modalities: it jailbreaks vision language models (VLMs) such as GPT-4o and audio language models (ALMs) like Gemini 1.5 Pro, using modality-specific augmentations. BoN reliably improves when we sample more augmented prompts. Across all modalities, ASR, as a function of the number of samples (N), empirically follows power-law-like behavior for many orders of magnitude. BoN Jailbreaking can also be composed with other black-box algorithms for even more effective attacks---combining BoN with an optimized prefix attack achieves up to a 35% increase in ASR. Overall, our work indicates that, despite their capability, language models are sensitive to seemingly innocuous changes to inputs, which attackers can exploit across modalities.

The method uses black-box access: it samples variations and checks whether a harmful response occurs. The research examines this behavior across text, vision, and audio systems, using variations appropriate to each input type.

title: Best-of-N Jailbreaking

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are bio-inspired networks that mimic how neurons in the brain communicate through discrete spikes, which have great potential in various tasks due to their energy efficiency and temporal processing capabilities. SNNs with self-attention mechanisms (spiking Transformers) have recently shown great advancements in various tasks, and inspired by traditional Transformers, several studies have demonstrated that spiking absolute positional encoding can help capture sequential relationships for input data, enhancing the capabilities of spiking Transformers for tasks such as sequential modeling and image classification. However, how to incorporate relative positional information into SNNs remains a challenge. In this paper, we introduce several strategies to approximate relative positional encoding (RPE) in spiking Transformers while preserving the binary nature of spikes. Firstly, we formally prove that encoding relative distances with Gray Code ensures that the binary representations of positional indices maintain a constant Hamming distance whenever their decimal values differ by a power of two, and we propose **Gray-PE** based on this property. In addition, we propose another RPE method called **Log-PE**, which combines the logarithmic form of the relative distance matrix directly into the spiking attention map. Furthermore, we extend our RPE methods to a two-dimensional form, making them suitable for processing image patches. We evaluate our RPE methods on various tasks, including time series forecasting, text classification, and patch-based image classification, and the experimental results demonstrate a satisfying performance gain by incorporating our RPE methods across many architectures. Our results provide fresh perspectives on designing spiking Transformers to advance their sequential modeling capability, thereby expanding their applicability across various domains. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/SeqSNN.

Previous work has used absolute positions, while this paper develops ways to approximate relative positional encoding without losing the binary nature of spikes. Relative information lets the architecture represent relationships based on distance between positions.

title: Toward Relative Positional Encoding in Spiking Transformers

abstract: The substantial memory demands of pre-training and fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) require memory-efficient optimization algorithms. One promising approach is layer-wise optimization, which treats each transformer block as a single layer and optimizes it sequentially, while freezing the other layers to save optimizer states and activations. Although effective, these methods ignore the varying importance of the modules within each layer, leading to suboptimal performance. Moreover, layer-wise sampling provides only limited memory savings, as at least one full layer must remain active during optimization. To overcome these limitations, we propose **M**odule-wise **I**mportance **SA**mpling (**MISA**), a novel method that divides each layer into smaller modules and assigns importance scores to each module. MISA uses a weighted random sampling mechanism to activate modules, provably reducing gradient variance compared to layer-wise sampling. Additionally, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ convergence rate under non-convex and stochastic conditions, where $K$ is the total number of training steps, and provide a detailed memory analysis showcasing MISA's superiority over existing baseline methods. Experiments on diverse learning tasks validate the effectiveness of MISA.

paragraphs: MISA reduces the memory needed to train large language models by changing which parts of the network are active during optimization. Existing layer-wise approaches update one transformer block while freezing others, saving optimizer-state and activation memory. However, they still keep a whole block active and do not account for differences in importance within that block.

The proposed method splits each layer into smaller modules and assigns them importance scores. It then uses weighted random sampling to choose which modules to activate. This finer selection creates opportunities for additional memory savings while directing updates according to module importance. The authors prove that the sampling method reduces gradient variance compared with layer-wise sampling.

The analysis also establishes a convergence rate of order 1/√K under non-convex, stochastic conditions, where K is the number of training steps. A separate memory analysis shows advantages over existing baselines, and experiments across diverse learning tasks support the method's effectiveness. Together, these results connect finer-grained update selection with both optimization guarantees and reduced memory requirements.
summary.tldr: MISA samples important sub-layer modules for updates, reducing training memory and gradient variance with a stated stochastic convergence guarantee.

title: MISA: Memory-Efficient LLMs Optimization with Module-wise Importance Sampling

abstract: Real-world objects frequently undergo state transformations. From an apple being cut into pieces to a butterfly emerging from its cocoon, tracking through these changes is important for understanding real-world objects and dynamics. However, existing methods often lose track of the target object after transformation, due to significant changes in object appearance. To address this limitation, we introduce the task of Track Any State: tracking objects through transformations while detecting and describing state changes, accompanied by a new benchmark dataset, VOST-TAS. To tackle this problem, we present TubeletGraph, a zero-shot system that recovers missing objects after transformation and maps out how object states are evolving over time. TubeletGraph first identifies potentially overlooked tracks, and determines whether they should be integrated based on semantic and proximity priors. Then, it reasons about the added tracks and generates a state graph describing each observed transformation. TubeletGraph achieves state-of-the-art tracking performance under transformations, while demonstrating deeper understanding of object transformations and promising capabilities in temporal grounding and semantic reasoning for complex object transformations. Code, additional results, and the benchmark dataset are available at https://tubelet-graph.github.io.
originalAbstract: Real-world objects frequently undergo state transformations. From an apple being cut into pieces to a butterfly emerging from its cocoon, tracking through these changes is important for understanding real-world objects and dynamics. However, existing methods often lose track of the target object after transformation, due to significant changes in object appearance. To address this limitation, we introduce the task of Track Any State: tracking objects through transformations while detecting and describing state changes, accompanied by a new benchmark dataset, VOST-TAS. To tackle this problem, we present TubeletGraph, a zero-shot system that recovers missing objects after transformation and maps out how object states are evolving over time. TubeletGraph first identifies potentially overlooked tracks, and determines whether they should be integrated based on semantic and proximity priors. Then, it reasons about the added tracks and generates a state graph describing each observed transformation. TubeletGraph achieves state-of-the-art tracking performance under transformations, while demonstrating deeper understanding of object transformations and promising capabilities in temporal grounding and semantic reasoning for complex object transformations. Code, additional results, and the benchmark dataset are available at https://tubelet-graph.github.io.

paragraphs: An object's appearance can change dramatically while it remains part of the same unfolding event. Cutting an apple into pieces illustrates why following appearance alone may lose the object of interest. This paper introduces Track Any State, a task that combines tracking through transformations with detecting and describing the associated state changes.

The authors provide the VOST-TAS benchmark and a zero-shot system called TubeletGraph. The system first searches for tracks that may have been overlooked after a transformation. It decides whether to integrate them using semantic relationships and proximity. It then reasons about the added tracks and constructs a state graph recording how the observed object states change over time.

TubeletGraph achieves state-of-the-art tracking performance under transformations in the reported evaluation. It also demonstrates deeper transformation understanding and promising abilities in temporal grounding and semantic reasoning. The contribution extends tracking beyond maintaining a location: the recovered tracks are linked into an account of what changed and when, connecting continuity of observation with an explanation of evolving object states.
summary.tldr: TubeletGraph recovers objects after transformations and builds state graphs describing their changes, alongside a new tracking benchmark.

title: Tracking and Understanding Object Transformations

abstract: Constructing accurate digital twins of articulated objects is essential for robotic simulation training and embodied AI world model building, yet historically requires painstaking manual modeling or multi-stage pipelines. In this work, we propose \textbf{URDF-Anything}, an end-to-end automatic reconstruction framework based on a 3D multimodal large language model (MLLM). URDF-Anything utilizes an autoregressive prediction framework based on point-cloud and text multimodal input to jointly optimize geometric segmentation and kinematic parameter prediction. It implements a specialized [SEG] token mechanism that interacts directly with point cloud features, enabling fine-grained part-level segmentation while maintaining consistency with the kinematic parameter predictions. Experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches regarding geometric segmentation (mIoU 17\% improvement), kinematic parameter prediction (average error reduction of 29\%), and physical executability (surpassing baselines by 50\%). Notably, our method exhibits excellent generalization ability, performing well even on objects outside the training set. This work provides an efficient solution for constructing digital twins for robotic simulation, significantly enhancing the sim-to-real transfer capability.

These results support jointly predicting structure and motion for constructing digital twins, with stated benefits for robotic simulation and transfer to real-world settings.
summary.tldr: URDF-Anything jointly reconstructs object parts and motion parameters from point clouds and text to build articulated digital twins.

title: URDF-Anything: Constructing Articulated Objects with 3D Multimodal Language Model

abstract: We study the problem of preconditioning in the setting of sequential prediction. From the theoretical lens of linear dynamical systems, we show that applying a convolution to the input sequence translates to applying a polynomial to the unknown transition matrix in the hidden space. With this insight, we develop a novel preconditioning method that convolves the input sequence with the coefficients of the Chebyshev or Legendre polynomials. We formally prove that this improves the regret of a wide family of prediction methods. We proceed to apply this preconditioning technique to the method of spectral filtering. This gives the first sublinear regret bound that is also hidden-dimension free (up to logarithmic factors) even when the hidden transition matrix is asymmetric. From rigorous experiments on synthetic data we show that our simple preconditioning method generalizes to both 1) settings where the data is \emph{not} from a linear dynamical system and 2) a broad range of learning algorithms, including recurrent neural networks.

paragraphs: Preconditioning transforms a problem so that a learning method can handle it more effectively. This paper studies that idea for sequential prediction. Through linear dynamical systems, it establishes that convolving an input sequence corresponds to applying a polynomial to the unknown transition matrix governing the hidden dynamics.

That connection motivates filtering input sequences with coefficients from Chebyshev or Legendre polynomials. The authors prove improved regret bounds for a broad family of prediction methods. When applied to spectral filtering, the technique gives a sublinear regret bound that avoids dependence on hidden-state dimension except for logarithmic factors, even when the hidden transition matrix is asymmetric.

Sublinear regret means the accumulated prediction disadvantage grows more slowly than the sequence length, making the theoretical improvement meaningful for sustained prediction. These experiments broaden the evidence for usefulness, while the formal guarantees arise from the paper's theoretical setting.
summary.tldr: Polynomial-based sequence filtering improves theoretical prediction regret and shows empirical benefits beyond linear dynamical systems.

title: Universal Sequence Preconditioning

abstract: Large language models are quickly becoming the foundation for intelligent agents that are capable of using tools. However, training such agents is challenging because it requires human creation and annotation of a diverse set of tasks, tools, and evaluation criteria. In this paper, we propose the Self-Challenging Agent framework for training an agent on high-quality tasks that are generated by itself. The agent first plays the role of challenger and generates a task after interacting with the given tools. The tasks take the form of a novel general class of problems termed Code-as-Task, which are defined by an instruction, a verification function and solution and failure cases which serve as tests, allowing to filter only for high-quality tasks. The agent then takes an executor role and trains on those tasks with reinforcement learning using the evaluation feedback as a reward. We show our method improves the performance of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on two existing multi-turn tool-use agent benchmarks, M$^3$ToolEval and TauBench, with a two-fold average success rate increase, despite using only self-generated training data.

paragraphs: Training a tool-using language-model agent usually requires people to create varied tasks and decide how success should be evaluated. The Self-Challenging Agent framework shifts task creation into the training process itself. An agent generates challenges and then learns to solve the tasks that pass quality checks.

In its challenger role, the agent interacts with the available tools before proposing a task. Each task uses the Code-as-Task format: an instruction, a verification function, and examples of successful and unsuccessful solutions that serve as tests. The reported average success rate doubles. This demonstrates that the framework's generated, testable challenges can provide useful training signals for improving tool-use behavior on the evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: A self-challenging agent creates verifiable tool-use tasks and learns from them, doubling average success on two evaluated benchmarks.

title: Self-Challenging Language Model Agents

abstract: Current benchmarks for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in social media moderation completely overlook a serious threat: covert advertisements, which disguise themselves as regular posts to deceive and mislead consumers into making purchases, leading to significant ethical and legal concerns. In this paper, we present the CHASM, a first-of-its-kind dataset designed to evaluate the capability of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in detecting covert advertisements on social media. CHASM is a high-quality, anonymized, manually curated dataset consisting of 4,992 instances, based on real-world scenarios from the Chinese social media platform Rednote. The dataset was collected and annotated under strict privacy protection and quality control protocols. It includes many product experience sharing posts that closely resemble covert advertisements, making the dataset particularly challenging.The results show that under both zero-shot and in-context learning settings, none of the current MLLMs are sufficiently reliable for detecting covert advertisements.Our further experiments revealed that fine-tuning open-source MLLMs on our dataset yielded noticeable performance gains. However, significant challenges persist, such as detecting subtle cues in comments and differences in visual and textual structures.We provide in-depth error analysis and outline future research directions. We hope our study can serve as a call for the research community and platform moderators to develop more precise defenses against this emerging threat.

paragraphs: CHASM examines whether multimodal language models can recognize advertisements disguised as ordinary social media posts. The central difficulty is that a genuine account of using a product may closely resemble covert promotion. Evaluating this distinction requires examples where promotional intent cannot be inferred simply from the presence of a product or an enthusiastic description.

The authors assemble 4,992 manually curated, anonymized instances based on real-world scenarios from Rednote, a Chinese social media platform. Collection and annotation follow privacy protection and quality control protocols. summary.tldr: CHASM provides a challenging Rednote dataset showing that covert advertising remains difficult for multimodal models to detect reliably.

title: CHASM: Unveiling Covert Advertisements on Chinese Social Media

paragraphs: Constrained expected improvement is a widely used strategy for optimizing a black-box objective while satisfying constraints. Despite its practical success, its theoretical convergence rate had not been established. This paper addresses that gap by bounding simple regret, which measures how far the best feasible result found remains from the optimum.

The analysis considers two mathematical settings. In the first, both the objective and constraint function belong to reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. In the second, both are sampled from Gaussian processes. For squared exponential kernels, the rate is t^(-1/2) times log(t)^((d+1)/2). The Gaussian-process setting obtains the same rates with high probability. These are guarantees under the stated function assumptions, connecting convergence to the selected kernel and problem dimension. Numerical experiments support the analysis. The contribution gives a theoretical basis for an established constrained optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes convergence rates for constrained expected improvement under kernel-space and Gaussian-process assumptions.

title: Convergence Rates of Constrained Expected Improvement

abstract: We introduce Equivariant Neural Eikonal Solvers, a novel framework that integrates Equivariant Neural Fields (ENFs) with Neural Eikonal Solvers. Our approach employs a single neural field where a unified shared backbone is conditioned on signal-specific latent variables – represented as point clouds in a Lie group – to model diverse Eikonal solutions. The ENF integration ensures equivariant mapping from these latent representations to the solution field, delivering three key benefits: enhanced representation efficiency through weight-sharing, robust geometric grounding, and solution steerability. This steerability allows transformations applied to the latent point cloud to induce predictable, geometrically meaningful modifications in the resulting Eikonal solution. By coupling these steerable representations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), our framework accurately models Eikonal travel-time solutions while generalizing to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds with regular group actions. This includes homogeneous spaces such as Euclidean, position–orientation, spherical, and hyperbolic manifolds. We validate our approach through applications in seismic travel-time modeling of 2D, 3D, and spherical benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance, scalability, adaptability, and user controllability compared to existing Neural Operator-based Eikonal solver methods.

title: Equivariant Eikonal Neural Networks: Grid-Free, Scalable Travel-Time Prediction on Homogeneous Spaces

abstract: The widespread use of AI-generated content from diffusion models has raised significant concerns regarding misinformation and copyright infringement. Watermarking is a crucial technique for identifying these AI-generated images and preventing their misuse. In this paper, we introduce *Shallow Diffuse*, a new watermarking technique that embeds robust and invisible watermarks into diffusion model outputs. Unlike existing approaches that integrate watermarking throughout the entire diffusion sampling process, *Shallow Diffuse* decouples these steps by leveraging the presence of a low-dimensional subspace in the image generation process. This method ensures that a substantial portion of the watermark lies in the null space of this subspace, effectively separating it from the image generation process. Our theoretical and empirical analyses show that this decoupling strategy greatly enhances the consistency of data generation and the detectability of the watermark. Extensive experiments further validate that *Shallow Diffuse* outperforms existing watermarking methods in terms of consistency.

paragraphs: Shallow Diffuse embeds watermarks in diffusion-generated images so that their artificial origin can be identified. The method aims for watermarks that remain detectable without becoming visible in the image. Its central concern is separating watermark insertion from image generation, since existing approaches incorporate watermarking throughout the diffusion sampling process.

It places a substantial portion of the watermark in that subspace's null space, separating much of the watermark signal from the generation process. This geometric construction is the mechanism for decoupling the two operations while retaining a signal that can be detected.

Theoretical and empirical analyses show improved generation consistency and watermark detectability from this separation. Further experiments report better consistency than existing watermarking methods. The contribution therefore links the placement of a watermark to how strongly it interacts with image generation, providing evidence that exploiting the process's subspace structure can support both consistent outputs and identifiable watermarks.
summary.tldr: Shallow Diffuse separates watermark signals from diffusion image generation through subspace structure, improving consistency and detectability.

title: Shallow Diffuse: Robust and Invisible Watermarking through Low-Dim Subspaces in Diffusion Models

abstract: Large language models are known to memorize parts of their training data, posing risk of copyright violations. To systematically examine this risk, we pretrain language models (1B/3B/8B) from scratch on 83B tokens, mixing web-scale data with public domain books used to simulate copyrighted content at controlled frequencies at lengths at least ten times longer than prior work. We thereby identified the offset effect, a phenomenon characterized by two key findings: (1) verbatim memorization is most strongly triggered by short prefixes drawn from the beginning of the context window, with memorization decreasing counterintuitively as prefix length increases; and (2) a sharp decline in verbatim recall when prefix begins offset from the initial tokens of the context window. We attribute this to positional fragility: models rely disproportionately on the earliest tokens in their context window as retrieval anchors, making them sensitive to even slight shifts. We further observe that when the model fails to retrieve memorized content, it often produces degenerated text. Leveraging these findings, we show that shifting sensitive data deeper into the context window suppresses both extractable memorization and degeneration. Our results suggest that positional offset is a critical and previously overlooked axis for evaluating memorization risks, since prior work implicitly assumed uniformity by probing only from the beginning of documents or training sequences.

summary.tldr: Controlled training experiments show that verbatim recall can depend sharply on prefix position, making positional offset important for memorization evaluation.

title: Positional Fragility in LLMs: How Offset Effects Reshape Our Understanding of Memorization Risks

abstract: Accurate identification and localization of objects in 3-D scenes are essential for advancing comprehensive 3-D scene understanding. Although diffusion models have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a broad spectrum of computer vision tasks, their potential in both 2-D and 3-D object detection remains underexplored. Existing approaches typically formulate detection as a ''noise-to-box'' process, but they rely heavily on direct coordinate regression, which limits adaptability for more advanced tasks such as grounding-based object detection. To overcome these challenges, we propose a promptable 3-D object recognition framework, which introduces a diffusion-based paradigm for flexible and conditionally guided 3-D object detection. Our approach encodes bounding boxes into latent representations and employs latent diffusion models to realize a ''promptable noise-to-box'' transformation. This formulation enables the refinement of standard 3-D object detection using textual prompts, such as class labels. Moreover, it naturally extends to grounding object detection through conditioning on natural language descriptions, and generalizes effectively to few-shot learning by incorporating annotated exemplars as visual prompts. We conduct thorough evaluations on three key 3-D object recognition tasks: general 3-D object detection, few-shot detection, and grounding-based detection. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art methods, validating its effectiveness, versatility, and broad applicability in 3-D computer vision.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional object detection must locate objects in a scene, and different applications may specify the desired object in different ways. Existing diffusion-based detectors often generate boxes through direct coordinate regression. This paper argues that this formulation limits adaptability, particularly when detection needs to follow a natural-language description.

The proposed framework encodes bounding boxes as latent representations and applies diffusion within that space. Prompts condition the transformation from noise to a box representation. Class labels can refine ordinary detection, natural-language descriptions enable grounding-based detection, and annotated examples act as visual prompts for few-shot detection. The shared formulation accommodates these different sources of guidance.

The authors evaluate the framework on general detection, few-shot detection, and grounding-based detection in three-dimensional scenes. Results are competitive with state-of-the-art methods across these tasks. The contribution is a flexible detection mechanism that connects latent box generation with several prompt types, showing how one diffusion-based formulation can support distinct ways of specifying which objects to find.
summary.tldr: Latent diffusion generates 3-D bounding boxes conditioned on class names, natural-language descriptions, or annotated visual examples.

title: Promptable 3-D Object Localization with Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: We introduce a simple, general framework for likelihood-free Bayesian reinforcement learning, through Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC). The advantage is that we only require a prior distribution on a class of simulators. This is useful when a probabilistic model of the underlying process is too complex to formulate, but where detailed simulation models are available. ABC-RL allows the use of any Bayesian reinforcement learning technique in this case. It can be seen as an extension of simulation methods to both planning and inference. We experimentally demonstrate the potential of this approach in a comparison with LSPI. Finally, we introduce a theorem showing that ABC is sound.

paragraphs: Bayesian reinforcement learning must connect observations of an environment with uncertainty about how that environment works. This can be difficult when a detailed simulator exists but writing down a probabilistic model of the underlying process is too complex. The paper proposes ABC-RL, a general framework that uses Approximate Bayesian Computation to support learning in this situation.

Its key requirement is a prior distribution over a class of simulators. This lets the framework approach inference without requiring an explicitly formulated likelihood for the process. The authors describe ABC-RL as allowing any Bayesian reinforcement learning technique to be used in this setting. Simulation consequently supports both planning what to do and inference about the environment.

The paper supplies an experimental comparison with LSPI to demonstrate the approach's potential. It also introduces a theorem establishing the soundness of ABC. These contributions address different questions: the experiments illustrate practical promise, while the theorem supplies theoretical support for the inference approach. The stated practical opportunity is to make detailed simulation models usable within Bayesian reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: ABC-RL enables likelihood-free Bayesian reinforcement learning using a prior over simulators, with theoretical support and an experimental demonstration.

title: ABC Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This work focuses on dynamic regret of online convex optimization that compares the performance of online learning to a clairvoyant who knows the sequence of loss functions in advance and hence selects the minimizer of the loss function at each step. By assuming that the clairvoyant moves slowly (i.e., the minimizers change slowly), we present several improved variation-based upper bounds of the dynamic regret under the true and noisy gradient feedback, which are \it optimal in light of the presented lower bounds. The key to our analysis is to explore a regularity metric that measures the temporal changes in the clairvoyant’s minimizers, to which we refer as path variation. Firstly, we present a general lower bound in terms of the path variation, and then show that under full information or gradient feedback we are able to achieve an optimal dynamic regret. Secondly, we present a lower bound with noisy gradient feedback and then show that we can achieve optimal dynamic regrets under a stochastic gradient feedback and two-point bandit feedback. Moreover, for a sequence of smooth loss functions that admit a small variation in the gradients, our dynamic regret under the two-point bandit feedback matches that is achieved with full information.

paragraphs: The paper evaluates online learning against a demanding comparator: a decision maker who knows all future loss functions and chooses a separate minimizer at every step. Dynamic regret measures the learner’s shortfall against this changing sequence. The analysis assumes that these minimizers move slowly and quantifies their movement through a measure called path variation.

The authors derive lower bounds in terms of that variation, then establish upper bounds that match them under several feedback settings. These include full information, exact gradients, stochastic gradients, and two-point bandit feedback. summary.tldr: Matching regret bounds characterize how well online learners can track slowly changing minimizers under exact, noisy, and bandit feedback.

title: Tracking Slowly Moving Clairvoyant: Optimal Dynamic Regret of Online Learning with True and Noisy Gradient

abstract: Low-Rank Representation (LRR) has been a significant method for segmenting data that are generated from a union of subspaces. It is also known that solving LRR is challenging in terms of time complexity and memory footprint, in that the size of the nuclear norm regularized matrix is n-by-n (where n is the number of samples). In this paper, we thereby develop a novel online implementation of LRR that reduces the memory cost from O(n^2) to O(pd), with p being the ambient dimension and d being some estimated rank (d < p < n). We also establish the theoretical guarantee that the sequence of solutions produced by our algorithm converges to a stationary point of the expected loss function asymptotically. Extensive experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets further substantiate that our algorithm is fast, robust and memory efficient.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Representation is used to separate data generated from a union of subspaces. Its computational burden includes working with a nuclear-norm-regularized matrix containing one row and column per sample. For n samples, that matrix has n squared entries, making memory consumption a substantial obstacle as the dataset grows.

This paper develops an online implementation that reduces memory cost from O(n^2) to O(pd). Here, p is the ambient dimension and d is an estimated rank, with d < p < n. The stated ordering makes the difference meaningful: storage depends on the ambient dimension and estimated rank instead of a matrix covering every pair of samples.

The authors prove that the generated solution sequence converges asymptotically to a stationary point of the expected loss. This is a stationary-point guarantee, rather than a claim of global optimality. Experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets further support the method's speed, robustness, and memory efficiency, connecting the storage improvement with practical evidence and an accompanying convergence result.
summary.tldr: An online Low-Rank Representation method reduces memory to O(pd) and converges asymptotically to a stationary point.

title: Online Low-Rank Subspace Clustering by Basis Dictionary Pursuit

abstract: Accelerated coordinate descent is widely used in optimization due to its cheap per-iteration cost and scalability to large-scale problems. Up to a primal-dual transformation, it is also the same as accelerated stochastic gradient descent that is one of the central methods used in machine learning. In this paper, we improve the best known running time of accelerated coordinate descent by a factor up to \sqrtn. Our improvement is based on a clean, novel non-uniform sampling that selects each coordinate with a probability proportional to the square root of its smoothness parameter. Our proof technique also deviates from the classical estimation sequence technique used in prior work. Our speed-up applies to important problems such as empirical risk minimization and solving linear systems, both in theory and in practice.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent updates selected coordinates of an optimization problem, keeping individual iterations inexpensive. Its accelerated form is useful for large problems and is connected, through a primal-dual transformation, to accelerated stochastic gradient descent. This paper improves the running-time guarantees by changing how the coordinate for each update is selected.

The proposed rule samples each coordinate with probability proportional to the square root of its smoothness parameter. Smoothness describes how sensitively the objective changes along a coordinate, so the sampling probabilities reflect differences in the optimization problem. The authors also introduce a proof approach that departs from the estimation-sequence technique used in earlier analyses.

The resulting improvement over the best known running time can be as large as a factor of the square root of n. That is a possible gain, rather than a fixed speedup promised for every problem. The paper reports theoretical and practical benefits for empirical risk minimization and linear-system solving, showing that the sampling change has consequences for important computational tasks.
summary.tldr: Sampling coordinates according to square-root smoothness improves accelerated coordinate descent by up to a square-root-of-n factor.

title: Even Faster Accelerated Coordinate Descent Using Non-Uniform Sampling

abstract: Gatys et al. recently demonstrated that deep networks can generate beautiful textures and stylized images from a single texture example. However, their methods requires a slow and memory-consuming optimization process. We propose here an alternative approach that moves the computational burden to a learning stage. Given a single example of a texture, our approach trains compact feed-forward convolutional networks to generate multiple samples of the same texture of arbitrary size and to transfer artistic style from a given image to any other image. The resulting networks are remarkably light-weight and can generate textures of quality comparable to Gatys et al., but hundreds of times faster. More generally, our approach highlights the power and flexibility of generative feed-forward models trained with complex and expressive loss functions.

paragraphs: This paper accelerates texture synthesis and artistic style transfer by moving expensive computation into a learning stage. The earlier approach discussed in the abstract generates images through a slow, memory-intensive optimization process. Here, a compact convolutional network is trained so that producing an image can subsequently use a feed-forward computation.

Given a single texture example, the trained network can generate multiple samples of that texture at arbitrary sizes. The approach also supports transferring the artistic style of a given image to other images. Training therefore constructs a reusable generator, allowing the learned computation to serve repeated synthesis requests.

The authors report texture quality comparable to the earlier method while generating textures hundreds of times faster. This speed claim concerns generation with the resulting networks, consistent with shifting work to training. More broadly, the paper demonstrates the usefulness of training feed-forward generative models with complex, expressive loss functions: an elaborate training objective can lead to a lightweight model for producing outputs.
summary.tldr: Compact trained networks generate textures of comparable quality to an optimization-based method hundreds of times faster.

title: Texture Networks: Feed-forward Synthesis of Textures and Stylized Images

abstract: Learning discrete representations of data is a central machine learning task because of the compactness of the representations and ease of interpretation. The task includes clustering and hash learning as special cases. Deep neural networks are promising to be used because they can model the non-linearity of data and scale to large datasets. However, their model complexity is huge, and therefore, we need to carefully regularize the networks in order to learn useful representations that exhibit intended invariance for applications of interest. To this end, we propose a method called Information Maximizing Self-Augmented Training (IMSAT). In IMSAT, we use data augmentation to impose the invariance on discrete representations. More specifically, we encourage the predicted representations of augmented data points to be close to those of the original data points in an end-to-end fashion. At the same time, we maximize the information-theoretic dependency between data and their predicted discrete representations. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that IMSAT produces state-of-the-art results for both clustering and unsupervised hash learning.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning compact discrete representations, including cluster assignments and hash codes. Deep networks can capture nonlinear patterns and handle large datasets, but their flexibility makes regularization important. A useful representation should preserve relevant information while remaining stable under transformations that an application intends to treat as equivalent.

Information Maximizing Self-Augmented Training, or IMSAT, combines two objectives. Data augmentation encourages an original example and its transformed versions to receive similar predicted representations. At the same time, the method maximizes the information-theoretic dependence between inputs and their discrete representations. Both goals are incorporated into end-to-end training.

The combination matters because stability alone does not express the need for informative representations. IMSAT explicitly asks for both the chosen invariances and a strong connection to the data. Extensive benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art results for clustering and unsupervised hash learning. These findings support the proposed pairing of augmentation-based regularization with information maximization across two tasks that share the need for compact, meaningful discrete outputs.
summary.tldr: IMSAT learns informative discrete representations by combining augmentation-based consistency with information maximization.

title: Learning Discrete Representations via Information Maximizing Self-Augmented Training

abstract: We examine the impact of learning Lipschitz continuous models in the context of model-based reinforcement learning. We provide a novel bound on multi-step prediction error of Lipschitz models where we quantify the error using the Wasserstein metric. We go on to prove an error bound for the value-function estimate arising from Lipschitz models and show that the estimated value function is itself Lipschitz. We conclude with empirical results that show the benefits of controlling the Lipschitz constant of neural-network models.
originalAbstract: We examine the impact of learning Lipschitz continuous models in the context of model-based reinforcement learning. We provide a novel bound on multi-step prediction error of Lipschitz models where we quantify the error using the Wasserstein metric. We go on to prove an error bound for the value-function estimate arising from Lipschitz models and show that the estimated value function is itself Lipschitz. We conclude with empirical results that show the benefits of controlling the Lipschitz constant of neural-network models.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned model to reason about how a system evolves. This paper examines the role of Lipschitz continuity in such models. A Lipschitz constraint controls how much a model's output can change when its input changes, making that sensitivity a quantity that can be analyzed and regulated.

The authors derive a bound on prediction error over multiple steps, measuring error with the Wasserstein metric. This connects model regularity to the accuracy of predictions obtained by repeatedly using the model. They also prove a bound on the resulting value-function estimation error, extending the analysis from predicting system evolution to estimating its value.

A further result shows that the estimated value function is itself Lipschitz continuous. The paper therefore links regularity of the learned model with both prediction accuracy and properties of the value estimate. Empirical results demonstrate benefits from controlling the Lipschitz constant of neural-network models, supporting the practical relevance of the quantities examined in the theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: Lipschitz constraints connect learned-model sensitivity to bounds on multistep prediction and value-estimation errors in reinforcement learning.

title: Lipschitz Continuity in Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We tackle the problem of optimizing a black-box objective function defined over a highly-structured input space. This problem is ubiquitous in science and engineering. In machine learning, inferring the structure of a neural network or the Automatic Statistician (AS), where the optimal kernel combination for a Gaussian process is selected, are two important examples. We use the \as as a case study to describe our approach, that can be easily generalized to other domains. We propose an Structure Generating Variational Auto-encoder (SG-VAE) to embed the original space of kernel combinations into some low-dimensional continuous manifold where Bayesian optimization (BO) ideas are used. This is possible when structural knowledge of the problem is available, which can be given via a simulator or any other form of generating potentially good solutions. The right exploration-exploitation balance is imposed by propagating into the search the uncertainty of the latent space of the SG-VAE, that is computed using variational inference. The key aspect of our approach is that the SG-VAE can be used to bias the search towards relevant regions, making it suitable for transfer learning tasks. Several experiments in various application domains are used to illustrate the utility and generality of the approach described in this work.

paragraphs: Optimizing a black-box objective becomes difficult when candidate inputs have rich structure, such as combinations of Gaussian-process kernels. This paper uses the Automatic Statistician as a case study for turning that structured search into a continuous optimization problem. A Structure Generating Variational Auto-encoder embeds kernel combinations into a low-dimensional continuous space.

Bayesian optimization then operates in this learned space. The approach requires structural knowledge, which can come from a simulator or another mechanism for generating potentially good solutions. Variational inference estimates uncertainty in the auto-encoder’s latent space, and that uncertainty is propagated into the search to balance exploring unfamiliar candidates against exploiting promising ones.

The learned representation can bias optimization toward relevant parts of the search space, making the method suitable for transfer-learning tasks. Experiments across several application domains illustrate its utility and generality. The contribution is a way to combine available structural knowledge, learned continuous representations, and uncertainty-aware search so that optimization can work with complex candidates through a more manageable space.
summary.tldr: A structure-generating variational auto-encoder enables uncertainty-aware Bayesian optimization over complex candidates using available structural knowledge.

title: Structured Variationally Auto-encoded Optimization

abstract: We propose a novel method for imputing missing data by adapting the well-known Generative Adversarial Nets (GAN) framework. Accordingly, we call our method Generative Adversarial Imputation Nets (GAIN). The generator (G) observes some components of a real data vector, imputes the missing components conditioned on what is actually observed, and outputs a completed vector. The discriminator (D) then takes a completed vector and attempts to determine which components were actually observed and which were imputed. To ensure that D forces G to learn the desired distribution, we provide D with some additional information in the form of a hint vector. The hint reveals to D partial information about the missingness of the original sample, which is used by D to focus its attention on the imputation quality of particular components. This hint ensures that G does in fact learn to generate according to the true data distribution. We tested our method on various datasets and found that GAIN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods.

paragraphs: GAIN adapts adversarial learning to filling missing entries in data. Its generator receives the observed components of a data vector and uses them to generate replacements for the missing components. The output is a completed vector that combines real observations with generated values.

The discriminator examines that vector and predicts which individual components were originally observed and which were filled in. The method also gives the discriminator a hint containing partial information about the original missingness pattern. This information focuses the discriminator’s attention on the quality of particular imputations. The hint is central to the authors’ argument that the generator learns the true data distribution.

This setup makes imputation depend on the available information within each sample, while adversarial feedback evaluates the generated components. Across the datasets tested, the authors report that GAIN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods. The findings support the proposed combination of component-level discrimination and missingness hints as an effective way to learn data completion.
summary.tldr: GAIN fills missing data through adversarial learning, using partial missingness hints to guide component-level discrimination.

title: GAIN: Missing Data Imputation using Generative Adversarial Nets

abstract: Active learning methods, like uncertainty sampling, combined with probabilistic prediction techniques have achieved success in various problems like image classification and text classification. For more complex multivariate prediction tasks, the relationships between labels play an important role in designing structured classifiers with better performance. However, computational time complexity limits prevalent probabilistic methods from effectively supporting active learning. Specifically, while non-probabilistic methods based on structured support vector ma-chines can be tractably applied to predicting cuts and bipartite matchings, conditional random fields are intractable for these structures. We propose an adversarial approach for active learning with structured prediction domains that is tractable for cuts and matching. We evaluate this approach algorithmically in two important structured prediction problems: multi-label classification and object tracking in videos. We demonstrate better accuracy and computational efficiency for our proposed method.

paragraphs: Active learning uses a prediction model to help decide which examples should receive labels. Probabilistic methods can support this process through uncertainty, but structured prediction makes the calculation harder: a prediction contains several related labels whose dependencies matter. Treating those labels separately can miss the structure the classifier needs to represent.

The paper focuses on predictions involving cuts and bipartite matchings. For these structures, it identifies a computational mismatch: structured support vector machines can make tractable non-probabilistic predictions, whereas conditional random fields are intractable. The authors propose an adversarial approach that makes active learning tractable for these structured domains, addressing the computational obstacle to using relationships among labels.

The approach is evaluated on multi-label classification and tracking objects in video. The authors report improvements in both accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution therefore concerns more than prediction quality alone: it provides a workable active learning approach for structures where prevalent probabilistic methods impose prohibitive computational demands.
summary.tldr: An adversarial approach makes active learning tractable for cuts and matchings, with reported accuracy and efficiency improvements on structured prediction tasks.

title: Active Learning for Probabilistic Structured Prediction of Cuts and Matchings

abstract: Dual Principal Component Pursuit (DPCP) is a recently proposed non-convex optimization based method for learning subspaces of high relative dimension from noiseless datasets contaminated by as many outliers as the square of the number of inliers. Experimentally, DPCP has proved to be robust to noise and outperform the popular RANSAC on 3D vision tasks such as road plane detection and relative poses estimation from three views. This paper extends the global optimality and convergence theory of DPCP to the case of data corrupted by noise, and further demonstrates its robustness using synthetic and real data.
