Experimentally, DPCP has proved to be robust to noise and outperform the popular RANSAC on 3D vision tasks such as road plane detection and relative poses estimation from three views. This paper extends the global optimality and convergence theory of DPCP to the case of data corrupted by noise, and further demonstrates its robustness using synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Dual Principal Component Pursuit learns a subspace from data containing outliers through non-convex optimization. Earlier work addressed noiseless data and subspaces of high relative dimension, including settings with outlier counts as large as the square of the inlier count. This paper extends the theoretical investigation to observations corrupted by noise.

The motivation is a gap between theory and observed behavior. DPCP had already shown experimental robustness to noise and had outperformed RANSAC on three-dimensional vision tasks, including road-plane detection and relative-pose estimation from three views. Those results suggested value beyond the noiseless setting covered by the earlier theory.

The paper extends both global-optimality and convergence theory to noisy data and adds demonstrations on synthetic and real datasets. These contributions address two connected questions: what can be established about the optimization solution, and how the method behaves when applied to contaminated observations. The earlier noiseless outlier tolerance provides context; the abstract does not state that the same quantitative tolerance transfers unchanged to noise.
summary.tldr: The paper extends DPCP’s global-optimality and convergence theory to noisy data and further demonstrates its robustness.

title: Noisy Dual Principal Component Pursuit

abstract: Most deep learning classification studies assume clean data. However, when dealing with the real world data, we encounter three problems such as 1) missing data, 2) class imbalance, and 3) missing label problems. These problems undermine the performance of a classifier. Various preprocessing techniques have been proposed to mitigate one of these problems, but an algorithm that assumes and resolves all three problems together has not been proposed yet. In this paper, we propose HexaGAN, a generative adversarial network framework that shows promising classification performance for all three problems. We interpret the three problems from a single perspective to solve them jointly. To enable this, the framework consists of six components, which interact with each other. We also devise novel loss functions corresponding to the architecture. The designed loss functions allow us to achieve state-of-the-art imputation performance, with up to a 14% improvement, and to generate high-quality class-conditional data. We evaluate the classification performance (F1-score) of the proposed method with 20% missingness and confirm up to a 5% improvement in comparison with the performance of combinations of state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Real-world classification data can have missing values, uneven class frequencies, and missing labels at the same time. Each problem can weaken a classifier, yet preprocessing methods often address them separately. HexaGAN is a generative adversarial framework designed to handle all three together through a shared perspective.

The framework contains six interacting components and loss functions designed for that architecture. Their joint operation supports both filling in missing values and generating data conditioned on class. The approach matters because it treats the three data problems as connected parts of one learning task, rather than assuming the other problems have already been resolved.

The authors report state-of-the-art imputation performance, with improvements of up to 14%, alongside high-quality class-conditional generation. In classification experiments with 20% missingness, they report F1-score improvements of up to 5% over combinations of state-of-the-art methods. These are reported upper-end improvements in the evaluated settings, supporting the promise of jointly addressing imperfect data within a single framework.
summary.tldr: HexaGAN jointly handles missing values, class imbalance, and missing labels, improving imputation and classification in the reported experiments.

title: HexaGAN: Generative Adversarial Nets for Real World Classification

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are instrumental in modelling sequential and time-series data. Yet, when using RNNs to inform decision-making, predictions by themselves are not sufficient {—} we also need estimates of predictive uncertainty. Existing approaches for uncertainty quantification in RNNs are based predominantly on Bayesian methods; these are computationally prohibitive, and require major alterations to the RNN architecture and training. Capitalizing on ideas from classical jackknife resampling, we develop a frequentist alternative that: (a) does not interfere with model training or compromise its accuracy, (b) applies to any RNN architecture, and (c) provides theoretical coverage guarantees on the estimated uncertainty intervals. Our method derives predictive uncertainty from the variability of the (jackknife) sampling distribution of the RNN outputs, which is estimated by repeatedly deleting “blocks” of (temporally-correlated) training data, and collecting the predictions of the RNN re-trained on the remaining data. To avoid exhaustive re-training, we utilize influence functions to estimate the effect of removing training data blocks on the learned RNN parameters. Using data from a critical care setting, we demonstrate the utility of uncertainty quantification in sequential decision-making.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks make predictions from sequences, but decisions based on those predictions also need an indication of uncertainty. The paper develops a frequentist approach that can be applied to any RNN architecture without changing its training or compromising predictive accuracy. Its uncertainty intervals come with theoretical coverage guarantees.

The method draws on jackknife resampling, estimating variability by considering what would happen if portions of the training data were removed. Because sequence observations are temporally correlated, the removed units are blocks of data. Predictions from models trained on the remaining data define the sampling variability used to construct uncertainty estimates.

Exhaustively retraining an RNN for these removals would be expensive. The authors instead use influence functions to estimate how deleting each block changes the learned parameters. This approximates the effects needed for blockwise jackknife estimation without carrying out every retraining operation. An application using critical-care data demonstrates the usefulness of the uncertainty estimates for sequential decision-making.
summary.tldr: Blockwise influence functions estimate jackknife uncertainty for RNN predictions without exhaustive retraining, with theoretical coverage guarantees.

title: Frequentist Uncertainty in Recurrent Neural Networks via Blockwise Influence Functions

abstract: We introduce a novel approach to endowing neural networks with emergent, long-term, large-scale memory. Distinct from strategies that connect neural networks to external memory banks via intricately crafted controllers and hand-designed attentional mechanisms, our memory is internal, distributed, co-located alongside computation, and implicitly addressed, while being drastically simpler than prior efforts. Architecting networks with multigrid structure and connectivity, while distributing memory cells alongside computation throughout this topology, we observe the emergence of coherent memory subsystems. Our hierarchical spatial organization, parameterized convolutionally, permits efficient instantiation of large-capacity memories, while multigrid topology provides short internal routing pathways, allowing convolutional networks to efficiently approximate the behavior of fully connected networks. Such networks have an implicit capacity for internal attention; augmented with memory, they learn to read and write specific memory locations in a dynamic data-dependent manner. We demonstrate these capabilities on exploration and mapping tasks, where our network is able to self-organize and retain long-term memory for trajectories of thousands of time steps. On tasks decoupled from any notion of spatial geometry: sorting, associative recall, and question answering, our design functions as a truly generic memory and yields excellent results.

The design aims to provide large memory capacity while allowing memory access to emerge through the network’s learned internal behavior.

Multigrid connectivity supplies short routes between internal locations, helping a convolutional network approximate fully connected behavior efficiently. With memory added, the network learns data-dependent reading and writing at particular locations. The authors observe coherent memory subsystems emerging from this organization, without requiring an external memory bank controlled by a separately crafted attention mechanism.

On exploration and mapping tasks, the network self-organizes and retains information over trajectories lasting thousands of time steps. It also performs well on sorting, associative recall, and question answering, which do not depend on spatial geometry. These results support the usefulness of the memory architecture beyond spatial tasks: a spatially organized network can learn memory operations for several kinds of information processing.
summary.tldr: A multigrid network learns internal memory access and retains information across long trajectories and nonspatial reasoning tasks.

title: Multigrid Neural Memory

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved great empirical successes in various domains. However, the large search space of neural networks requires a large amount of data, which makes the current RL algorithms not sample efficient. Motivated by the fact that many environments with continuous state space have smooth transitions, we propose to learn a smooth policy that behaves smoothly with respect to states. We develop a new framework — \textbf{S}mooth \textbf{R}egularized \textbf{R}einforcement \textbf{L}earning ($\textbf{SR}^2\textbf{L}$), where the policy is trained with smoothness-inducing regularization. Such regularization effectively constrains the search space, and enforces smoothness in the learned policy. Moreover, our proposed framework can also improve the robustness of policy against measurement error in the state space, and can be naturally extended to distribubutionally robust setting. We apply the proposed framework to both on-policy (TRPO) and off-policy algorithm (DDPG). Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our method achieves improved sample efficiency and robustness.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning searches a large space of neural-network policies, which can demand substantial amounts of experience. This paper draws on the observation that many continuous-state environments have smooth transitions. It proposes encouraging a corresponding smoothness in the policy, so that small changes in the observed state do not produce unnecessarily abrupt changes in behavior.

The resulting framework, Smooth Regularized Reinforcement Learning, adds smoothness-inducing regularization during policy training. This constrains the space of policies the learner explores while directly shaping how the learned policy responds to nearby states. The same mechanism can improve robustness to state measurement errors, because those errors perturb the inputs on which decisions depend.

The authors apply the framework to TRPO, an on-policy algorithm, and DDPG, an off-policy algorithm. Their experiments report improvements in both sample efficiency and robustness. They also describe a natural extension to a distributionally robust setting. The contribution is a training framework that can strengthen existing learning algorithms by encoding a useful smoothness preference, motivated by the behavior of many continuous environments.
summary.tldr: Smoothness regularization improves sample efficiency and robustness in experiments with both on-policy and off-policy reinforcement learning.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Robust and Smooth Policy

abstract: We consider the problem of the limited-bandwidth communication for multi-agent reinforcement learning, where agents cooperate with the assistance of a communication protocol and a scheduler. The protocol and scheduler jointly determine which agent is communicating what message and to whom. Under the limited bandwidth constraint, a communication protocol is required to generate informative messages. Meanwhile, an unnecessary communication connection should not be established because it occupies limited resources in vain. In this paper, we develop an Informative Multi-Agent Communication (IMAC) method to learn efficient communication protocols as well as scheduling. First, from the perspective of communication theory, we prove that the limited bandwidth constraint requires low-entropy messages throughout the transmission. Then inspired by the information bottleneck principle, we learn a valuable and compact communication protocol and a weight-based scheduler. To demonstrate the efficiency of our method, we conduct extensive experiments in various cooperative and competitive multi-agent tasks with different numbers of agents and different bandwidths. We show that IMAC converges faster and leads to efficient communication among agents under the limited bandwidth as compared to many baseline methods.

paragraphs: When learning agents communicate over limited bandwidth, they must choose both useful messages and useful connections. A communication protocol determines message content, while a scheduler helps determine who communicates with whom. This paper treats those choices together, since an informative message can still waste resources if the communication connection is unnecessary.

The proposed Informative Multi-Agent Communication method, or IMAC, draws on the information bottleneck principle to learn compact, valuable messages. The authors first establish a communication-theoretic result connecting bandwidth limits to the need for low-entropy messages during transmission. They then combine the learned protocol with a weight-based scheduler, addressing message content and communication allocation within the same method.

Experiments cover cooperative and competitive tasks with different numbers of agents and different bandwidths. IMAC converges faster and communicates efficiently under bandwidth limits compared with many baseline methods. These findings support jointly learning what to transmit and which connections to establish, with the information bottleneck supplying a principled motivation for keeping messages compact.
summary.tldr: IMAC jointly learns compact messages and communication scheduling to help agents coordinate under limited bandwidth.

title: Learning Efficient Multi-agent Communication: An Information Bottleneck Approach

abstract: We propose Zeno++, a new robust asynchronous Stochastic Gradient Descent(SGD) procedure, intended to tolerate Byzantine failures of workers. In contrast to previous work, Zeno++ removes several unrealistic restrictions on worker-server communication, now allowing for fully asynchronous updates from anonymous workers, for arbitrarily stale worker updates, and for the possibility of an unbounded number of Byzantine workers. The key idea is to estimate the descent of the loss value after the candidate gradient is applied, where large descent values indicate that the update results in optimization progress. We prove the convergence of Zeno++ for non-convex problems under Byzantine failures. Experimental results show that Zeno++ outperforms existing Byzantine-tolerant asynchronous SGD algorithms.

paragraphs: Distributed training can receive faulty or malicious updates from workers, a problem described as Byzantine failure. Zeno++ is an asynchronous SGD procedure designed to tolerate such failures while relaxing restrictions on communication. It allows anonymous workers, arbitrarily stale updates, and the possibility of an unbounded number of Byzantine workers.

The central idea is to estimate how much the loss would decrease after applying a candidate gradient. A larger estimated decrease indicates that the update would contribute to optimization progress. This makes the proposed update's effect on the objective the key signal for assessing it, fitting the setting where worker identity and update freshness may be unreliable.

The authors prove convergence for nonconvex problems under Byzantine failures. Experiments also show better performance than existing Byzantine-tolerant asynchronous SGD algorithms. The contribution combines a progress-based assessment of candidate gradients with a communication model that supports fully asynchronous operation. Its theoretical and empirical results address robustness while accommodating worker updates that previous approaches restricted.
summary.tldr: Zeno++ assesses updates by estimated loss reduction to support Byzantine-tolerant SGD with anonymous workers and arbitrarily stale asynchronous updates.

title: Zeno++: Robust Fully Asynchronous SGD

abstract: Weighted model integration (WMI) is an appealing framework for probabilistic inference: it allows for expressing the complex dependencies in real-world problems, where variables are both continuous and discrete, via the language of Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT), as well as to compute probabilistic queries with complex logical and arithmetic constraints. Yet, existing WMI solvers are not ready to scale to these problems. They either ignore the intrinsic dependency structure of the problem entirely, or they are limited to overly restrictive structures. To narrow this gap, we derive a factorized WMI computation enabling us to devise a scalable WMI solver based on message passing, called MP-WMI. Namely, MP-WMI is the first WMI solver that can (i) perform exact inference on the full class of tree-structured WMI problems, and (ii) perform inter-query amortization, e.g., to compute all marginal densities simultaneously. Experimental results show that our solver dramatically outperforms the existingWMI solvers on a large set of benchmarks.

They either ignore the intrinsic dependency structure of the problem entirely, or they are limited to overly restrictive structures. To narrow this gap, we derive a factorized WMI computation enabling us to devise a scalable WMI solver based on message passing, called MP-WMI. paragraphs: Weighted model integration, or WMI, supports probabilistic reasoning with both discrete and continuous variables under logical and arithmetic constraints. Its expressive language can capture complex dependencies, but exploiting those dependencies computationally is difficult. The paper argues that existing solvers either ignore the dependency structure or support structures that are too restrictive.

The authors derive a factorized form of WMI computation and use it to build MP-WMI, a message-passing solver. This formulation enables exact inference across the full class of tree-structured WMI problems. The structural scope matters: the stated exact-inference capability applies to tree-structured problems, rather than all possible dependency graphs.

MP-WMI also shares computation across different queries, a capability called inter-query amortization. For example, it can compute all marginal densities simultaneously instead of treating each as an independent task. Experiments show dramatic improvements over existing WMI solvers across a large benchmark collection. The contribution combines broader structural support with reusable computation to make expressive hybrid probabilistic inference more scalable.
summary.tldr: MP-WMI uses factorization and message passing for exact tree-structured hybrid inference while sharing computation across queries.

title: Scaling up Hybrid Probabilistic Inference with Logical and Arithmetic Constraints via Message Passing

abstract: Markov decision processes (MDPs) are known to be sensitive to parameter specification. Distributionally robust MDPs alleviate this issue by allowing for \textit{ambiguity sets} which give a set of possible distributions over parameter sets. The goal is to find an optimal policy with respect to the worst-case parameter distribution. We propose a framework for solving Distributionally robust MDPs via first-order methods, and instantiate it for several types of Wasserstein ambiguity sets. By developing efficient proximal updates, our algorithms achieve a convergence rate of $O\left(NA^{2.5}S^{3.5}\log(S)\log(\epsilon^{-1})\epsilon^{-1.5} \right)$ for the number of kernels $N$ in the support of the nominal distribution, states $S$, and actions $A$; this rate varies slightly based on the Wasserstein setup. Our dependence on $N,A$ and $S$ is significantly better than existing methods, which have a complexity of $O\left(N^{3.5}A^{3.5}S^{4.5}\log^{2}(\epsilon^{-1}) \right)$. Numerical experiments show that our algorithm is significantly more scalable than state-of-the-art approaches across several domains.

paragraphs: A policy for a Markov decision process can be sensitive to how its parameters are specified. Distributionally robust MDPs address this by considering a set of possible probability distributions over those parameters. The objective is to choose a policy that performs optimally against the worst distribution in that set, making parameter uncertainty part of the decision problem.

This paper proposes a framework based on first-order optimization and develops it for several Wasserstein ambiguity sets. Efficient proximal updates are the main computational ingredient. The analysis tracks how computation depends on the number of transition kernels in the nominal distribution, the number of actions, the number of states, and the desired solution accuracy.

The resulting bounds substantially improve dependence on the numbers of kernels, actions, and states compared with existing methods; the precise rate varies slightly with the Wasserstein setup. Numerical experiments across several domains also show greater scalability than state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution makes this form of robust planning computationally more accessible as the modeled decision problem grows.
summary.tldr: First-order methods with efficient proximal updates improve the scalability of Wasserstein distributionally robust MDP optimization.

title: First-Order Methods for Wasserstein Distributionally Robust MDP

abstract: Although stochastic optimization is central to modern machine learning, the precise mechanisms underlying its success, and in particular, the precise role of the stochasticity, still remain unclear. Modeling stochastic optimization algorithms as discrete random recurrence relations, we show that multiplicative noise, as it commonly arises due to variance in local rates of convergence, results in heavy-tailed stationary behaviour in the parameters. Theoretical results are obtained characterizing this for a large class of (non-linear and even non-convex) models and optimizers (including momentum, Adam, and stochastic Newton), demonstrating that this phenomenon holds generally. We describe dependence on key factors, including step size, batch size, and data variability, all of which exhibit similar qualitative behavior to recent empirical results on state-of-the-art neural network models. Furthermore, we empirically illustrate how multiplicative noise and heavy-tailed structure improve capacity for basin hopping and exploration of non-convex loss surfaces, over commonly-considered stochastic dynamics with only additive noise and light-tailed structure.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how randomness in optimization shapes the behavior of learned parameters. It models optimizer updates as discrete random recurrence relations and focuses on multiplicative noise, which can arise when local convergence rates vary. This differs from treating randomness only as an added disturbance of otherwise fixed update dynamics.

The authors show that multiplicative noise produces heavy-tailed stationary parameter behavior across a large class of models and optimizers. Heavy tails assign more probability to extreme values than light-tailed descriptions do. Their theory includes nonlinear and nonconvex models, along with momentum, Adam, and stochastic Newton methods. They also characterize dependence on step size, batch size, and data variability.

Those dependencies qualitatively resemble previously observed neural-network behavior. Further experiments illustrate that multiplicative noise and heavy-tailed structure improve movement between basins and exploration of nonconvex loss surfaces compared with the considered additive, light-tailed dynamics. This offers a mechanism linking optimizer randomness to exploration, supported by broad theoretical results and specific empirical demonstrations rather than a universal claim about training success.
summary.tldr: Multiplicative optimizer noise can produce heavy-tailed parameter behavior, with experiments linking that structure to better exploration of nonconvex losses.

title: Multiplicative Noise and Heavy Tails in Stochastic Optimization

abstract: We investigate the distributions of Conjugate Kernel (CK) and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) for ReLU networks with random initialization. We derive the precise distributions and moments of the diagonal elements of these kernels. For a feedforward network, these values converge in law to a log-normal distribution when the network depth $d$ and width $n$ simultaneously tend to infinity and the variance of log diagonal elements is proportional to ${d}/{n}$. For the residual network, in the limit that number of branches $m$ increases to infinity and the width $n$ remains fixed, the diagonal elements of Conjugate Kernel converge in law to a log-normal distribution where the variance of log value is proportional to ${1}/{n}$, and the diagonal elements of NTK converge in law to a log-normal distributed variable times the conjugate kernel of one feedforward network. Our new theoretical analysis results suggest that residual network remains trainable in the limit of infinite branches and fixed network width. The numerical experiments are conducted and all results validate the soundness of our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: The paper studies the randomness of the Conjugate Kernel and Neural Tangent Kernel in ReLU networks at initialization. It derives exact distributions and moments for their diagonal entries. The focus is on how these quantities behave as network size changes, distinguishing ordinary feedforward networks from residual architectures.

For feedforward networks, when depth and width both tend to infinity, the diagonal values converge in distribution to log-normal variables. The variance of their logarithms scales with the depth-to-width ratio. For residual networks with infinitely many branches but fixed width, Conjugate Kernel diagonals instead approach a log-normal distribution whose log variance scales inversely with width.

The residual network’s Neural Tangent Kernel diagonals have a different limit: a log-normal variable multiplied by the Conjugate Kernel of a feedforward network. The authors interpret these results as suggesting that residual networks remain trainable with infinitely many branches and fixed width. Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis. The trainability statement is presented as an implication suggested by the kernel results, rather than a blanket guarantee for every training problem.
summary.tldr: Kernel-distribution results distinguish feedforward and residual scaling and suggest residual networks can remain trainable at fixed width with infinitely many branches.

title: On the Random Conjugate Kernel and Neural Tangent Kernel

abstract: We present a message passing method for 0{–}1 integer linear programs. Our algorithm is based on a decomposition of the original problem into subproblems that are represented as binary deci- sion diagrams. The resulting Lagrangean dual is solved iteratively by a series of efficient block coordinate ascent steps. Our method has linear iteration complexity in the size of the decomposi- tion and can be effectively parallelized. The char- acteristics of our approach are desirable towards solving ever larger problems arising in structured prediction. We present experimental results on combinatorial problems from MAP inference for Markov Random Fields, quadratic assignment, discrete tomography and cell tracking for develop- mental biology and show promising performance.

Our algorithm is based on a decomposition of the original problem into subproblems that are represented as binary deci- sion diagrams. The resulting Lagrangean dual is solved iteratively by a series of efficient block coordinate ascent steps. Our method has linear iteration complexity in the size of the decomposi- tion and can be effectively parallelized. The char- acteristics of our approach are desirable towards solving ever larger problems arising in structured prediction. We present experimental results on combinatorial problems from MAP inference for Markov Random Fields, quadratic assignment, discrete tomography and cell tracking for develop- mental biology and show promising performance.

paragraphs: A 0–1 integer linear program expresses an optimization problem through binary choices, linear constraints, and a linear objective. Such formulations arise in structured prediction and other combinatorial tasks. This paper develops a message passing approach that splits the original problem into subproblems represented by binary decision diagrams.

The decomposition produces a Lagrangean dual problem, which the method improves through repeated block coordinate ascent steps. This gives the algorithm a way to coordinate its subproblems through iterative updates. Each iteration costs an amount proportional to the size of the decomposition, and the computation can be effectively parallelized. Both properties are useful when scaling to larger structured problems.

The authors evaluate the method on problems from Markov random field inference, quadratic assignment, discrete tomography, and cell tracking in developmental biology, reporting promising performance. These applications demonstrate the breadth of the proposed representation and optimization strategy. The linear complexity statement applies to individual iterations; the abstract's empirical conclusion concerns the overall performance observed in the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: Binary decision diagrams enable a parallelizable message passing method for binary integer programs with linear cost per iteration in decomposition size.

title: Efficient Message Passing for 0–1 ILPs with Binary Decision Diagrams

abstract: We tackle the problem of conditioning probabilistic programs on distributions of observable variables. Probabilistic programs are usually conditioned on samples from the joint data distribution, which we refer to as deterministic conditioning. However, in many real-life scenarios, the observations are given as marginal distributions, summary statistics, or samplers. Conventional probabilistic programming systems lack adequate means for modeling and inference in such scenarios. We propose a generalization of deterministic conditioning to stochastic conditioning, that is, conditioning on the marginal distribution of a variable taking a particular form. To this end, we first define the formal notion of stochastic conditioning and discuss its key properties. We then show how to perform inference in the presence of stochastic conditioning. We demonstrate potential usage of stochastic conditioning on several case studies which involve various kinds of stochastic conditioning and are difficult to solve otherwise. Although we present stochastic conditioning in the context of probabilistic programming, our formalization is general and applicable to other settings.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs usually incorporate observations as samples from a joint data distribution. The paper calls this deterministic conditioning. In practice, available evidence may instead consist of marginal distributions, summary statistics, or a mechanism that generates samples. Conventional probabilistic programming systems do not adequately support modeling and inference for all these forms of information.

The authors introduce stochastic conditioning, which conditions on a variable's marginal distribution having a specified form. They formally define the concept, examine its properties, and show how to carry out inference with it. This expands the kinds of observational information that a probabilistic program can directly express and use in reasoning about its model.

Several case studies demonstrate potential uses involving different forms of stochastic conditioning and problems that are otherwise difficult to solve. The contribution includes both a formal description of the new conditioning operation and methods for working with it. Although developed within probabilistic programming, the authors state that the formalization is general enough to apply in other settings.
summary.tldr: Stochastic conditioning extends probabilistic programming to incorporate evidence about marginal distributions, with a formal definition and inference methods.

title: Probabilistic Programs with Stochastic Conditioning

abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of learning an $\epsilon$-optimal policy for a discounted Markov Decision Process (MDP). Given an MDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions, the discount factor $\gamma \in (0,1)$, and an approximation threshold $\epsilon > 0$, we provide a model-free algorithm to learn an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with sample complexity $\tilde{O}(\frac{SA\ln(1/p)}{\epsilon^2(1-\gamma)^{5.5}})$ \footnote{In this work, the notation $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides poly-logarithmic factors of $S,A,1/(1-\gamma)$, and $1/\epsilon$.} and success probability $(1-p)$. For small enough $\epsilon$, we show an improved algorithm with sample complexity $\tilde{O}(\frac{SA\ln(1/p)}{\epsilon^2(1-\gamma)^{3}})$. While the first bound improves upon all known model-free algorithms and model-based ones with tight dependence on $S$, our second algorithm beats all known sample complexity bounds and matches the information theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors.
originalAbstract: In this paper we consider the problem of learning an $\epsilon$-optimal policy for a discounted Markov Decision Process (MDP). Given an MDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions, the discount factor $\gamma \in (0,1)$, and an approximation threshold $\epsilon > 0$, we provide a model-free algorithm to learn an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with sample complexity $\tilde{O}(\frac{SA\ln(1/p)}{\epsilon^2(1-\gamma)^{5.5}})$ \footnote{In this work, the notation $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides poly-logarithmic factors of $S,A,1/(1-\gamma)$, and $1/\epsilon$.} and success probability $(1-p)$. For small enough $\epsilon$, we show an improved algorithm with sample complexity $\tilde{O}(\frac{SA\ln(1/p)}{\epsilon^2(1-\gamma)^{3}})$. While the first bound improves upon all known model-free algorithms and model-based ones with tight dependence on $S$, our second algorithm beats all known sample complexity bounds and matches the information theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many samples a model-free algorithm needs to learn a policy within epsilon of optimal in a discounted Markov decision process. The analysis tracks the number of states S, actions A, discount factor gamma, desired accuracy epsilon, and allowed failure probability p.

The first algorithm has sample complexity of order SA ln(1/p) divided by epsilon squared and (1−gamma) to the power 5.5, up to polylogarithmic factors. It succeeds with probability at least 1−p. The authors state that this improves on previously known model-free bounds and model-based bounds with tight dependence on the number of states.

For sufficiently small epsilon, a second algorithm improves the exponent on (1−gamma) from 5.5 to 3 while keeping the stated dependence on the other quantities. This bound matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. The small-epsilon condition is essential to the stronger result. Together, the guarantees show that model-free learning can attain nearly optimal sample complexity in that regime.
summary.tldr: The paper gives improved model-free sample-complexity bounds, matching the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors for sufficiently small epsilon.

title: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning: from Clipped Pseudo-Regret to Sample Complexity

abstract: We study the global convergence of policy gradient for infinite-horizon, continuous state and action space, and entropy-regularized Markov decision processes (MDPs). We consider a softmax policy with (one-hidden layer) neural network approximation in a mean-field regime. Additional entropic regularization in the associated mean-field probability measure is added, and the corresponding gradient flow is studied in the 2-Wasserstein metric. We show that the objective function is increasing along the gradient flow. Further, we prove that if the regularization in terms of the mean-field measure is sufficient, the gradient flow converges exponentially fast to the unique stationary solution, which is the unique maximizer of the regularized MDP objective. Lastly, we study the sensitivity of the value function along the gradient flow with respect to regularization parameters and the initial condition. Our results rely on the careful analysis of the non-linear Fokker–Planck–Kolmogorov equation and extend the pioneering work of \cite{mei2020global} and \cite{agarwal2020optimality}, which quantify the global convergence rate of policy gradient for entropy-regularized MDPs in the tabular setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether policy-gradient learning reaches a globally optimal solution in entropy-regularized decision problems. The setting has an infinite time horizon and continuous state and action spaces. Policies use a softmax representation with a one-hidden-layer neural network, analyzed in a mean-field regime through a probability measure describing the network.

The authors add entropy regularization to that mean-field measure and examine the resulting gradient flow using the 2-Wasserstein metric. They prove that the objective increases along this flow. When the additional regularization is sufficiently strong, the flow converges exponentially fast to a unique stationary solution, which is also the unique maximizer of the regularized objective.

The paper also examines how the value function along training responds to regularization parameters and initialization. Its analysis relies on a nonlinear Fokker–Planck–Kolmogorov equation and extends convergence research from tabular policies to the stated neural approximation setting. The sufficient-regularization condition is central: the global convergence result concerns this particular regularized mean-field flow.
summary.tldr: With sufficient additional mean-field regularization, a neural policy-gradient flow converges exponentially to the unique optimum of its regularized objective.

title: Convergence of Policy Gradient for Entropy Regularized MDPs with Neural Network Approximation in the Mean-Field Regime

abstract: Understanding the latent causal factors of a dynamical system from visual observations is considered a crucial step towards agents reasoning in complex environments. In this paper, we propose CITRIS, a variational autoencoder framework that learns causal representations from temporal sequences of images in which underlying causal factors have possibly been intervened upon. In contrast to the recent literature, CITRIS exploits temporality and observing intervention targets to identify scalar and multidimensional causal factors, such as 3D rotation angles. Furthermore, by introducing a normalizing flow, CITRIS can be easily extended to leverage and disentangle representations obtained by already pretrained autoencoders. Extending previous results on scalar causal factors, we prove identifiability in a more general setting, in which only some components of a causal factor are affected by interventions. In experiments on 3D rendered image sequences, CITRIS outperforms previous methods on recovering the underlying causal variables. Moreover, using pretrained autoencoders, CITRIS can even generalize to unseen instantiations of causal factors, opening future research areas in sim-to-real generalization for causal representation learning.

paragraphs: CITRIS aims to recover the hidden causal factors behind a changing visual scene. It learns from image sequences in which those factors may have been intervened upon. Its key sources of information are how observations evolve over time and which underlying factors are known to have been targeted by interventions.

The framework uses a variational autoencoder to learn causal representations, including factors with multiple components, such as three-dimensional rotation angles. The authors prove identifiability in a setting that allows an intervention to affect only some components of a factor. A normalizing-flow extension also lets CITRIS separate causal factors within representations supplied by an already pretrained autoencoder.

On rendered three-dimensional image sequences, CITRIS recovers underlying causal variables better than the previous methods evaluated. With pretrained autoencoders, it can also generalize to unseen instantiations of causal factors. These findings suggest a route toward broader causal representation learning, while the abstract presents transfer from simulation to reality as a future research direction rather than an established result.
summary.tldr: CITRIS combines temporal images and observed intervention targets to identify scalar and multidimensional causal factors.

title: CITRIS: Causal Identifiability from Temporal Intervened Sequences

abstract: Modern neural models trained on textual data rely on pre-trained representations that emerge without direct supervision. As these representations are increasingly being used in real-world applications, the inability to control their content becomes an increasingly important problem. In this work, we formulate the problem of identifying a linear subspace that corresponds to a given concept, and removing it from the representation. We formulate this problem as a constrained, linear minimax game, and show that existing solutions are generally not optimal for this task. We derive a closed-form solution for certain objectives, and propose a convex relaxation that works well for others. When evaluated in the context of binary gender removal, the method recovers a low-dimensional subspace whose removal mitigates bias by intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation. Surprisingly, we show that the method—despite being linear—is highly expressive, effectively mitigating bias in the output layers of deep, nonlinear classifiers while maintaining tractability and interpretability.

paragraphs: Pretrained text representations can contain concepts that users did not explicitly choose to encode. This paper studies how to identify a linear subspace associated with a chosen concept and remove that subspace from the representation. The goal is to make representation content more controllable through an operation that remains tractable and interpretable.

The authors formulate erasure as a constrained linear minimax game and show that existing solutions are generally not optimal for that formulation. They derive closed-form solutions for some objectives and propose a convex relaxation for others. These results turn concept removal into an explicit optimization problem, with solution methods matched to the objective being used.

In evaluations of binary gender removal, the method finds a low-dimensional subspace whose removal mitigates bias under intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation. It also reduces bias in the output layers of deep nonlinear classifiers despite using a linear operation. The findings demonstrate the reach of this linear formulation in the evaluated setting; mitigation does not mean that every trace of a concept or every possible bias has been eliminated.
summary.tldr: The paper formulates linear concept erasure as a minimax problem and shows that removing a learned low-dimensional subspace can mitigate evaluated gender bias.

title: Linear Adversarial Concept Erasure

abstract: The primary goal in recommendation is to suggest relevant content to users, but optimizing for accuracy often results in recommendations that lack diversity. To remedy this, conventional approaches such as re-ranking improve diversity by presenting more diverse items. Here we argue that to promote inherent and prolonged diversity, the system must encourage its creation . Towards this, we harness the performative nature of recommendation, and show how learning can incentivize strategic content creators to create diverse content. Our approach relies on a novel form of regularization that anticipates strategic changes to content, and penalizes for content homogeneity. We provide analytic and empirical results that demonstrate when and how diversity can be incentivized, and experimentally demonstrate the utility of our approach on synthetic and semi-synthetic data.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems aim to present relevant content, but optimizing accuracy can produce a narrow selection. Conventional diversification methods change which existing items are shown, for example through re-ranking. This paper considers an additional source of diversity: influencing the kinds of content that creators choose to produce.

The approach uses the performative nature of recommendation, meaning that the system's choices can change the content it will encounter later. Creators respond strategically to recommendation incentives. The proposed regularization anticipates those responses and penalizes content homogeneity, bringing expected changes in the supply of content into the learning objective.

The authors provide analytical and empirical results describing when and how these incentives can encourage diversity. Experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic data demonstrate the approach's utility. The contribution shifts attention toward the feedback between recommendations and content creation, offering a mechanism intended to support inherent, sustained diversity. Its evidence concerns the modeled strategic responses and the stated experimental settings, where anticipating creator behavior can help shape a more diverse content supply.
summary.tldr: A recommendation regularizer anticipates creators' strategic responses to encourage the production of diverse content.

title: Performative Recommendation: Diversifying Content via Strategic Incentives

abstract: Recent complicated problems require large-scale datasets and complex model architectures, however, it is difficult to train such large networks due to high computational issues. Significant efforts have been made to make the training more efficient such as momentum, learning rate scheduling, weight regularization, and meta-learning. Based on our observations on 1) high correlation between past eights and future weights, 2) conditions for beneficial weight prediction, and 3) feasibility of weight prediction, we propose a more general framework by intermittently skipping a handful of epochs by periodically forecasting near future weights, i.e., a Weight Nowcaster Network (WNN). As an add-on module, WNN predicts the future weights to make the learning process faster regardless of tasks and architectures. Experimental results show that WNN can significantly save actual time cost for training with an additional marginal time to train WNN. We validate the generalization capability of WNN under various tasks, and demonstrate that it works well even for unseen tasks. The code and pre-trained model are available at https://github.com/jjh6297/WNN.

paragraphs: Training a large network requires many costly updates to its weights. This paper explores whether some near-future weights can be predicted from earlier ones, allowing training to advance without explicitly executing every intervening epoch. The approach builds on observations about correlations between past and future weights, conditions under which prediction helps, and the feasibility of predicting those weights.

The proposed Weight Nowcaster Network, or WNN, operates as an add-on module. Periodically, it forecasts the weights the main network is expected to reach in the near future, skipping a handful of training epochs. The framework is intended to apply across tasks and architectures, making weight evolution itself the object of learning.

Experiments show substantial savings in actual training time, with only marginal additional time spent training WNN. The authors also evaluate its ability to generalize across tasks and report that it works well on unseen tasks. These findings support periodically forecasting short stretches of training as a practical acceleration mechanism, with the reported benefit accounting for the extra cost of the forecasting model.
summary.tldr: WNN periodically predicts near-future model weights to skip training epochs, yielding reported time savings with little forecasting overhead.

title: Learning to Boost Training by Periodic Nowcasting Near Future Weights

abstract: Unsupervised multiplex graph representation learning (UMGRL) has received increasing interest, but few works simultaneously focused on the common and private information extraction. In this paper, we argue that it is essential for conducting effective and robust UMGRL to extract complete and clean common information, as well as more-complementarity and less-noise private information. To achieve this, we first investigate disentangled representation learning for the multiplex graph to capture complete and clean common information, as well as design a contrastive constraint to preserve the complementarity and remove the noise in the private information. Moreover, we theoretically analyze that the common and private representations learned by our method are provably disentangled and contain more task-relevant and less task-irrelevant information to benefit downstream tasks. Extensive experiments verify the superiority of the proposed method in terms of different downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Learning representations of a multiplex graph requires handling information shared across its layers and information specific to individual layers. The paper argues that both matter: shared information should be complete and clean, while layer-specific information should add useful complementary content without retaining unnecessary noise.

The proposed unsupervised method explicitly separates these common and private representations. It uses disentangled representation learning to capture shared information and a contrastive constraint to shape private information. The latter is designed to preserve what individual layers contribute beyond the common representation while removing noise that does not help subsequent tasks.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis establishing disentanglement of the learned common and private representations. Their analysis also supports greater retention of task-relevant information and less task-irrelevant information. Experiments across different downstream tasks report superior performance. Together, these contributions connect the separation of shared and layer-specific content to the practical usefulness of the resulting graph representations.
summary.tldr: The method separates shared and layer-specific graph information while using a contrastive constraint to preserve complementary content and reduce noise.

title: Disentangled Multiplex Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Robustness to adversarial attacks is typically evaluated with adversarial accuracy. While essential, this metric does not capture all aspects of robustness and in particular leaves out the question of how many perturbations can be found for each point. In this work, we introduce an alternative approach, adversarial sparsity, which quantifies how difficult it is to find a successful perturbation given both an input point and a constraint on the direction of the perturbation. We show that sparsity provides valuable insight into neural networks in multiple ways: for instance, it illustrates important differences between current state-of-the-art robust models them that accuracy analysis does not, and suggests approaches for improving their robustness. When applying broken defenses effective against weak attacks but not strong ones, sparsity can discriminate between the totally ineffective and the partially effective defenses. Finally, with sparsity we can measure increases in robustness that do not affect accuracy: we show for example that data augmentation can by itself increase adversarial robustness, without using adversarial training.

paragraphs: Adversarial accuracy is an important measure of whether a model withstands attacks, but it does not describe how many successful perturbations surround an input. Two models can therefore differ in aspects of robustness that this measure misses. This paper introduces adversarial sparsity to examine how difficult it is to find a successful perturbation when its direction is constrained.

The authors use this perspective to reveal differences among leading robust models that accuracy-based analysis does not capture. It also distinguishes defenses that are entirely ineffective from those that retain partial effectiveness despite failing against stronger attacks. This gives a more detailed account of what a defense accomplishes than a single accuracy result.

The paper further shows that robustness can improve under the sparsity measure without changing adversarial accuracy. In particular, data augmentation alone can produce such an improvement without adversarial training. The contribution is an additional evaluation perspective that exposes changes in vulnerability and can suggest ways to improve robustness, while retaining adversarial accuracy as an essential measure.
summary.tldr: Adversarial sparsity reveals differences in model vulnerability and defense effectiveness that adversarial accuracy alone can miss.

title: How Many Perturbations Break This Model? Evaluating Robustness Beyond Adversarial Accuracy

abstract: We study the gradients of a maxout network with respect to inputs and parameters and obtain bounds for the moments depending on the architecture and the parameter distribution. We observe that the distribution of the input-output Jacobian depends on the input, which complicates a stable parameter initialization. Based on the moments of the gradients, we formulate parameter initialization strategies that avoid vanishing and exploding gradients in wide networks. Experiments with deep fully-connected and convolutional networks show that this strategy improves SGD and Adam training of deep maxout networks. In addition, we obtain refined bounds on the expected number of linear regions, results on the expected curve length distortion, and results on the NTK.

paragraphs: Training a deep network becomes difficult when its gradients shrink toward zero or grow excessively. This paper studies that problem for maxout networks by analyzing gradients with respect to both inputs and model parameters. The goal is to derive initialization choices from the network’s gradient behavior rather than treating initialization as an isolated tuning decision.

The authors bound gradient moments in terms of the architecture and the distribution of parameters. They find that the distribution of the input-output Jacobian depends on the input, adding a complication to stable initialization. Using their moment analysis, they formulate initialization strategies that avoid vanishing and exploding gradients in wide networks.

Experiments with deep fully connected and convolutional maxout networks show improvements in training with both SGD and Adam. The paper also develops refined bounds on the expected number of linear regions, analyzes expected distortion of curve lengths, and gives results concerning the neural tangent kernel. Together, these contributions connect practical initialization to a broader mathematical account of how maxout networks transform inputs and propagate gradients.
summary.tldr: Gradient-moment analysis yields initialization strategies that stabilize wide maxout networks and improve evaluated SGD and Adam training.

title: Expected Gradients of Maxout Networks and Consequences to Parameter Initialization

abstract: To mitigate the bias exhibited by machine learning models, fairness criteria can be integrated into the training process to ensure fair treatment across all demographics, but it often comes at the expense of model performance. Understanding such tradeoffs, therefore, underlies the design of fair algorithms. To this end, this paper provides a complete characterization of the inherent tradeoff of demographic parity on classification problems, under the most general multi-group, multi-class, and noisy setting. Specifically, we show that the minimum error rate achievable by randomized and attribute-aware fair classifiers is given by the optimal value of a Wasserstein-barycenter problem. On the practical side, our findings lead to a simple post-processing algorithm that derives fair classifiers from score functions, which yields the optimal fair classifier when the score is Bayes optimal. We provide suboptimality analysis and sample complexity for our algorithm, and demonstrate its effectiveness on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Fairness requirements can change the best classification accuracy a model can achieve. This paper characterizes that tradeoff for demographic parity in settings with multiple demographic groups, multiple classes, and noise. Its analysis concerns classifiers that may randomize their decisions and use demographic attributes, making those features part of the stated optimization setting.

The authors show that the lowest achievable classification error under the fairness requirement equals the solution of a Wasserstein-barycenter problem. This mathematical characterization turns the fairness–accuracy tradeoff into an explicit optimization target. It describes the best attainable error within the specified classifier class, rather than merely comparing a collection of particular training procedures.

The theory leads to a simple post-processing method that converts score functions into fair classifiers. When the supplied scores are Bayes optimal, the resulting fair classifier is optimal as well. The paper also analyzes suboptimality and sample complexity and evaluates the method on benchmark datasets. Its practical significance is that fairness can be imposed through a principled transformation of scores, with the strongest optimality conclusion explicitly tied to the quality of those scores.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the demographic-parity accuracy tradeoff and derives post-processing that is optimal when its input scores are Bayes optimal.

title: Fair and Optimal Classification via Post-Processing

abstract: Large language models can be prompted to pro- duce fluent output for a wide range of tasks without being specifically trained to do so. Nevertheless, it is notoriously difficult to control their generation in such a way that it satisfies user-specified constraints. In this paper, we present InstructCTG, a simple controlled text generation framework that incorporates different constraints by verbalizing them as natural language instructions. We annotate natural texts through a combination of off-the-shelf NLP tools and simple heuristics with the linguistic and extra-linguistic constraints they satisfy. Then, we verbalize the constraints into natural language instructions to form weakly supervised training data, i.e., we prepend the natural language verbalizations of the constraints in front of their corresponding natural language sentences. Next, we fine-tune a pre-trained language model on the augmented corpus. Compared to existing methods, InstructCTG is more flexible in terms of the types of constraints it allows the practitioner to use. It also does not require any modification of the decoding procedure. Finally, InstructCTG allows the model to adapt to new constraints without re-training through the use of in-context learning.

paragraphs: A language model can produce fluent text without reliably following every constraint a user supplies. InstructCTG addresses this gap by expressing constraints as natural-language instructions and training the model to generate sentences that satisfy them. The framework accommodates both linguistic constraints and constraints concerning other properties of the text.

The training data comes from existing natural text. Off-the-shelf language-processing tools and simple heuristics identify constraints that each sentence already satisfies. The method then turns those annotations into instructions, places them before the corresponding sentence, and fine-tunes a pretrained language model on the resulting pairs. This creates weak supervision from automatically annotated examples rather than requiring every instruction-and-answer pair to be written manually.

The approach makes constraint following part of what the model learns during fine-tuning. The abstract reports greater flexibility in supported constraint types than existing methods, without changing the decoding procedure. It also states that in-context learning lets the trained model adapt to new constraints without another round of training.
summary.tldr: InstructCTG trains language models to follow text-generation constraints by converting automatically identified properties of sentences into natural-language instructions.

title: Controlled Text Generation with Natural Language Instructions

abstract: In view of the complexity of the dynamics of learning in games, we seek to decompose a game into simpler components where the dynamics’ long-run behavior is well understood. A natural starting point for this is Helmholtz’s theorem, which decomposes a vector field into a potential and an incompressible component. However, the geometry of game dynamics - and, in particular, the dynamics of exponential / multiplicative weights (EW) schemes - is not compatible with the Euclidean underpinnings of Helmholtz’s theorem. This leads us to consider a specific Riemannian framework based on the so-called Shahshahani metric, and introduce the class of incompressible games, for which we establish the following results: First, in addition to being volume-preserving, the continuous-time EW dynamics in incompressible games admit a constant of motion and are Poincaré recurrent - i.e., almost every trajectory of play comes arbitrarily close to its starting point infinitely often. Second, we establish a deep connection with a well-known decomposition of games into a potential and harmonic component (where the players’ objectives are aligned and anti-aligned respectively): a game is incompressible if and only if it is harmonic, implying in turn that the EW dynamics lead to Poincaré recurrence in harmonic games.

paragraphs: Learning in a game can produce complicated behavior because each player's updates interact with everyone else's. This paper studies that behavior by separating games into components with more understandable dynamics. It draws inspiration from a decomposition of vector fields into potential and incompressible parts, but argues that the usual Euclidean geometry does not fit exponential, or multiplicative, weights learning.

The authors instead use a Riemannian geometry based on the Shahshahani metric and define incompressible games within that framework. For these games, they prove that continuous-time exponential weights dynamics preserve volume and possess a quantity that remains constant along trajectories. They also establish Poincaré recurrence: almost every trajectory returns arbitrarily close to its initial position infinitely often.

The paper then connects this dynamical classification to an existing decomposition into potential and harmonic games. It proves that incompressibility and harmonicity are equivalent. Consequently, the recurrence result applies to harmonic games as well, providing a precise explanation of persistent revisiting behavior for this class under continuous-time exponential weights.
summary.tldr: A geometry adapted to exponential weights reveals that continuous-time learning in harmonic games returns near its starting point infinitely often for almost every trajectory.

title: A Geometric Decomposition of Finite Games: Convergence vs. Recurrence under Exponential Weights

abstract: In the past couple of years, various approaches to representing and quantifying different types of predictive uncertainty in machine learning, notably in the setting of classification, have been proposed on the basis of second-order probability distributions, i.e., predictions in the form of distributions on probability distributions. A completely conclusive solution has not yet been found, however, as shown by recent criticisms of commonly used uncertainty measures associated with second-order distributions, identifying undesirable theoretical properties of these measures. In light of these criticisms, we propose a set of formal criteria that meaningful uncertainty measures for predictive uncertainty based on second-order distributions should obey. Moreover, we provide a general framework for developing uncertainty measures to account for these criteria, and offer an instantiation based on the Wasserstein distance, for which we prove that all criteria are satisfied.

paragraphs: A classifier can express uncertainty through probabilities over possible labels. A second-order prediction goes further by placing a distribution over those probability distributions. This richer representation has motivated methods for separating and measuring types of predictive uncertainty, but recent criticism has identified undesirable theoretical behavior in some commonly used measures.

The paper responds by proposing formal criteria for what a meaningful uncertainty measure based on second-order distributions should satisfy. This makes the desired behavior of the measure explicit before choosing a particular formula. The authors then introduce a general framework for constructing measures with those requirements in mind, linking the definition of uncertainty to mathematical properties.

They instantiate the framework using Wasserstein distance and prove that the resulting measures satisfy all the proposed criteria. The contribution is therefore both a set of standards and a construction meeting them. The guarantee is specifically about those formal criteria, providing a principled answer to the theoretical concerns motivating the work without establishing that every question about predictive uncertainty has been settled.
summary.tldr: The paper defines criteria for second-order uncertainty measures and proves that a Wasserstein-based construction satisfies them.

title: Second-Order Uncertainty Quantification: A Distance-Based Approach

abstract: In this paper, we study the feature learning ability of two-layer neural networks in the mean-field regime through the lens of kernel methods. To focus on the dynamics of the kernel induced by the first layer, we utilize a two-timescale limit, where the second layer moves much faster than the first layer. In this limit, the learning problem is reduced to the minimization problem over the intrinsic kernel. Then, we show the global convergence of the mean-field Langevin dynamics and derive time and particle discretization error. We also demonstrate that two-layer neural networks can learn a union of multiple reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces more efficiently than any kernel methods, and neural networks aquire data-dependent kernel which aligns with the target function. In addition, we develop a label noise procedure, which converges to the global optimum and show that the degrees of freedom appears as an implicit reguralization.

Under that setup, training becomes an optimization problem over the network's intrinsic kernel.

The authors prove global convergence for the resulting mean-field Langevin dynamics. They also derive errors associated with discretizing time and representing the dynamics with a finite number of particles. The learned kernel depends on the data and aligns with the target function. Together, these results describe feature learning as adaptive kernel learning under the paper's specified limiting assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under a two-timescale mean-field limit, two-layer networks learn adaptive kernels with global convergence guarantees and characterized discretization errors.

title: Mean-field Analysis on Two-layer Neural Networks from a Kernel Perspective

abstract: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are able to understand visual concepts, describe and decompose complex tasks into sub-tasks, and provide feedback on task completion. In this paper, we aim to leverage these capabilities to support the training of reinforcement learning (RL) agents. In principle, VLMs are well suited for this purpose, as they can naturally analyze image-based observations and provide feedback (reward) on learning progress. However, inference in VLMs is computationally expensive, so querying them frequently to compute rewards would significantly slowdown the training of an RL agent. To address this challenge, we propose a framework named Code as Reward (VLM-CaR). VLM-CaR produces dense reward functions from VLMs through code generation, thereby significantly reducing the computational burden of querying the VLM directly. We show that the dense rewards generated through our approach are very accurate across a diverse set of discrete and continuous environments, and can be more effective in training RL policies than the original sparse environment rewards.

Code as Reward addresses this by having the vision-language model generate code for dense reward functions. These functions provide feedback during learning without requiring direct model queries at the same frequency. The approach turns a model’s task understanding into an executable source of training feedback, reducing the burden of using that understanding throughout reinforcement learning.

The authors report accurate generated rewards across a diverse collection of discrete and continuous environments. They also find that these rewards can train policies more effectively than the environments’ original sparse rewards. The practical significance is that useful feedback need not be limited to occasional success signals, while the expensive model need not directly judge every learning step.
summary.tldr: Code as Reward uses vision-language models to generate executable reward functions that can improve reinforcement learning while reducing model-query costs.

title: Code as Reward: Empowering Reinforcement Learning with VLMs

paragraphs: A coreset is a small, weighted selection of examples that preserves a larger dataset’s usefulness for an analysis task. This paper constructs coresets for linear regression with multiple responses and an ℓp objective. Its central advance is that the subset size does not depend on the number of responses, overcoming a gap in earlier constructions.

The guarantee preserves the regression objective throughout its domain within relative error ε. If preserving a subspace-constrained minimizer is enough, the bounds improve by a factor of ε for p above 1. The authors describe these bounds as nearly tight.

Two applications show what this compression enables. The results determine tight uniform-sampling requirements for approximating ℓp Euclidean power means. They also establish that, for p between 1 and 2, a small subset of matrix rows spans a nearly optimal low-dimensional subspace. summary.tldr: The paper constructs nearly tight coresets for multiple-response ℓp regression whose sizes are independent of the response count.

title: Coresets for Multiple $\ell_p$ Regression

abstract: Mixup, which generates synthetic training samples on the data manifold, has been shown to be highly effective in augmenting Euclidean data. However, finding a proper data manifold for graph data is non-trivial, as graphs are non-Euclidean data in disparate spaces. Though efforts have been made, most of the existing graph mixup methods neglect the intrinsic geodesic guarantee, thereby generating inconsistent sample-label pairs. To address this issue, we propose GeoMix to mixup graphs on the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) geodesics. A joint space over input graphs is first defined based on the GW distance, and graphs are then transformed into the GW space through equivalence-preserving transformations. We further show that the linear interpolation of the transformed graph pairs defines a geodesic connecting the original pairs on the GW manifold, hence ensuring the consistency between generated samples and labels. An accelerated mixup algorithm on the approximate low-dimensional GW manifold is further proposed. Extensive experiments show that the proposed GeoMix promotes the generalization and robustness of GNN models.

paragraphs: Mixup creates synthetic training examples by interpolating between existing examples and their labels. For graphs, deciding what lies between two examples is difficult because graphs do not naturally share an ordinary Euclidean space. The paper argues that neglecting the geometry of this interpolation can produce inconsistent synthetic graph-label pairs.

GeoMix defines a shared space using Gromov–Wasserstein distance and maps input graphs into it through transformations that preserve their equivalence. The authors show that linear interpolation between transformed graphs traces a geodesic connecting the original graphs on the corresponding manifold. This supplies a geometric basis for keeping generated samples consistent with their mixed labels.

To make the approach more practical, the paper also introduces an accelerated algorithm operating on an approximate, lower-dimensional Gromov–Wasserstein manifold. Experiments show improvements in graph neural networks’ generalization and robustness. The contribution therefore combines a justification for graph interpolation with an approximation designed to make that interpolation usable in training, rather than treating graph mixing as an arbitrary combination of structures.
summary.tldr: GeoMix gives graph mixup a geometric foundation and uses a lower-dimensional approximation to improve GNN generalization and robustness.

title: Graph Mixup on Approximate Gromov–Wasserstein Geodesics

abstract: The development of deep generative models for tabular data is currently a very active research area in machine learning. These models, however, tend to be computationally heavy and require careful tuning of multiple model parameters. In this paper, we propose TabSDS - a lightweight, non-parametric, and model free alternative to tabular deep generative models which leverages rank and data shuffling transformations for generating synthetic data which closely approximates the joint probability distribution of the real data. We evaluate TabSDS against multiple baselines implemented in the Synthcity Python library across several datasets. TabSDS showed very competitive performance against all baselines (including TabDDPM - a strong baseline model for tabular data generation). Importantly, the execution time of TabSDS is orders of magnitude faster than the deep generative baselines, and also considerably faster than other computationally efficient baselines such as adversarial random forests.

paragraphs: Generating synthetic tabular data requires reproducing relationships among columns as well as the behavior of individual columns. Deep generative approaches can do this, but they often demand substantial computation and careful parameter tuning. TabSDS explores a lightweight alternative based on direct transformations of the data rather than a trained generative model.

The method is fully non-parametric and model free. It uses rank transformations and data shuffling to produce synthetic records whose joint probability distribution closely approximates that of the original data. The joint-distribution objective matters because it concerns how variables occur together, which is central to retaining the structure of a table.

The authors compare TabSDS with multiple baselines from the Synthcity library across several datasets. They report very competitive performance, including against TabDDPM, alongside execution times orders of magnitude lower than deep generative baselines. It is also considerably faster than adversarial random forests. These results suggest that the evaluated data-generation tasks can benefit from a simple transformation-based approach with substantially lower computational demands.
summary.tldr: TabSDS generates competitive synthetic tabular data through rank and shuffling transformations, with much shorter execution times than evaluated generative baselines.

title: TabSDS: a Lightweight, Fully Non-Parametric, and Model Free Approach for Generating Synthetic Tabular Data

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce incorrect or outdated information, necessitating efficient and precise knowledge updates. Current model editing methods, however, struggle with long-form knowledge in diverse formats, such as poetry, code snippets, and mathematical derivations. These limitations arise from their reliance on editing a single token’s hidden state, a limitation we term as “efficacy barrier”. To solve this, we propose AnyEdit, a new autoregressive editing paradigm. It decomposes long-form knowledge into sequential chunks and iteratively edits the key token in each chunk, ensuring consistent and accurate outputs. Theoretically, we ground AnyEdit in the Chain Rule of Mutual Information, showing its ability to update any knowledge within LLMs. Empirically, it outperforms strong baselines by 21.5% on benchmarks including UnKEBench, AKEW, and our new EditEverything dataset for long-form diverse-formatted knowledge. Additionally, AnyEdit serves as a plug-and-play framework, enabling current editing methods to update knowledge with arbitrary length and format, significantly advancing the scope and practicality of LLM knowledge editing. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jianghoucheng/AnyEdit.
