paragraphs: This paper analyzes stochastic gradient descent when gradient noise has heavy tails in weakly convex optimization. Heavy tails allow unusually large noise values, complicating convergence analysis. The work extends understanding beyond the convexity and smoothness settings that underpin much of the existing theory.

The guarantees distinguish both noise assumptions and optimization domains. For ordinary SGD on a bounded constrained domain, the authors establish convergence in expectation when the noise has a bounded p-th central moment. On an unbounded domain, they establish a high-probability guarantee under a heavy-tailed sub-Weibull noise assumption. These are different statements: an expectation guarantee describes average behavior, while a high-probability guarantee controls failure likelihood.

With gradient clipping, SGD obtains high-probability convergence on an unbounded domain under the bounded p-th central moment assumption. All reported high-probability bounds depend on failure probability through polynomial-logarithmic factors. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution clarifies how clipping, domain constraints, and noise assumptions change the convergence guarantees available in the weakly convex setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes assumption-specific convergence guarantees for ordinary and clipped SGD under heavy-tailed noise in weakly convex optimization.

abstract: Synchronous reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms with linear function approximation are representable as inhomogeneous matrix iterations of a special form (Schoknecht & Merke, 2003). In this paper we state conditions of convergence for general inhomogeneous matrix iterations and prove that they are both necessary and sufficient. This result extends the work presented in (Schoknecht & Merke, 2003), where only a sufficient condition of convergence was proved. As the condition of convergence is necessary and sufficient, the new result is suitable to prove convergence AND divergence of RL algorithms with function approximation. We use the theorem to deduce a new concise proof of convergence for the synchronous residual gradient algorithm (Baird, 1995). Moreover, we derive a counterexample for which the uniform RL algorithm (Merke & Schoknecht, 2002) diverges. This yields a negative answer to the open question if the uniform RL algorithm converges for arbitrary multiple transitions.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether synchronous reinforcement learning algorithms settle to a limit when they use linear function approximation. Such algorithms can be represented as particular matrix iterations whose updates vary across iterations. The authors work at this matrix level, deriving convergence conditions that can then be applied to reinforcement learning procedures.

The key theoretical contribution is a condition proved to be both necessary and sufficient for convergence of general inhomogeneous matrix iterations. Earlier work had supplied only a sufficient condition. That distinction matters: a sufficient condition can certify convergence when it holds, but its failure alone does not establish divergence. The stronger characterization supports conclusions in both directions.

The paper demonstrates the theorem through two applications. It gives a concise new convergence proof for the synchronous residual gradient algorithm and constructs a case where the uniform reinforcement learning algorithm diverges. The counterexample answers negatively the question of whether the uniform algorithm converges for arbitrary multiple transitions. It establishes a failure case, rather than claiming that the algorithm always diverges.
summary.tldr: A necessary-and-sufficient convergence theorem yields a residual gradient convergence proof and a counterexample to general convergence of uniform reinforcement learning.

title: Convergence of synchronous reinforcement learning with linear function approximation

abstract: Consider the following problem: given sets of unlabeled observations, each set with known label proportions, predict the labels of another set of observations, also with known label proportions. This problem appears in areas like e-commerce, spam filtering and improper content detection. We present consistent estimators which can reconstruct the correct labels with high probability in a uniform convergence sense. Experiments show that our method works well in practice.
originalAbstract: Consider the following problem: given sets of unlabeled observations, each set with known label proportions, predict the labels of another set of observations, also with known label proportions. This problem appears in areas like e-commerce, spam filtering and improper content detection. We present consistent estimators which can reconstruct the correct labels with high probability in a uniform convergence sense. Experiments show that our method works well in practice.

paragraphs: The learning problem starts with groups of observations whose individual labels are unknown. What is available for each group is the proportion belonging to each label. The goal is to predict individual labels for another group, whose label proportions are also known. Supervision therefore comes from group summaries rather than directly labeled examples.

The paper introduces consistent estimators for recovering labels from this information. It establishes that correct labels can be reconstructed with high probability in a uniform convergence sense. This is a probabilistic theoretical claim about the estimators’ behavior, giving the approach support beyond an observation that aggregate proportions sometimes seem useful.

Experiments indicate that the method also works well in practice. The abstract identifies e-commerce, spam filtering, and improper content detection as settings where the problem arises. The central contribution is a way to connect information about label frequencies across groups to predictions for individual observations, with both a stated convergence result and empirical evidence supporting that connection.
summary.tldr: The paper learns individual labels from known group label proportions, with high-probability reconstruction results and positive experimental evidence.

title: Estimating labels from label proportions

abstract: EM algorithm is a very popular method to estimate the parameters of Gaussian Mixture Model from a large observation set. However, in most cases, EM algorithm is not guaranteed to converge to the global optimum. Instead, it stops at some local optimums, which can be much worse than the global optimum. Therefore, it is usually required to run multiple procedures of EM algorithm with different initial configurations and return the best solution. To improve the efficiency of this scheme, we propose a new method which can estimate an upper bound on the logarithm likelihood of the local optimum, based on the current configuration after the latest EM iteration. This is accomplished by first deriving some region bounding the possible locations of local optimum, followed by some upper bound estimation on the maximum likelihood. With this estimation, we can terminate an EM algorithm procedure if the estimated local optimum is definitely worse than the best solution seen so far. Extensive experiments show that our method can effectively and efficiently accelerate conventional EM algorithm.

paragraphs: Expectation-maximization, or EM, is widely used to fit Gaussian mixture models, but it is generally not guaranteed to find the global optimum. Different initial configurations can lead to substantially different local optima. A common response is to run EM several times and retain the best result, which makes the cost of unsuccessful runs an important concern.

This paper proposes estimating an upper bound on the log likelihood that a run's local optimum can achieve, using its current configuration after an EM iteration. The method first bounds the region in which that optimum may lie. It then uses this region to estimate an upper bound on the achievable likelihood.

A run can be stopped when this bound establishes that its eventual result is worse than the best solution already found. The method therefore saves work by identifying runs that cannot improve the current answer. Extensive experiments report effective and efficient acceleration of conventional EM. This improves the multiple-run procedure without claiming to eliminate EM's underlying susceptibility to local optima.
summary.tldr: Upper bounds on a run's eventual local optimum allow unpromising Gaussian-mixture EM runs to stop early.

title: Estimating local optimums in EM algorithm over Gaussian mixture model

abstract: Iterative methods that take steps in approximate subgradient directions have proved to be useful for stochastic learning problems over large or streaming data sets. When the objective consists of a loss function plus a nonsmooth regularization term, whose purpose is to induce structure (for example, sparsity) in the solution, the solution often lies on a low-dimensional manifold along which the regularizer is smooth. This paper shows that a regularized dual averaging algorithm can identify this manifold with high probability. This observation motivates an algorithmic strategy in which, once a near-optimal manifold is identified, we switch to an algorithm that searches only in this manifold, which typically has much lower intrinsic dimension than the full space, thus converging quickly to a near-optimal point with the desired structure. Computational results are presented to illustrate these claims.

When the objective consists of a loss function plus a nonsmooth regularization term, whose purpose is to induce structure (for example, sparsity) in the solution, the solution often lies on a low-dimensional manifold along which the regularizer is smooth. This paper shows that a regularized dual averaging algorithm can identify this manifold with high probability. This observation motivates an algorithmic strategy in which, once a near-optimal manifold is identified, we switch to an algorithm that searches only in this manifold, which typically has much lower intrinsic dimension than the full space, thus converging quickly to a near-optimal point with the desired structure. Computational results are presented to illustrate these claims.

paragraphs: Stochastic learning methods often use approximate subgradient steps to handle large datasets or streaming observations. When their objective includes a nonsmooth regularizer, that term can encourage a structured solution, such as a sparse one. The paper examines how an optimization algorithm can recognize the lower-dimensional structure that the regularizer is trying to produce.

The key observation is that a solution often lies on a low-dimensional manifold where the otherwise nonsmooth regularizer becomes smooth. The authors show that regularized dual averaging can identify this manifold with high probability. Identifying it means learning a useful restriction on where to search, in addition to making progress toward a good objective value.

This result motivates a two-stage strategy. Once a near-optimal manifold has been identified, optimization switches to a method that searches only within it. Because this space typically has much lower intrinsic dimension, the restricted search can converge quickly to a near-optimal point with the intended structure. Computational results illustrate these claims, while the identification guarantee remains probabilistic.
summary.tldr: Regularized dual averaging can identify a solution's low-dimensional manifold with high probability, motivating faster optimization restricted to that structure.

title: Manifold Identification of Dual Averaging Methods for Regularized Stochastic Online Learning

abstract: When learning multiple related tasks with limited training data per task, it is natural to share parameters across tasks to improve generalization performance. Imposing the correct notion of task relatedness is critical to achieve this goal. However, one rarely knows the correct relatedness notion a priori. We present a generative model that is based on the weight vector of each task being drawn from a nonparametric mixture of nonparametric factor analyzers. The nonparametric aspect of the model makes it broad enough to subsume many types of latent task structures previously considered in the literature as special cases, and also allows it to learn more general task structures, addressing their individual shortcomings. This brings in considerable flexibility as compared to the commonly used multitask learning models that are based on some a priori fixed notion of task relatedness. We also present an efficient variational inference algorithm for our model. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets, on both regression and classification problems, establish the efficacy of the proposed method.

paragraphs: When several related prediction tasks each have little training data, sharing information can improve generalization. The difficulty is deciding how the tasks are related. A fixed assumption about their relationship may be inappropriate, and the right form of sharing is rarely known before learning begins.

The paper introduces a generative model in which each task's weight vector comes from a nonparametric mixture of nonparametric factor analyzers. This supplies a flexible model for the hidden structure connecting tasks. It includes many previously studied task structures as special cases while also allowing more general relationships, broadening the ways parameters can be shared.

An efficient variational inference algorithm makes the model usable for learning. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets cover both regression and classification and support the method's effectiveness. The main contribution is to make task relatedness something the model can learn more flexibly, reducing dependence on a single relationship pattern fixed in advance.
summary.tldr: A flexible Bayesian multitask model learns hidden relationships among tasks instead of requiring one fixed form of parameter sharing.

title: Flexible Modeling of Latent Task Structures in Multitask Learning
